# About this book

This is a digital copy of a book that has been preserved for generations on library shelves before being digitized by Google as part of a project aimed at making the world’s books available online.
It has survived long enough to no longer be protected by copyright and has entered the public domain. A public domain book is a book that was never protected by copyright or whose legal copyright terms have expired. Whether a book is classified as being in the public domain may vary from country to country. Public domain books are a link to the past; they represent a heritage of history, culture, and knowledge that is often difficult to discover.
Comments, notes, and other marginalia <note>original: "annotazioni a margine"</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file as a testament to the long journey the book has taken—from the original publisher to the library, and finally to you.

## Guidelines for Use

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them universally available. Public domain books belong to the public, and we are merely their custodians. However, this work is costly; therefore, in order to continue offering this service, we have taken steps to prevent misuse by commercial entities, including the imposition of restrictions on automated querying.
We also ask that you:

+ *Do not use these files for commercial purposes* We designed Google Book Search for use by individual private users, and we ask that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.
+ *Do not send automated queries* Do not send automated queries of any kind to Google. If you are conducting research in the fields of machine translation, optical character recognition (OCR), or other fields where you need to use large amounts of text, we invite you to contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help you.
+ *Keep the watermark* The Google "watermark" that appears in each file is essential for informing users about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.
+ *Use it legally* Regardless of how you use it, remember that it is your responsibility to ensure your use is legal. Do not assume that because a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, it is also in the public domain for users in other countries. The criteria for determining whether a book is protected by copyright vary from country to country, and we cannot offer guidance on whether a specific use of a book is permitted. Do not assume that because a book appears in Google Book Search, it can be used in any way or in any country in the world. The penalties for copyright infringement can be very severe.

# The Candle-Bearer.
<term>Candelaio</term> — <note>original: "The Candle-Bearer" or "The Chandler"</note>. While literally a maker or seller of candles, the title serves as a metaphor for the one who provides light to see the truth amidst social and moral darkness. It also contains several bawdy double entendres typical of Renaissance comedy.

## A Comedy by Bruno the Nolan

### Academic of no Academy; known as "the Annoyed One."
<note>Bruno often used the moniker "the Nolan" to signify his birthplace in Nola, near Naples. His self-description as an "Academic of no Academy" is a satirical strike against the rigid, dogmatic scholarly institutions of his time. "The Annoyed One" (il fastidito) reflects his characteristic impatience with social hypocrisy and academic pedantry.</note>

->Cheerful in sadness; sad in cheerfulness.<-
<note>original Latin: "In Tristitia hilaris: in Hilaritate tristis." This motto reflects the philosopher’s belief in the "coincidence of opposites"—the idea that every emotion or state contains its own contrary.</note>

<meta>The text continues the dedication to Lady Morgana. Bruno is transitioning from the self-deprecating sonnet of the previous page to an elaborate, philosophical, and highly satirical prose address. He positions his play, *The Candlebearer*, as a literal and metaphorical offering to her.</meta>

# The Candlebearer.

<margin>1</margin> Resistance? No. To her Highness, her most Illustrious and most Reverend Ladyship?
No, no. By my faith, there is no prince, cardinal, king, emperor, or
Pope who shall take this candle from my hand in this most solemn
offertory. It belongs to you, to you it is given, and you shall either hang it in
<margin>5</margin> your study, or fix it in your candlestick. To my superlatively
learned, wise, beautiful, and generous Lady Morgana. You are the cultivator
of the field of my soul; after having broken the clods of its 
hardness and refined its style—so that the dusty fog
raised by the wind of levity might not offend the eyes of this one or
<margin>10</margin> that one—with divine water that flows from the fountain of your spirit, you
watered my intellect. Therefore, at the time when we could first touch hands,
I addressed to you my *Gay Thoughts*. Next, *The Trunk of Living Water*.
Now, while you rejoice in the bosom of Abraham, and I,
without waiting for that help of yours which used to refresh my tongue,
<margin>15</margin> desperately burn and sparkle, a great Chaos—all too 
envious of my well-being—intervenes between us. To show you
that this same chaos cannot prevent my love, with some proper hostage and
material gift, from crossing despite its rotten malice: here is the candle
being offered to you by this Candlebearer who departs from me. This candle,
<margin>20</margin> in this country where I find myself, may somewhat illuminate certain shadows of
the Ideas, which in truth frighten the beasts, and as if they were
Dantean devils, cause the asses to stay far behind. And in that homeland
where you are, it will allow many to contemplate my soul, and let them
see that it is not entirely discarded. Greet on my behalf that other
<margin>25</margin> Candlebearer of flesh and bone, of whom it is said that <note>original: "Regnum Dei non possidebunt"</note> they shall not possess the kingdom of God; and tell him not to rejoice so much that my memory is said to be 
trampled there by the force of pigs' feet and the kicks
of asses; for by this hour the asses' ears are cropped, and
the pigs will pay me for it some December. And let him not rejoice so much
<margin>30</margin> with that saying of his, <note>original: "abiit in regionem longinquam"</note> "he went into a far country." For if it should
ever happen that the heavens grant that I may effectively say,
<note>original: "Surgam et ibo"</note> "I will arise and go," then that fatted calf will undoubtedly be part of
our feast.
In the meantime, let him live and manage himself, and see to making himself fatter
<margin>35</margin> than he is; because on the other hand, I hope to recover the lard where I
lost the greens. If not under one cloak, then under another. If not in
one life, then in another. Remember, my Lady, what I believe 
need not be taught to you: Time takes everything and gives everything. Everything
changes, nothing is annihilated. There is only One who cannot change; only One is
<margin>40</margin> eternal, and can persevere eternally as one, similar, and the same. With

<summary>In this dedication to "Lady Morgana," Bruno presents his play as a symbolic candle to illuminate philosophical truths (the "Ideas") while mocking his critics as "asses" and "pigs." He employs a series of Biblical metaphors—specifically the Parable of the Prodigal Son—to warn his enemies that he may yet return to have the last laugh.</summary>

# The Candlebearer.

Through this philosophy my soul grows great, and my intellect is magnified. <margin>1</margin>
Therefore, whatever the point of this evening I await might be—if
change is true: I, who am in the night, await the day; and those
who are in the day, await the night. Everything that is, is either here,
or there; near, or far; now, or later; soon, or late. Rejoice, <margin>5</margin>
then, and if you can, stay healthy, and love those who love you.

### [6] Argument and order of the comedy

There are three main subjects woven together in the present comedy:
the love of Bonifacio, the alchemy of Bartolomeo, and the pedantry
of Mamphurio. However, for a clear understanding of the subjects, the <margin>10</margin>
logic of the order, and the evidence of the artful weaving: let us
first present the insipid lover by himself; second, the sordid miser;
third, the clumsy pedant. Of these, the insipid man is not without clumsiness
and sordidness. The sordid one is likewise insipid and clumsy. And the clumsy
one is no less sordid and insipid than he is clumsy. <margin>15</margin>
<note>Bruno is explaining that while the play follows three different men, their character flaws—lust, greed, and intellectual vanity—are all interconnected and equally foolish.</note>

->Bonifacio then<-

*In Act 1.* Scene one: in love with Lady Vittoria, and realizing
that his love could not be reciprocated (the reason being that
she was a lover—as they say—of "flowers of beards and fruits of purses" <note>An idiomatic way of saying she prefers men who are both young and wealthy.</note>;
and he was neither young nor generous), he places his hope in the va- <margin>20</margin>
nity of magical superstitions to achieve his amorous goals. For
this reason, he sends his servant to find Scaramuré, who had
[7] been described | to him as an effective magician. *Scene 2.* Having sent Ascanio,
he discourses with himself, calling to mind the value of that art.
*Scene 3.* Bartolomeo comes upon him and, with a certain artful trick, <margin>25</margin>
makes him "vomit up" <note>original: "vomitare." Here used metaphorically to mean confessing or blurting out a secret.</note> his secret, and shows the difference in the object
of his love. *Scene 4.* Sanguino, father and shepherd of rogues, and
a student who studied under Mamphurio, who had heard
these discussions from the side: they discuss that event. Sanguino par-
ticularly begins to take the lead in weaving some web against <margin>30</margin>
Bonifacio. *Scene 6.* <note>Bruno skips Scene 5 in this summary, a common occurrence in early drafts or printers' errors.</note> Lucia the procuress <term>ruffiana: a woman who acts as a go-between in illicit affairs or manages prostitutes.</term> appears with a small gift
that Bonifacio was sending; she performs an "anatomy" of it <note>A detailed, piece-by-piece inspection.</note>, and prepares to
take her "tithe" from it, and she was nearly caught in the act. *Scene 7*
*and 8.* Bonifacio arrives all full of pride for a certain poem of <margin>35</margin>
his, written in a new style in honor and glory of his lady. In this celebration
he was found by Gioan Bernardo the painter, to whom he would have dis-
closed his new poetic frenzy; but he was distracted by the thought of the
portrait, and by a thought regarding a doubt that Gioan Bernardo left with him.

<margin>40</margin> they are very well satisfied.

# The Candlebearer.

<margin>1</margin> *In the fourth act.* **Scene i.** Lady Vittoria comes out, annoyed from 
waiting so long. She discusses the stingy love of Bonifacio and his vain 
hopes. She shows herself resolved to give him a "bitter taste" <note>original: "insapore" — likely a pun on giving him something "unsavory" or a "distasteful" trick</note> of 
his own medicine. She is together with the man pretending to be the captain of the 
guards, and Giovanni Bernardo. Meanwhile, Lucia 
<margin>5</margin> arrived. **Scene ii.** She shows that she has not wasted her time, nor was 
her labor in vain: she explains how she has informed and instructed Carubina, the 
wife of Bonifacio. **Scene iii.** Overtaken by Bartolomeo, they depart 
indignantly. **Scene iiii.** Bartolomeo remains, discussing his own 
affairs <note>literally "his matter," likely referring to his alchemical obsessions</note>. 
And behold, **scene v.** he encounters Bonifacio, and they talk for a while 
<margin>10</margin> together, mocking one another. Meanwhile, Lucia, who was not "sleeping 
on the job," **[10]** **scene vi.** finds Master Bonifacio. Having been 
released from Bartolomeo, he is easily persuaded by the extraordinary news 
she tells him: namely, that at the very least, Lady Vittoria would have 
given him her all, on the condition that he go to sleep with her that 
<margin>15</margin> night; otherwise, she would die of longing. Given the things that had 
already happened regarding the magical spell <note>referring to a fake enchantment Bonifacio believes is working</note>, it was not difficult to make 
him believe it. He was ordered to disguise himself as Giovanni Bernardo. 
Lucia departs with Vittoria’s clothes to mask Carubina <note>disguising the wife as the mistress to trick the husband</note>. **Scene vii.** Bonifacio 
remains, celebrating within himself the effect he sees from his 
<margin>20</margin> enchantment. Next, in **scene viii.** he mocks Martha, the wife of 
Bartolomeo, for a while. Then it is likely he went immediately to the 
mask-maker to prepare himself as Saint Cresconio <note>A fictional or obscure saint's name used as a disguise</note>. **Scene xii.**

->Mamphurio<-

In **Act One, Scene 5**, he begins to thunder in a high-flown style <note>original: "altitonare," a mock-Latinism typical of Mamphurio’s pedantic speech</note> and comes to be known by Sanguino as a "sheep for the pasture," <margin>15</margin> meaning that the rogues <term>marioli; street-wise swindlers or thieves</term> began to form a plan regarding his affairs.

In **Act Three**, he unsheathes a poem against Signor Ottaviano in <margin>25</margin> revenge for the low esteem he showed for his verses; while he discusses these with his servant Pollula, Master Giovanni Bernardo arrives in **Scene 7**, with whom he converses until [Giovanni Bernardo] loses his patience. He returns in **Scene 11**, appearing with Corcovizzo | who acted in such a way that he took the **[16]** <margin>30</margin> coins <term>scudi; Italian gold or silver currency</term> from his hand. Now, while he laments this and makes a racket in **Scene 12**, he encounters Barra and Marca, and in **Scene 13**, Sanguino; these men, giving him hope of finding the thief and recovering the stolen goods, made him change his clothes and led him away.
In **Act Four, Scene 2**, he returns as poorly dressed as he was, <margin>35</margin> complaining that the second set of swindlers had taken his academic robes <note>original: "vestimenta talari," robes reaching the ankles, signifying his status as a scholar</note> and his precious cap, leaving him alone while passing through a certain room. Because of this, he was ashamed to return home. He waits until later, retreating into a small corner, until in **Scene 15** <margin>40</margin> he steps into the middle, walking about and discussing what he had heard and seen there. Meanwhile, in **Scene 16**, Sanguino, Marca, and others arrive in the guise of guards <term>birri; police officers or constables, often portrayed as corrupt</term>, and as Mamphurio wishes to withdraw in secret, they take him prisoner under that and other pretenses and deposit him in the next room.

<header>The Candlebearer.</header>

<margin>1</margin> *In the next-to-last scene of the fifth act,* it is proposed to him that he make a choice of one of three things to avoid going to prison: either to pay a "good tip" <note>original: "bona strena"; a bribe or gratuity often expected by officials</note> to the constables and the captain, or to receive ten blows to the palms, or fifty lashes with his breeches down. He would have accepted any other <margin>5</margin> thing rather than go to prison in that manner. Therefore, of the three, he chooses the ten blows to the palms; but when he was at the third, he said, "I would rather have fifty lashes on the buttocks." Of which, having received many, and the count being confused now for one reason, now for another: it <margin>10</margin> happened that he received both the blows to the palms and the lashes, and he paid however many coins <note>original: "scudi"</note> he had left in his pouch; and he left his cloak there, which was not even his own. And all this being done, dressed like Don Paulino, in the *last scene* he gives and delivers the *Applause* <note>original: "Plaudite"; the traditional closing request for the audience to clap at the end of a Roman comedy</note>.

## [18] | Anti-prologue.

Yes, sir. Well considered. Well noted. Well ordered.
Perhaps I did not prophesy that this comedy would not be performed <margin>15</margin> tonight? That hussy who is appointed to represent Vittoria and Carubina has I-know-not-what "sickness of the mother" <note>original: "mal di madre"; a contemporary term for hysteria or uterine distress</note>. He who is to represent Bonifacio is so drunk that he has seen neither heaven nor earth from midday until now; and as if he had nothing to do, he does not want to get <margin>20</margin> out of bed. He says, "Leave me, leave me, for in three and a half days and seven evenings, with four or two oarsmen, I shall be among the butterflies and bats. Let it be; row, row, let it be." To me was committed the prologue, and I swear to you it is so intricate and bedeviled that I have sweated over it for four days and nights; and all the trumpets and <margin>25</margin> [19] drums of those harlot Muses of Helicon <note>The mountain home of the Muses in Greek mythology</note> are not enough to stick| a single straw of it into my memory. Now go, do the prologue! Be the boat for this discarded, shattered, broken, poorly-tarred great old hulk of a ship; which looks as if it had been pulled by force from the deep abyss with hooks, grapples, and harpoons. Water enters it from many sides, it is not caulked at all; <margin>30</margin> and it wants to go out, and it wants to reach the high seas? To leave this safe port of the *Mantracchio*? <term>Mantracchio; a busy inner harbor in Naples</term> To depart from the *Mole of Silence*? If you knew the author, you would say he has a bewildered face. It seems he is always contemplating the pains of hell. He looks as if he has been under the press like felt caps. A man who laughs only to do as others <margin>35</margin> do. For the most part, you will see him annoyed, stubborn, and bizarre; he is satisfied with nothing, as cranky as an eighty-year-old man, as flighty as a dog that has been beaten a thousand times, fed on onions. By the [20] blood—I won't say whose—he and all these other philosophers...

<margin>1</margin> For poets and pedants, the greatest enemy they have is wealth and property; while they perform an anatomy <note>original: "nothomia"; a detailed dissection or analysis</note> with their brains, for fear of being truly torn apart, quartered, and dissipated by these riches, they flee from them like a hundred thousand devils, and go to find those who keep them used and in reserve. In conclusion, I want to go and become a monk, and whoever wants to do the prologue, let them do it.

<margin>10</margin> ### | Pre-prologue. [21]

Where has that rogue gone, whose back is meant for beatings, who was supposed to perform the prologue? Gentlemen, the comedy will be without a prologue. And it doesn't matter, because it is not necessary for there to be one. The matter, the subject, the manner, and the order and circumstances of it, I tell you that they will be presented to you in order, and will be placed before your eyes in order: which is much better than if they were narrated to you in order. This is a kind of <margin>15</margin> fabric that has the warp and the weaving together. Let him who can understand it, understand it. Let him who wants to comprehend it, comprehend it. But I will not fail to warn you that you must imagine yourself to be in the most royal city of Naples, near the Seat of Nilo <note>original: "seggio di Nilo"; one of the historical noble administrative districts of Naples</note>. This house that you see formed here, for tonight, will serve for certain tricksters, <margin>20</margin> rogues, and rascals (watch yourselves, that they don't make you "widowers" <note>meaning to be robbed or deprived of something</note> of something you are carrying on you). Here these men will spread their nets: and hazard <note>original: "zara"; a game of dice, here meaning "bad luck" or "risk"</note> to whom it touches. On this side is the room of the Candlebearer, *that is* <note>original: "id est"</note> Master <margin>25</margin> Bonifacio, and Carubina his wife, and that of Master Bartholomeo. On this other side is the room of Signora Vittoria, and of Giovanni Bernardo the painter, and Scaramuré who acts as a necromancer. Around these parts—I know not for what occasions—a most solemn pedant named Manphurio is very often seen wandering about. I am sure you will see them all. And the procuress <margin>30</margin> Lucia, because of her many affairs, must come and go many times. You will mostly see Poll with his teacher; this is a scholar of black and white ink. You will see Bonifacio’s page, Ascanio—a servant for sun and candle <note>meaning he serves day and night, or perhaps a joke on Bonifacio's obsession</note>. Mochione, Bartholomeo’s boy, is neither hot nor cold; he doesn't smell or stink. In Sanguino, Barra, Marca, and Corcovizzo, <margin>35</margin> you will contemplate in part the dexterity of the rascally discipline. You will recognize the form of alchemical deceits <note>original: "barrarie"</note> in Cencio. And as a pastime, you will be presented with Consalvo the apothecary, Martha, Bartholomeo’s wife, and the most witty Signor Ottaviano. Consider who goes, who [comes...]

Masculine mockeries, illuminated jests, <margin>10</margin>hungry flatteries, fox-like excuses, wolf-like accusations, and oaths that die of hunger; praising those present, blaming those absent, serving everyone, and loving no one. She whets your appetite, and then you fast. You will also see the personification and majesty of a man of the "masculine gender" <note>Bruno is mocking the redundant, hyper-grammatical speech of pedants.</note>. One who brings you certain sweetmeats <note>original: "suauioli"; likely a pun on sweet words or small kisses.</note> to turn the <margin>15</margin>stomach of a pig or a hen; a restorer of that ancient Latium <note>A reference to scholars obsessed with restoring "pure" classical Latin.</note>, an emulator of Demosthenes; one who summons Cicero <note>original: "Tullio"; Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator.</note> from the deepest and darkest center. An arranger of the deeds of heroes. Here before you is a sharp wit to make the eyes water, [28] the hair stand on end, the teeth feel numb; to fart, to rise <note>original: "rizzar"; implies an erection, part of Bruno's mix of high and low register.</note>, to cough, and <margin>20</margin>to sneeze. Behold one of those composers of books "well-deserving of the republic," annotators, glossers, constructors, methodists, adders, commentators, translators, interpreters, makers of compendiums, new-fangled dialecticians, attendants with a new grammar, a new dictionary, a lexicon, a variant reading, a prover of authors, an authentic proven one, with Greek, <margin>25</margin>Hebrew, Latin, Italian, Spanish, and French epigrams placed at the front of the books. Whereby the one and the other and the other and the one are consecrated to immortality, as benefactors of the present and future centuries; for this, people are obliged to dedicate statues and colossi to them in the Mediterranean seas and the ocean, and other uninhabitable places of the earth. The <term>eternal light</term> <note>original Latin: "lux perpetua"; a phrase from the Requiem Mass, here used to mock the "divine" status of scholars.</note> comes to <margin>30</margin>tip its hat to them, and <term>forever and ever</term> <note>original Latin: "secula seculorum".</note> bows with profound reverence. Fame is obliged to make their voices heard at both poles, and to deafen with shrieks, noise, and crashes the North Wind and the South Wind, and the Indian and Atlantic seas. How well a Latin discourse stands out (it seems to me I see so many pearls and margarites on a field of gold) in the middle of Italian. A Greek discourse in the middle of Latin; and they do not <margin>35</margin>let a page of paper pass where there does not appear at least one little word, a verse, a concept, from an exotic character and language. Ah, they give me life when, whether by force or of their own free will, in speaking and writing they bring in a verse of Homer, of Hesiod, a little scrap of Plato, or Greek Demosthenes. How well they <margin>40</margin>demonstrate that they are the only ones on whom Saturn has pissed the ju[ice]... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "giu-"; likely "giusquiamo" (henbane), a plant associated with madness or melancholy.</note>

<margin>1</margin>In his head, the nine handmaidens of Pallas <note>The Muses, serving Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note> have unloaded a cornucopia of vocabulary into his *pia* and *dura mater* <note>original: "pia et dura matre"; these are the inner and outer membranes surrounding the brain, here used to mock the pedant's "stuffed" intellect.</note>; and therefore it is | quite appropriate that they walk with such pomposity, with that heavy-stepping gait <note>original: "incesso grauigrado".</note>, torso upright, head steady, and eyes in an attitude of modest, <margin>5</margin>haughty circumspection. Furthermore: sweet disgusts, bitter pleasures, foolish determinations, failed <margin>15</margin>faiths, lame hopes, and | scarce charities. Great and grave judgments regarding the deeds of others, but little feeling for one's own. Manly women, effeminate men. So many voices from the head and not from the chest. He who believes most of all is most deceived. Universal love is a matter of coins. From this proceed quartan fevers, spiritual cancers, thoughts of little weight, <margin>20</margin>overflowing follies, scholarly stumbles, masterly blunders, and slips that would break one's neck. Besides the "will" that pushes, the "knowing" that approaches, the "doing" that bears fruit. And diligence, the mother of results. In conclusion, you will see that in everything there is nothing certain; but plenty of business, enough defects, little of beauty, and nothing of good. I think I hear the characters coming. Farewell.

Ber.** Since he is now in the state of misery that you were in, by having six hundred scudi less, and you are in the comfort in which he was, by having over six hundred scudi more: therefore, as you have changed fortune, change also your cloaks and caps. For in the end, it is not fitting <margin>10</margin> that he goes in that outfit, and you in | this. <margin>19</margin>
**Cencio.** Oh, you are always joking.
**Gio. Ber.** Yes, yes, I joke. The first time I see you together I will say: here is your cape, Cencio; here is your cape, Bartholomeo. But tell me as a gentleman (let us speak seriously), didn't you fasten it <margin>15</margin> onto him just as Gigio fastened it onto Perrotino?
**Cencio.** And what did he do?
**Gio. Ber.** Do you not know what he did? I can tell you. That man hollowed out a piece of wood and inserted gold inside it; then he charred the outside, making it look like any other piece of charcoal. At the right moment, with a beautiful <margin>20</margin> dexterity, he took it from his pocket and, setting his hands to two other pieces of charcoal that were near the furnace, he found the opportunity to place that "pregnant" charcoal <note>original: "carbone pregnante"; a term for charcoal rigged with hidden precious metals to fool observers during an alchemical demonstration.</note> in a spot where, quickly turned to ash by the force of the fire, the powdered gold trickled | through the holes to the bottom.
**Cencio.** Oh, God save me, I could never have imagined such <margin>25</margin> a piece of <term>gagloffaria</term> <note>A term for roguery or knavery.</note>. Me, to deceive? Master Bartholomeo, let himself be deceived? Now I believe that he has been informed of this trick. Not only did he not want me to touch a single thing, but he even made me sit six paces away from the furnace the first time he operated in my presence for the demonstration of the recipe's practice. And the <margin>30</margin> second time, he wanted to be alone, making me be entirely absent, | having only my recipe for a guide. So, because the experiment has been done twice with little material and very little expense, now he has resolved to go all in, and as I told you, he is doing a great sowing to reap a great harvest.
<margin>35</margin> **Gio. Ber.** How so: has he increased the doses?
**Cenc.** So much so that in this first batch, he will draw five hundred <margin>20</margin> scudi like fifty soldi.
**Gio. Ber.** I believe it will be more like fifty soldi than fifty more scudi. Now indeed you have prophesied better than a <term>Caiaphas</term> <note>original: "Caifasso." A reference to the biblical High Priest; here it implies making a prophecy that comes true in a disastrous or unintended way.</note>. <margin>40</margin> Now let us wait for the "birth," and then we shall see if it is male or female. Goodbye.

### Cencio alone.

In truth, if Bartholomeo had the brains of this fellow, and if everyone were so ill-advised, I would have spread my nets in this land in vain. Now let us act with good grace since the bird is in the net. Let us <margin>5</margin> not be like the man who lured the bird to the snare and then let it escape **B** from his hand. I will never consider myself the owner of these | scudi, nor will I call them mine, until I am out of the kingdom. I have ordered the post-horses, and I am going to mount them this very hour; it will not be necessary for me to go and collect any other baggage. When the innkeeper opens the valise he has in his <margin>10</margin> hands, he will find it full of stones, and he will see that what is on the outside is worth more than what is inside. I believe he, too, will not wait long to see how his account stands. I must not stay here until the time comes when Bartholomeo might send someone to find the "Christ's powder." <note>original: "puluis Christi." An alchemical substance or projection powder used in the attempt to transmute base metals into gold.</note> I think I see his wife. I do not want her to see me so "stuffed." <margin>15</margin> <note>original: "imbottato." Likely referring to Cencio having the stolen money hidden or padded under his clothes.</note>

### Martha alone.

I believe that Satan, Barsabucco, <note>A folkloric name for a demon or devil.</note> and all those who melt souls will take him as a companion; for he will surely know how to stir the fires of hell to fry and roast the souls of the damned. The face of my husband resembles a man who has spent <margin>20</margin> thirty years making charcoal on the mountain of Scaruaita, which lies beyond Mount Cicala. <note>Local geography near Nola, Italy, the author's birthplace. The area was known for its woods and charcoal production.</note> A fish does not stay so willingly in the water as he does near those glowing coals, smoking himself all day long—I do not wish to speak ill of him. Then he comes before me with those red eyes, scorched in such a way that he resembles Lucifer. In the end, there is no labor so heavy that love does not make <margin>25</margin> not only light, but pleasant. Look at this man: because the hope of making the philosopher's stone has been hammered into his brain, he has come to such a state that eating is a nuisance to him, and being in bed is a source of restlessness. The night always seems as long to him as it does to children who have a new suit of clothes to put on. Everything annoys him; every other <margin>30</margin> moment is bitter to him. His only paradise is the furnace. His **B** gems and | precious stones are the coals; his angels are the glass vessels <note>original: "bozzole." Glass flasks or containers used in distillation.</note> that are attached in order in the furnaces with those glass noses—so many iron alembics <note>term: "lambicchi" (alembics). A chemical apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling liquids.</note> here and there, some larger, some smaller, and some medium-sized. And how that <margin>35</margin> wretch leaps, and dances, and sings, reminding me of a donkey. A little while ago, to see what he was doing, I put my eye to a crack in the door, and I saw him seated upon his chair like a professor <note>original: "cathedrante." One who sits in a "cathedra" or academic chair to lecture.</note> with one leg...

<margin>1</margin> ...of a fresh nature, without a wrinkle, with milky breath, of rosy little lips, <note>original Latin: "recentis naturae... roseorum labellulorum." Mamphurio is describing the ideal physical traits of youth in his characteristically pedantic Latin.</note> of a sweet little tongue, of honeyed simplicity; of those living in the flower, not in the seed, having bright little eyes, a matter of indifference to girls.
*Ottavio.* Oh noble Master, trim, most eloquent, most gallant master-steward and cupbearer of the Muses. <margin>5</margin> <note>original: "architriclino, et pincerna." These are high-flown terms for a headwaiter or steward and a cupbearer.</note>
*Mamphurio.* Oh, a beautiful apposition! <note>A grammatical term referring to placing two nouns together to describe the same thing.</note>
*Ottavio.* Patriarch of the Apollonian choir. <note>Referring to the choir of Apollo, leader of the Muses.</note>
*Mamphurio.* It would be better said: *Apollinean*. <note>original: "Melius diceretur Apollineo." Mamphurio is correcting Ottavio's Latinate suffix.</note>
*Ottavio.* Trumpet of Phoebus, let me give you a kiss on the left cheek; for I do not deem myself worthy to kiss that most sweet mouth. <margin>10</margin>
*Mamphurio.* So that I do not envy Jupiter his ambrosia and nectar. <note>original: "Ch' Ambrosia et Nectar non inuidio à Gioue."</note>
*Ottavio.* That mouth, I say, which breathes forth such varied and beautiful maxims and unheard-of phrases.
*Mamphurio.* I shall add even more: on the very threshold of age, in the very beginnings of life, in the very rudiments of the business of this worldly or cosmic architecture, <margin>15</margin> from the very vestibule, in the very spring of age, as those who desire to marry, not even among the parsley. <note>original Latin: "Addam et plura... ne in apijs quidem." To be "not even among the parsley" was a classical idiom meaning to be at the very start of something, referring to parsley being planted at the borders of gardens.</note>
*Ottavio.* Oh Master of the Caballine fount, <note>The spring of Hippocrene, created by the hoof of the winged horse Pegasus, sacred to the Muses.</note> for mercy's sake do not let me die of sweetness before I confess my fault; speak no more, I pray you, for you make me swoon. <margin>20</margin>
*Mamphurio.* I shall be silent, then, because he is overwhelmed by the glory of majesty, <note>original: "Silebo igitur quia opprimitur a gloria maiestatis."</note> just as happened to that wretched woman mentioned by Ovid in the *Metamorphoses*, whose thread of life the greedy Fates cut short, upon seeing the thundering Jupiter in his own majesty. <note>A reference to the myth of Semele, who was consumed by fire when she saw Jupiter in his true divine form.</note>
*Ottavio.* By your grace, I beseech you by that god Mercury who has <margin>25</margin> flooded you with eloquence.
*Mamphurio.* I am compelled to comply. <note>original Latin: "Cogor morem gerere."</note>
*Ottavio.* Have pity on me and hurl no more of those darts at me, which make me go out of my mind.
*Mamphurio.* Admiration draws him into a profound ecstasy. <margin>30</margin> <note>original: "In Echstasim profundam trahit ipsum admiratio."</note> I shall therefore be silent about these things henceforth; I shall add nothing: "mute as fishes," having spoken so much, "his voice stuck in his throat." <note>original: "muti pisces... vox faucibus hesit." Mamphurio uses classical clichés for silence.</note>
*Ottavio.* Master Mamphurio, most pleasant river of eloquence, most serene sea of learning.
*Mamphurio.* Tranquility of the sea, serenity of the air. <margin>35</margin>
*Ottavio.* Do you have any beautiful composition of yours? For I have a great desire to have a copy of your most learned papers.
*Mamphurio.* I believe, sir, that in the whole course of your life <note>original Latin: "in toto vitae curriculo."</note> and throughout the discourse of various and diverse pages, you have never encountered songs of <term>callisymmetry</term>. <note>A pedantic neologism meaning "beautiful proportion" or "beautiful symmetry."</note>

<margin>1</margin>...so well adapted, like these that at present I am about to demonstrate to you, here written down.
<margin>25</margin>*Ottavio.* What is the matter of your verses?
*Mamphurio.* Letters, syllables, diction, and speech—both the near and remote parts. <note>original Latin: "Litterae, Syllabae, dictio, et oratio, partes propinquae et remotae." Mamphurio answers the question "what is the matter" as a grammarian might, focusing on the components of language rather than the theme.</note>
<margin>5</margin>*Ottavio.* I mean, what is the subject and the purpose?
*Mamphurio.* You mean "of what is it treated?" the "matter concerning which?" or "around which?" <note>original: "de quo agitur? materia de qua? circa quam?"</note> It is the throat, gluttony, and <term>gastrimargia</term> <note>From the Greek word for "belly-madness" or excessive gluttony.</note> of that glutton Sanguino (the living image of Philoxenus, who wished for the neck of a crane <margin>10</margin> <note>Philoxenus of Leucas was a famous Greek glutton who wished for a long neck so he could enjoy the taste of his food for a longer duration.</note>) along with his other peers, associates, adherents, likes, and side-kicks.
*Ottavio.* Please, let me hear them.
*Mamphurio.* Most gladly. Secrets should not be hidden from the learned: <note>original: "Lubentissime. Eruditis non sunt operienda archana."</note> behold, I unfold the paper worked and ruled by my own fingers. But I want you to take note that Ovid of Sulmona (for Sulmo is my homeland <note>original: "Sulmo mihi patria est." Mamphurio is quoting Ovid's "Tristia" to claim a scholarly kinship with the Roman poet.</note>) <margin>15</margin> described the Calydonian Boar with many epithets in the eighth book of his *Metamorphoses*; in imitation of which I go about outlining this domestic pig.
*Ottavio.* For heaven's sake, read them quickly.
*Mamphurio.* Let it be so. He who gives quickly, gives twice. <note>original: "Fiat. Qui cito dat, bis dat." A common Latin proverb suggesting that a prompt favor is worth more than a delayed one.</note> The beginning is from the emotion of one who marvels. <margin>20</margin> <note>original: "Exordium ab admirantis affectu."</note>

> O filthy pig, vile, useless life:
> Who have nothing else but that fatuous grunting
> With which you think to acquire food. <image-desc>Oval library stamp: REGENTS OF THE UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA</image-desc>

*Ottavio.* Certainly, for a work by one of your profession, they are not without beautiful consideration.

*Mamphurio.* Unconditionally and absolutely <note>original Latin: "Sine conditione, et absolutè"</note> they must be judged worthy of deep scrutiny—these fruits gathered from the best plants that the Heliconian mount <note>Mount Helicon was the home of the Muses in Greek mythology.</note> ever produced, irrigated also by the Parnassian spring, tempered by blonde Apollo, and cultivated by the sacred Muses. <margin>B</margin> *Mamphurio.* No.
*Ottavio.* Did you exhaust yourself in making them?
*Mamphurio.* Not in the least. <note>original Latin: "Minime."</note>
*Ottavio.* Did you expend great care and thought?
*Mamphurio.* By no means. <note>original Latin: "Nequaquam."</note>
*Ottavio.* Did you make and remake them?
*Mamphurio.* Not at all. <note>original Latin: "Haud quaquam."</note>
*Ottavio.* Did you correct them?
*Mamphurio.* Not in the least in the world; <note>original Latin: "Minime gentium"</note> there was no need.
*Ottavio.* Did you perhaps skillfully take them—not to say "stole" them—from some other author?
*Mamphurio.* Not at all; let envy be absent from the word; may the gods avert it; may the powers above not allow such a thing! <note>original Latin: "Neutiquam, absit verbo inuidia, dij auertant. ne faxint ista superi."</note> You wish to see too much of my erudition. Believe me, I have drunk no small amount from the Horse’s Spring <note>original: "fonte Caballino," referring to Hippocrene, the spring on Mount Helicon created by the hoof of the winged horse Pegasus; drinking its water was said to bring poetic inspiration.</note>; nor has the daughter born of Jove’s brain <note>Minerva (Athena), the goddess of wisdom, who was born fully formed from the head of Jupiter (Zeus).</note> infused me with little liquid: I mean the chaste Minerva, to whom wisdom is
<margin>27</margin> attributed. Do you believe I would be | less happily resolved if I were provoked to explain the marks of one who affirms or asserts? They have not failed my memory: Yes, so, also, truly, indeed, openly, truly, certainly, without a doubt, especially, who doubts it? certainly, why not? By Hercules! By Pollux! By the god of Truth! and so forth. <note>original: "Sic, ita, etiam, sanè, profecto, palam, verum, certè, procul dubio, maxime, cui dubium? vtique, quidni? <margin>1</margin> *Ottaviano.* Please, instead of that "and so forth," tell me another negation.

There was a time when the lion and the donkey were <margin>15</margin> companions; and traveling together on a pilgrimage, they agreed that when crossing rivers, they would take turns carrying each other: that is to say, one time the donkey would carry the lion, and another time the lion would carry the donkey. Having then to go to Rome, and having neither boat nor bridge at their <margin>20</margin> service, they reached the river Garigliano <note>A river in central Italy, often mentioned in historical and literary contexts.</note>. The donkey took the lion upon his back; as he swam toward the other bank, the lion—for fear of falling—dug his claws deeper and deeper into the donkey's skin, so that they penetrated that poor animal right to the <margin>25</margin> bone. And the poor wretch (as one who makes a profession of patience) crossed as best he could without saying a word. Except that, having reached safety out of the water, he shook his back a little, rolled on his spine three or four times in the warm sand, and they moved on. Eight days later, on their return journey, it was the lion’s turn to carry the <margin>30</margin> donkey. The donkey, being on top of him and fearing he would fall into the water, gripped the lion’s neck with his teeth; and as this was not enough to keep him up, he thrust his "instrument"—or whatever we want to call it... you understand me, to speak decently—into the void under the tail where the skin is missing <note>A crude joke implying the donkey sodomized the lion to maintain his grip.</note>. Thus the lion felt <margin>33</margin> greater anguish than a woman in the pains of childbirth, crying out: "Whoa, whoa! Ay, ay, ay, ay! Alas! Whoa, <margin>35</margin> you traitor!" To which the donkey replied with a severe face and a grave tone: "Patience, my brother; you see that I have no other claw than this to hold on with." And so it was necessary for the lion to suffer and endure until they had crossed the river. To this point: there is a change in all things <note>original: "Omnio rero vicissitudo este," a mangled version of the Latin proverb *Omnium rerum vicissitudo est*.</note>. # Act Third.
## Scene I.
### *Master Bartholomeo Alone.*

Who was that great beast of a bell-ringer who draws such a huge herd after him? While it is commonly considered <margin>20</margin> where the power <note>original: 'virtú,' referring to the inherent efficacy or occult property of a thing</note> of things consists, people make that division into words, herbs, and stones <note>original: 'in verbis, in herbis, et in lapidibus'</note>. Oh, may the sickness of Saint Lazarus <note>leprosy</note> take them, and every other thing I wouldn't wish for myself! Why, before they mention those three miserable things, don't they mention metals? Metals, like gold and silver, are **39** the source of | everything. These, these bring about words, herbs, <margin>25</margin> stones, linen, wool, silk, fruit, grain, wine, oil; and everything desirable upon the earth is drawn from these. These, I say, are so necessary that without them, not one of those other things can be acquired or possessed. Therefore gold is called the "matter of the sun," and silver the "moon": for <margin>30</margin> if you take these two planets from the sky, where would the generation of things be? Where would the light of the universe be? Take these two from the earth: where would the participation, possession, and enjoyment of things be? Therefore, how much better that first "animal" <note>likely referring to the first human or primeval philosopher</note> would have done to put into the mouth of the common people that one single subject of power, rather than all those other three without <margin>35</margin> this one! Unless, of course, this was introduced so that not everyone should understand and possess what I understand and possess. Herbs, words, **B** and stones are the subject of power only among | certain mad and senseless philosophers who are hated by God, by nature, and by fortune.

<margin>1</margin> they see themselves dying of hunger, complaining without a poor single penny in their purse; to temper the poison of envy they feel toward the wealthy, they curse gold, silver, and those who possess them. Then, when I take notice: look there, they all go like little dogs to the tables of the <margin>5</margin> rich. Truly they are dogs who know how to earn their bread with nothing but barking. Where? At the tables of the rich—of those fools, I say, who, for four words spoken out of turn by those beggars, with certain shaggy eyebrows, astonished eyes, and an air of wonder, allow the bread to be taken from their cupboards and the <margin>10</margin> money from their purses; and they make them conclude with truth that **in words there are powers** <note>original: 'in verbis sunt virtutes.' This is a play on a famous medieval/Renaissance maxim: 'In verbis, herbis, et lapidibus sunt virtutes' (In words, herbs, and stones there are powers/virtues).</note>. But they would be in a fine mess if they expected any result from their chatter on my part: seeing as I do not know how to feed anyone with anything else but the very same; he who feeds me with words <margin>12</margin> [gets the same in return]. Now let the beasts value herbs, the madmen value stones, and the charlatans <note>original: 'saltainbanco,' literally 'bench-jumpers'—itinerant performers or quacks.</note> value words: for I, for my part, value nothing but that by which <margin>15</margin> everything is valued. Money contains all the other four <note>Referring either to the triad of words, herbs, and stones plus money itself, or the four elements mentioned next.</note>. To him who lacks money: not only are stones, herbs, and words lacking, but the air, the earth, the water, the fire, and life itself. This gives temporal life; and eternal life as well, if one knows how to use it by giving <margin>20</margin> alms: which must also be done with great discretion: and without knowing your own account, you must not deprive the purse of its soul <note>Bartholomeo views money as the 'soul' of the purse.</note>. Therefore the wise man says: **If you do good, see to whom you do it** <note>original: 'Si bene feceris, vide cui.' A quote from the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 12:1, advising against giving to the ungodly.</note>. But in this theory, there is no profit. I have heard that there is an order in the Kingdom that the coins of twenty-one <margin>23</margin> <term>carlini</term> <note>A silver coin used in the Kingdom of Naples.</note> shall no longer be worth more than twenty <term>tornesi</term> <note>A smaller copper coin.</note>; I want to go and change the three I have before the edict is published. Meanwhile, my <margin>25</margin> boy will return from fetching the **Christ’s powder** <note>original: 'puluis Christi.' This could refer to an alchemical preparation or a common medicine of the time.</note>.

**Gio.Ber.** What I want to say is this: I would like to know from you what "pedant" means.

**Mam.** Most gladly I wish to tell it to you, teach it to you, declare it to you, explain it to you, make it known to you, make it public to you, insinuate it to you, and—the conjunctive particle being added to the final word—crack it open for you. <note>original: "enuclearuelo." Manfurio uses an absurd string of synonyms to show off his vocabulary.</note> Just as, like, as if, just as, I have cracked open the Ovidian nut before my disciples so that they might better eat its kernel. <note>original: "nucem Ouidianam... enucleaui." A reference to the poem 'The Walnut' attributed to Ovid; "enucleate" literally means to remove the kernel from a nut, metaphorically to explain.</note> "Pedant" means, as it were, "foot before." <margin>47</margin> <note>original: "pede ante."</note> That is because he has a following gait, with which he makes the youths being educated go forward. Or, by a stricter and narrower etymology: *Pe*, "perfect" [perfectos]; *Dan*, "giving" [dans]; *Te*, "treasures" [thesauros]. Now, what do you say to both?

**Gio.Ber.** They are good; but neither one pleases me, nor does it seem to the point.

**Mam.** It is permissible for you to say that, provided a better one is brought into the open: that is, when you have brought forward another more worthy.

**Gio.Ber.** Here it is: *Pe*, "big sheep" [pecorone]; *Dan*, "good-for-nothing" [da nulla]; *Te*, "donkey-head" [testa d'asino].

**Mam.** The elder Cato said: Do not lie; and believe nothing rashly. <note>original: "Nil mentire; et nihil temere credideris."</note>

**Gio.Ber.** That is to say, whoever says the opposite lies through his throat.

**Mam.** Go, go. <note>original: "Vade, vade."</note>
> Against the wordy, do not strive to contend with words.
> Against the wordy, do not strive to contend with words.
> With words, do not strive to contend against the wordy.
<note>Manfurio repeats the same Latin maxim—"Contra verbosos, verbis contendere noli"—three times, merely rearranging the word order to display his grammatical "skill."</note>

<margin>B |</margin> **Gio.Ber.** I give to the devil as many pedants as there are! Stay here with a hundred thousand of those angels with the scorched faces. <note>A sarcastic reference to demons in hell.</note>

**Mam.** Take them indeed as your own companions, with you. Are you there, Pollula? Pollula, what do you say? Do you see what a nefarious, abominable, turbulent, and portentous age this is?
> This tedious age in which I find myself
> Is void of all valor, full of all pride.
But let us hasten toward the house, since I wish to exercise you further in those adverbs of place: Movement from a place, to a place, and through a place. <note>original: "Motu de loco, ad locum, et per locum." Standard categories in Latin grammar.</note>

# The Torch-Bearer.

<margin>1</margin> Of metals, they say that gold is the **heaviest**: and yet nothing makes a man move more freely, lightly, and nimbly than this. Not every weight, nor every thing added to us, weighs us down; rather, one is found that is so light that the greater it is, the more it makes one swift and <margin>5</margin> agile. A man without silver and gold is like a bird without feathers: whoever wants to catch him, catches him; whoever wants to eat him, eats him. However, if he has them, he flies, and the more he has, the more he flies and the higher he perches. Master Bonifacio, once he has shaken out <margin>65</margin> his purse | and his back, will feel heavier, in | defiance of all his <margin>10</margin> enemies. <note>The speaker suggests that losing money makes a man "heavy" with sorrow or social stagnation, contrasting with the physical weight of gold.</note>

Just as one "moreover begat" leads to another <note>original: "autem genuit," a reference to the long genealogies in the Latin Bible</note>, and that to another, and another to <margin>25</margin> another; and just as one "from the tribe" and "thousands sealed" <note>original: "ex tribu, et millia signati," Latin phrases referring to the counting of the tribes of Israel in the Book of Revelation</note> follows in a certain line from the one before it; and just as one cherry pulls another; so do troubles and inconveniences usually act: for one follows close upon the other. It is a universal proverb that misfortunes never come alone. First, for my master’s first ill-fortune, he met Cencio. For the second, he <margin>30</margin> left six hundred scudi there. For <margin>35</margin> the eighth, he has gone to prison. For the ninth, some other disaster will surely happen before he gets out of jail, and it will cost him both time and money. *Scar.* The conclusion is that prostitutes in Naples, Venice, and Rome—
<margin>That is to say, in | all of Italy.</margin> <note>original: "ideste," a Latinism for "that is to say"</note> —are permitted, favored, have their own statutes, their laws, their taxes, and even privileges.
*Sang.* You must tell me, what sort of privileges?
*Scar.* And therefore, consequently, people are not deprived of the opportunity to visit courtesans, and they are not persecuted by justice.
*Sang.* I am beginning to understand this fellow.
*Bon.* And I; he is getting closer. Praise and glory to Our Lady of Loreto! <note>The Santa Casa di Loreto was a major pilgrimage site; Bonifacio is expressing relief as the defense seems to be working</note>
*Scar.* And not only this: but justice also very zealously abstains from proceeding against, persecuting, and seizing those who go to women of honor <note>meaning respectable or married women, as opposed to professional courtesans</note>; because our princes consider it a barbaric thing to take the "horns" <note>In the Renaissance, "horns" were the symbolic mark of a cuckold. Scaramuré argues that publicizing a scandal "attaches" these metaphorical horns to a man's forehead for all to see</note> that a gentleman—a man of esteem and some reputation—carries in his breast, and attach them to his
<margin>121</margin> forehead. Therefore, however notorious the act may be, it is not customary to proceed against it; except when the party (who is always of the vilest condition) is not ashamed to make a formal demand. As for the honorable parties, justice would do them a great wrong and injury; because the punishment given to the one who "plants the horns" does not outweigh the disgrace brought upon a personage by making his shame public and notorious to the eyes of the whole world. So it is that the offense suffered from justice is greater than that from the delinquent; and even if the whole world already knew of it, nonetheless the "horns" always become more solemn
<margin>B</margin> and glorious <note>Scaramuré uses "glorious" ironically here to mean "highly visible" or "prominent"</note> through an act of justice. Every man capable of judgment therefore considers that this feigned ignorance by justice prevents many inconveniences: because a shamed man whose disgrace is hidden (if indeed such a man can be called shamed whose reputation is not yet corrupted), for fear of being discovered, or because he cares less for those "horns" that no one sees (which in fact are nothing), abstains from taking that vengeance which he would be obliged to take according to the ways of the world when the case is manifest to many. The custom of Italy and other non-barbaric countries where "horns" are not cheap <note>meaning they are not taken lightly; honor is expensive</note> therefore not only tolerates and ignores such excesses, but also strives to cover them. Whence in a certain way those who
<margin>122</margin> permit brothels are to be praised, for through them the greatest inconveniences that can happen in our regions are avoided.
*Sang.* Conclude quickly, I tell you.
*Bon.* Alas, he makes me die of thirst; a paroxysm <note>original: "parasisismo," a malapropism or variant of "parossismo," indicating Bonifacio's extreme nervous agitation</note> is coming over me.
*Scar.* Finally, I say to Your Lordship, that the excess of Master Bonifacio has been...

**Gioan Bernardo.** Messer Bonifacio, I am a Christian, and I profess to be a good Catholic. I confess my sins generally and receive communion on all the principal feast days of the year. My trade is to paint and present to the eyes of worldly folk the image of our Lord, of our Lady, and of other saints of paradise. **Mamphurio.** At the heel, at the end. For I too am not stretching my sides with laughter. <note>original Latin: "In calce, in fine. neque enim et ego risu ilia tendo." A variation of a line from the Roman satirist Persius, indicating his lack of amusement.</note>

**Mamphurio.**
> How poorly can I clap,
> Tested by endurance,
<margin>15</margin>> For the Applause made by me
> Has long since been miserable;
> With both my buttocks, and my hands,
> And with the sound of gold coins. Amen. <note>Mamphurio delivers this as a mock-liturgical chant in Latin. The "sound of gold coins" refers to the money the rogues have just stolen from him.</note>

**Ascio.** Give the applause, I say: and strive to do it yourself as well,
<margin>20</margin>and do it all well, like the master and man of letters that you are; otherwise, people will return to the stage, to your misfortune.
**Mamphurio.** I shall do so with a cheerful heart, in the following manner. <note>original Latin: "Hilari efficiam animo, forma quae sequitur."</note> Just as sailors, even though they have a broken mast, a lost sail, torn rigging,
<margin>145</margin>and a strayed rudder | because of the turbulent storm; are nevertheless
<margin>25</margin>accustomed to applaud for having reached the port; and according to the Maronian maxim <note>Referring to the Roman poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note>:
> Saved sailors shall pay their vows on the shore
> To Glaucus, and Panopea, and Melicertes son of Ino. <note>original Latin: "Votaque seruati soluent in littore nautae / Glauco, et Panopeae, et Inóo Melicertae." A quote from Virgil’s Georgics regarding the deities of the sea.</note>

Likewise I, Mamphurio, professor of Greek, Latin, and Vernacular letters—not, I say, a royal [regius] nor a common [gregius] one, but an extraordinary [egregius] one (which by etymology means
<margin>30</margin>"taken from the flock" <note>Mamphurio is punning on the Latin word "egregius," which usually means "excellent," but literally means "separated from the herd."</note>); also doctor of Philosophy, Medicine, and of both laws <note>Civil and Canon Law.</note>, and of Theology if I had so desired; for having reached the port of my sorrowful and calamitous events (intending to fulfill my vows after this), I applaud. Therefore, I say to you, most noble spectators (upon whom I see all faces and eyes are cast),
<margin>35</margin>just as I, finding myself at the end of my role as a tragic subject; if not
<margin>B</margin>with my hands, <term>giornea</term> <note>A short, sleeveless surcoat.</note>, and clothes; yet in heart and spirit I applaud: | So, and better still, may you who have been moved by better fortune until now, and who have been joyful and happy spectators of our annoying and troublesome misfortunes, fare well, and applaud. <note>original Latin: "Valete, et Plavdite." The traditional closing of Roman comedies.</note>

<margin>[2]</margin> <margin>1</margin> ## | To the Discontented One.

If you are pierced by the Cynic tooth, <note>The "Cynic tooth" refers to biting criticism, traditionally associated with the Cynics who were compared to dogs for their barking at social conventions.</note>
Complain of yourself, you barbaric dog: <note>original: "perro," the Spanish word for dog, used here as a sharp insult.</note>

If you do not take care to avoid spiting me.
<margin>5</margin>Because you approached me with wrong against right,
Therefore I tear your skin and lay you open:
And if it happens that my body is then cast down,
Your disgrace is written in diamond. <note>Meaning the critic's shame will be permanent and indelible.</note>
<margin>10</margin>Do not go naked to take honey from the bees.
Do not bite if you do not know if it is stone or bread.
Do not go barefoot to sow thorns.
Do not, as a fly, despise the spider’s webs.
If you are a mouse, do not follow the frogs. <note>A reference to the "Battle of Frogs and Mice," a mock-epic poem often attributed to Homer.</note>

And believe the Gospel,
Which says with good zeal,
From our field, he reaps penitence
Who sowed the seeds of error there.

Also other Metaphysical, other Mathematical, and other Natural speculations.

### Argument of the Fourth Dialogue.

1 Theophilo and Frulla [might seem] to touch the backs of certain subjects <margin>1</margin> too heavily and rigidly: but consider, Sir, that these animals do not have such tender hides; so that even if the blows were a hundredfold greater, [10] they would not care a bit, nor would they feel it more than if they were being 5 stroked by a young girl. Nor would I wish you to judge me worthy of reproach because, upon such ineptitudes and such an unworthy field as these doctors have provided us, we have chosen to elaborate on such grave and worthy propositions: for I am certain you know there is a difference between taking 10 a thing as a foundation and taking it as an occasion. Foundations, in truth, must be proportioned to the greatness, condition, and nobility of the building. But occasions can be of all sorts, for all effects: because the smallest and most sordid things are the seeds of 15 great and excellent things. Foolishness and madness are wont to provoke great counsel, judgments, and inventions. I leave aside that it is manifest how errors and crimes have many times provided the occasion for the greatest rules of justice and goodness.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If, in the portrayal, it seems to you that the colors do not correspond perfectly 20 to the life, and the outlines do not seem to you entirely proper: know that the defect has arisen from this, that the painter could not examine the portrait with those spaces and distances that the masters of the art are accustomed to take: because, besides the fact that the panel, or the field, was too 25 close to the face and the eyes, he could not withdraw even a single step backward or move aside to one side or the other, without fear of making that leap which the son of the famous defender of Troy <note>Astyanax, the son of the Trojan hero Hector; according to legend, he was thrown from the city walls during the fall of Troy.</note> once made. Furthermore, I am certain that your generous soul will direct the eye of consideration more to the gratitude of the affection with which it is given, than to the gift of the hand that offers it to you. This has been directed to you, who are closer, and show yourself more propitious and more favorable to our Nolan <note>The "Nolan" is Giordano Bruno himself, so called because he was born in Nola, Italy.</note>. # The Ash Wednesday Supper.

->**There was never a Greek free of malice.**<-
<note>This is a common Renaissance proverb, "Non fu mai Greco di malitia netto," often used to contrast Italian or modern sincerity with the perceived duplicity of ancient or academic authorities.</note>

Beyond the fact that I cannot fall in love with something I do not see, there are others—others indeed—who have enchained my soul. To you others, then, I speak: gracious, gentle, mellow, soft, young, beautiful, delicate ones, with blond hair, white cheeks, vermilion cheeks, succulent lips, divine eyes, breasts of enamel, and hearts of diamond. For you, I build so many thoughts in my | **5** mind, gather so many affections in my spirit, conceive so many passions in my life. So many tears I shed from my eyes; so many sighs I discharge from my chest; and from my heart, I spark so many flames. To you, Muses of England <note>Bruno is addressing the noblewomen of the Elizabethan court, whom he famously praised for their beauty and intellect.</note>, I say: inspire me, breathe into me, warm me, kindle me, distill me, and resolve me into liquid; turn me into sap, and make me appear not with a tiny, delicate, narrow, short, and succinct epigram, but with a copious and wide vein of long, flowing, great, and solid prose; so that, not as from a narrow reed, but as from a wide channel, I may pour forth my streams. And you, my Mnemosyne <note>The Greek goddess of memory and mother of the Muses.</note>, hidden under thirty seals <note>A reference to Bruno's own book, *The Thirty Seals of Ideas*, which deals with the art of memory.</note> and enclosed in the dark prison of the shadows of Ideas, intone a little in my ear.

In days past, two men came to the Nolan <note>The "Nolan" is Giordano Bruno himself, named after his birthplace, Nola.</note> on behalf of a Royal Esquire, making him understand how much that man desired his conversation to understand his Copernicus, and other paradoxes of his new philosophy. To which the Nolan replied that he did not see through the eyes of Copernicus, nor of Ptolemy, but through his own as far as judgment and determination were concerned; although, as for observations, he felt he owed much to these and other diligent <term>mathematicians</term> <note>In the 16th century, "mathematician" was the standard term for what we now call an "astronomer."</note> who, successively from age to age, adding light to light, have given us sufficient principles by which we are brought to such judgment—a judgment which could not have been born except after many active ages.

He added that these men [the astronomers] are, in effect, like those interpreters who translate words from one language to another; but it is others [the philosophers] who then penetrate the meanings, and not the translators themselves. They are like those rustics who report the details and the form of a battle to an absent | **5†** captain; they themselves do not understand the business, the reasons, and the art by which the victory was won; but he who has experience and better judgment in the military art understands it. Thus, to the Theban Manto, who saw but did not understand, the blind Tiresias <note>In Greek mythology, Tiresias was the blind prophet of Thebes, and Manto was his daughter who possessed the gift of sight but lacked his prophetic insight.</note>, the divine interpreter, said:

> A great part of the truth is hidden from one lacking sight,
> But where my country, where Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of prophecy.</note> calls me, I shall follow.
> You, daughter, guiding your father who is destitute of light,
> Report the manifest signs of the sacred prophecy.
<note>original: "Visu carentem magna pars ueri latet, / Sed quo uocat me patria, quo Phoebus sequar. / Tu lucis inopem gnata genitorem regens, / Manifesta sacri signa fatidici refer." These lines are from Seneca's tragedy *Oedipus*.</note>

<meta>This page continues the First Dialogue. Following the invocation to the Muses and the ladies of England, Teofilo begins to discuss the nature of scientific observation and the specific merit of Nicolaus Copernicus. # The Ash Wednesday Supper.

<margin>1</margin>Similarly, how could we judge the many and diverse verifications of the appearances of superior or surrounding bodies, if they had not been declared and placed before the eyes of reason? Certainly not at all. Nevertheless, after having given thanks to the gods—the distributors of gifts that proceed from the first and infinite, omnipotent light—and after having magnified the study of these generous spirits, we know most clearly that we must open our eyes to what they have observed and seen, but not give our consent to what they have conceived, understood, and determined.

<margin>10</margin>    **Smith:** Please, let me understand what opinion you have of Copernicus?

    **Teofilo:** He possessed a serious, elaborate, diligent, and mature genius; a man who is inferior to no astronomer who came before him, except by sequence of time and place. A man who, in terms of natural judgment, was far superior to Ptolemy, Hipparchus, Eudoxus, and all the others who followed in their footsteps. He achieved this by freeing himself from certain false presuppositions of common and vulgar philosophy <note>By "vulgar philosophy," Bruno refers to the Aristotelian-scholastic tradition dominant in the universities of his time.</note>—I will not say blindness. But for all that, he did not distance himself much from it; because he, being more a student of mathematics than of nature, was not able to go deep enough or penetrate far enough to completely remove the roots of inconvenient and vain principles. Thus, he could not perfectly resolve all the opposing difficulties, nor succeed in freeing both himself and others from so many vain inquiries, nor fix contemplation upon things that are constant and certain. Despite this, who could fully praise the magnanimity of this German <note>original: "Germano." Although Copernicus was from Toruń (modern Poland), Bruno refers to him as "German" or "Alemano," as was common in the 16th century for those from that region under the Holy Roman Empire's influence.</note>, who, having little regard for the foolish multitude, stood so firm against the torrent of the opposing faith? And although he was almost unarmed with "living reasons" <note>Bruno suggests that Copernicus lacked the physical and philosophical proofs of an infinite universe that Bruno himself would later propose.</note>, by taking up those abject and rusty fragments <note>A reference to the ancient heliocentric theories of the Pythagoreans, which had been neglected for centuries.</note> that he was able to get his hands on from antiquity, he polished, assembled, and soldered them together. He did this with a discourse that was more mathematical than natural, so much so that he made a cause once considered ridiculous, abject, and despised into something honored, prized, and more plausible than its opposite; and certainly more convenient and expeditious for theoretical and calculating reason. Thus this German, although he did not have sufficient means to do more than resist—not enough to fully conquer, defeat, and suppress falsehood—nevertheless stood his ground. He determined in his mind and most openly confessed that one must finally conclude, of necessity, that it is rather this globe <note>The Earth.</note> that moves in relation to the universe, than that it is possible for the generality of so many innumerable bodies—many of which are known to be more magnificent and larger—to do so. This would be despite nature and reason, which cry out the contrary with the most sensible motions; to recognize this as the center...

<summary>Teofilo discusses the legacy of Nicolaus Copernicus, praising him for reviving ancient heliocentric ideas and surpassing previous astronomers like Ptolemy, while critiquing him for being more of a mathematician than a natural philosopher who understood the true physical nature of the universe.</summary>

What then should be done for this man who has found the way to climb to the
<margin>10</margin>heavens, to travel the circumference of the stars, and leave behind the convex surface of the firmament? The Tiphis <term>Tiphis</term> <note>Tiphys was the pilot of the *Argo* in Greek mythology; Bruno uses the name here to represent all navigators and explorers.</note> have found the way to disturb the peace of others, to violate the native spirits of various regions, to confound what provident nature has kept distinct, and through commerce to double the defects and add vice to vice from one generation to another; with violence they propagate new follies and plant unheard-of madness where it does not exist, concluding in the end that he who is strongest is the wisest. They show new studies, instruments, and the art of tyrannizing and robbing one another; by grace of which deeds, a time will come when those people, having learned at their own painful expense, and by the force of the vicissitude of things, will know how to, and be able to, return to us similar and even worse fruits of such pernicious inventions.

The Nolan, to bring about entirely opposite effects, has liberated the human spirit and knowledge, which was enclosed in the very narrow prison of the turbulent air, from where it could barely, as if through certain holes, have the power to look at the most distant stars; its wings were clipped so that it could not fly to pull back the veil of these clouds and see what was truly found up there, and to free itself from the chimeras of those who, having emerged from the mud and caves of the earth as if they were Mercuries and Apollos descended from heaven, have—with multi-faceted imposture—[filled the world with folly].

# The Ash Wednesday Supper.

<margin>1</margin>...filled the world with infinite follies, bestiality, and vices, as if they were so many virtues, divinities, and disciplines; snuffing out that light that made the souls of our ancient fathers divine and heroic, while approving and confirming the darkness.
<margin>5</margin>For so long a time human reason has been oppressed, yet sometimes in its lucid intervals, weeping for its so low condition, it turns toward the divine and provident mind—which always whispers in its internal ear—with words such as these:

->Who will ascend to heaven for me, my lady,<-

# The Ash Wednesday Supper.

> *Learn, but from the learned; you yourself should teach the unlearned.*
<note>original: "Disce, sed a' doctis, indoctos ipse doceto." A Latin maxim from the Distichs of Cato, a medieval schoolbook.</note>

What you say regarding doctrine is also useful to many, and therefore it is advice that concerns the crowd; for this burden is not fit for just anyone’s shoulders, but for those who can carry it like the Nolan—or at least move it | toward its goal without **13** encountering unseemly difficulty, as Copernicus was able to do.

Furthermore, those who possess this truth should not communicate it to every kind of person, unless they wish to "wash the donkey's head" <note>An Italian idiom meaning to waste one's effort on something or someone beyond help.</note>, as they say, or see what pigs do with pearls, and reap those fruits of their study and labor which reckless and foolish ignorance usually produces, along with the presumption and incivility that are its perpetual and faithful companions. Of those unlearned, then, we can be teachers, and of those blind, we can be enlighteners; those who are called blind not due to natural inability or lack of talent and discipline, but solely for failing to notice and consider: which occurs by the absence of the act alone, and not yet of the faculty. Among these, some are so malicious and wicked that, out of a certain lazy envy, they become angry and proud toward the one who seems to want to teach them; being regarded as learned, and (what is worse) believing themselves to be doctors, they are outraged that someone dares to show they know what they themselves do not. Here you will see them catch fire and go mad.

*FRULLA.* As happened to those two barbarian doctors <note>The "doctors" are the Oxford professors Bruno debated in 1583.
