# The Ash Wednesday Supper.

<margin>1</margin>the Nolan will gain the assent and the love. These are those most noble wits who are capable of hearing him and disputing with him. Because in truth, no one is worthy of opposing him regarding these matters; for if one does not come away content to agree with him entirely, not being capable of it, <margin>5</margin>at least one does not subscribe against him in the many, greater, and principal things, and must confess that what he cannot know for certain to be more true is surely more likely.

*Prudentio.* Be that as it may, I do not wish to depart from the opinion of the ancients, because the Sage says: *In antiquity is wisdom.* <note>original: "Ne l’ antiquitá é la sapienza." A reference to Job 12:12: "With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding."</note>

<margin>10</margin>*Theophilo.* And he adds: *In many years is prudence.* <note>original: "in molti anni la prudenza."</note> If you understood well what you were saying, you would see that from your own foundation, one infers the contrary of what you think. I mean to say that we are older and have a longer age than our predecessors—I mean in what pertains to certain judgments, as in this subject. <margin>15</margin>The judgment of Eudoxus <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 390–337 BC) who proposed a system of concentric spheres to explain planetary motion.</note>, who lived shortly after the rebirth of astronomy—if indeed it did not beget itself in him—could not have been as mature as that of Calippus <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 370–300 BC) who refined Eudoxus's model.</note>, who lived thirty years after the death of Alexander the Great; | who, as he added years to years, could also add observations to observations. Hipparchus <note>Often considered the greatest ancient astronomical observer (c. 190–120 BC); he discovered the precession of the equinoxes.</note>, for the same reason, ought to have known <margin>20</margin>more than Calippus, because he saw the changes made up to one hundred and ninety-six years after the death of Alexander. Menelaus the Roman Geometer <note>Menelaus of Alexandria (c. 70–140 AD), a mathematician and astronomer who worked in Rome.</note>, because he saw the difference in motion four hundred and sixty-two years after Alexander's death, by reason understood more than Hipparchus. Even more should have been seen by Al-Battani <note>original: "Machometto Aracense." Referring to the Arab astronomer Albategnius (c. 858–929 AD), born in Harran (Aracca).</note> one thousand two hundred and two years <margin>25</margin>after that. Even more has been seen by Copernicus, almost in our own times, around the year one thousand eight hundred and forty-nine after the same [death of Alexander]. But the fact that some of these who have come after were not, for all that, more shrewd than those who were first, and that the multitude of those who are in our own times do not have more wit <note>original: "piu sale," literally "more salt," a common Renaissance metaphor for wisdom or sharp intelligence.</note>, <margin>30</margin>this happens because those others did not live, and these do not live, the years of others; and (what is worse) both those and these lived as dead men within their own years.

*Prudentio.* Say what you please, pull it to your own pleasure wherever you like; I am a friend of antiquity, and as far as your opinions or paradoxes are concerned, I do not believe that so many and so wise men have been as ignorant as <margin>35</margin>you and other friends of novelty think.

*Theophilo.* Well, Master Prudentio, if this common and personal opinion of yours is true simply because it is ancient, then certainly it was false when it was new. # The Ash Wednesday Supper.

<margin>1</margin> these senseless and vain logicians and mathematicians rebelled, being enemies not so much of antiquity as they are estranged from the truth. It is <margin>10</margin> like two blind beggars at the gate of the archbishopric of Naples: one called himself a Guelph and the other a Ghibelline <note>The Guelphs and Ghibellines were rival political factions in Italy. At this point, a good man approached them and said: <margin>15</margin> "Come here, you and you, blind scoundrel! What is a Guelph? What is a Ghibelline? What does it mean to be a Guelph and to be a Ghibelline?" In truth, the first one did not know how to answer or what to say at all. The other resolved it by saying: "Lord Pietro Costanzo, who is my master and whom I love very much, is a Ghibelline." Just so, <margin>20</margin> there are many Peripatetics who get angry, heat up, and catch fire for Aristotle; they want to defend the doctrine of Aristotle, they are enemies of those who are not friends of Aristotle, and they want to live and die for Aristotle—yet they do not even understand the meaning of the titles of Aristotle's books. *The.* Please, <margin>17</margin> do not interrupt our discourse any further. <margin>30</margin> *Sm.* Continue, Signor Theophilo.

*The.* Your Aristotle noted, I say, that just as there is a cycle of change in all other things, it is no less so with opinions and various effects. Are we in darkness, or are they? <header>The Ash Wednesday Supper.</header>

<note>The speaker Smitho is addressing Theophilo regarding the difficulty of unlearning childhood prejudices.</note>
Whether by the choice of those who governed me—fathers and teachers—or by my own whim and imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note>, or by the reputation of a doctor; I would consider myself to have gained no less satisfaction of mind under the arrogant and fortunate ignorance of a horse than under anyone else less ignorant, or even learned. Since in the mind of that person there is perhaps less inclination to attend to your propositions than to those of a thousand others who differ?

**Theophilo.** This is a gift of the gods, if they guide you and dispense the fates to make you encounter a man who not only has the reputation of a true guide, but in truth is such, and they illuminate your internal spirit to make the choice of that which is better.

**Smitho.** However, one commonly follows common judgment, so that if an error is made, it will not be without great favor and company.

**Theophilo.** A thought most unworthy of a man. For this reason, wise and divine men are very few: and the will of the gods is this, considering that what is common and general is neither esteemed nor precious.

**Smitho.** I well believe that the truth is known by few, and prized things are possessed by very few: but it confuses me that many things are few, among few, and perhaps held by only one, which ought not to be esteemed, are worth nothing, and may be the greatest follies and vices.

**Theophilo.** Well; but in the end it is safer to seek the true and the fitting outside of the multitude: because the multitude never brought anything precious and worthy. And things of perfection and value were always found among the few; which, if they were only rare and among rare men, everyone—even if they did not know how to find them—could at least recognize them: and thus they would not be so precious by way of knowledge, but of possession only.

**Smitho.** Let us leave these discourses then, and stay a while to hear and observe the thoughts of the Nolan <note>The "Nolan" refers to Giordano Bruno himself, born in Nola.</note>. It is indeed enough that until now he has won so much faith that he is esteemed worthy of being heard.

**Theophilo.** This is quite enough for him. Now attend to how strong his philosophy is in preserving itself, defending itself, discovering vanity, and making...

Theophilo. Then Sir Fulke Greville <note>Sir Fulke Greville (1554–1628) was an English poet and statesman who hosted the debate described in this book.</note> said to him: "Please, Mr. Nolan, let me understand the reasons for which you judge the earth to be in motion." To which he replied that he could not give him any reason at all, not knowing his capacity; and not knowing how he might be understood by him, he feared doing as those who tell their reasons to statues and go about speaking with the dead.

Therefore, let it please him first to make himself known by proposing those reasons that persuade him of the contrary; because, according to the light and strength of the intellect he demonstrates in bringing those forward, resolutions could then be given to him.

He added to this that, because of the desire he has to show the weakness of contrary opinions through the very same principles with which they think they are confirmed, it would give him no <page-num>24</page-num> small pleasure to find people who were judged sufficient for this undertaking; and he would always be prepared and ready to respond. In this way, the virtue of the foundations of this philosophy of his against the common one could be seen all the better, the greater the occasion presented to him to respond and declare himself. This response greatly pleased Sir Fulke. He said: "You do me a most gracious service. I accept your proposal, and I wish to set a day on which people will oppose you who perhaps will not fail to give you material to bring your ideas into the field. Wednesday in eight days, which will be <term>Ash Wednesday</term><note>The first day of Lent; the title of the book refers to this specific dinner party in London in 1584.</note>, you shall be invited with many gentlemen and learned personages, so that after eating there may be a discussion of fine and varied things." "I promise you," said the Nolan, "that I shall not fail to be present at that time, and every time such an occasion presents itself; because there is nothing within my choice that could delay me from the study of wanting to understand and know. But I pray you that you do not bring before me ignoble people, ill-bred, and of little understanding in such..."

1 Like a man who lies and long laments

What must I do? What must I say, alas?
From this side, our lodging called us back: because Master Big-Toad and Master Slough <note>original: "maestro Buazzo et maestro Pantano." These are derogatory nicknames for the boatmen who had just left them in the mud.</note> had so thoroughly stuffed us with drink that we could hardly move our legs. Furthermore, the rules of **Odomantia** <note>A pseudo-scientific term likely referring to the "divination of paths" or the omens of travel.</note> and the usual practice of augury importunately advised us not to continue that journey. The stars, being entirely covered under a dark and gloomy mantle and leaving the air misty for us, forced us to return. The weather dissuaded us from going so far forward and exhorted us to turn back that little bit. The nearby place applauded us kindly. Opportunity, which with one hand had pushed us back this far, now with two stronger pulses made the greatest impetus in the world. Fatigue, finally (no less than a stone is moved toward the center by its intrinsic principle and nature), showed us the same path and made us incline toward the right. On the other hand, we were called by the many labors, travails, and hardships which would have been spent in vain; but the worm of conscience said: if this little bit of path has cost us so much, which is not even twenty-five paces, what will become of the great distance that remains? *Better to lose, than to lose more.* <note>original: "Meior es perdere, che mas perdere." A Spanish proverb.</note> From there, we were invited by the desire we had not to defraud the expectation of those knights and noble personages; on the other hand, cruel remorse responded that since those men had neither care nor thought to send a horse or a boat to gentlemen at this time, hour, and occasion, they would likewise have no scruple regarding our failure to go. From that side, we were accused of being ultimately discourteous, or of being men who stand too much on ceremony <note>original: "pontiglio" (punctilio).</note>, who measure things by merits and favors, and make a profession more of receiving courtesy than of giving it; and like villains and ignoble men, would rather be defeated in that than conquer. From this side, we were excused because where there is force, there is no reason.
From there, the particular interest of the **Nolan** <note>Giordano Bruno himself, who was from Nola.</note> attracted us, for he had promised, and they might have been able to attach some sort of stigma to him. Besides, he has a great desire that an opportunity be offered to him to see customs, to know wits, to perceive if some new truth might be possible, to confirm the good habit of knowledge, and to notice anything he lacks. From this side, we were delayed by common boredom and by some sort of spirit that spoke certain reasons more true than worthy to report. To whom does it belong to determine this contradiction? Who is to triumph over this free will? To whom does reason consent? What has fate determined? Behold, this fate, by means of reason, opening the door of the intellect, enters within and commands the choice <note>original: "elettione" (the faculty of choosing).</note> to dispatch the consent to continue the journey. Oh, heavy steps!

<margin>Proverb: A neat exaggeration.</margin>
...now (as it is said), oh you faint-hearted, oh you light, inconstant men of little spirit.

**Theophilus**: It is not, it is not impossible, although this undertaking may be difficult; difficulty is that which is ordained to make the lazy stay behind. Ordinary and easy things are for the commoners and ordinary people. Rare, heroic, and divine men pass along this path of difficulty so that necessity is forced to grant them the palm of immortality. Add to this that even if it were not possible to reach the finish line to win the prize: run anyway, and make your effort in a matter of such great importance, and resist until the final breath. Not only is the winner praised, but also the one who does not die as a coward and a sluggard; such a man casts the blame for his loss and death onto fate, and shows the world that it was not through his own defect, but through the wrong of fortune <note>original: "fortuna"</note> that he reached such an end. Not only is that one man worthy of honor who has earned the prize: but also that one, and that other, who has run so well that he is judged worthy and capable of having earned it, even though he did not win it. And those are shameful who, despairing in the middle of the race, stop and do not go (even if they are last) to touch the goal with that breath and vigor which is possible for them.

Let perseverance, therefore, conquer; for if the labor is so great, the reward will not be mediocre. All precious things are placed in difficulty: narrow and thorny is the path to blessedness; perhaps heaven promises us a great thing.

<note>The following is a quote from Virgil's Georgics, Book I, lines 121-124</note>
*The Father of tillage himself*
*Did not wish the way to be easy, and he first through art*
*Moved the fields, sharpening mortal hearts with cares,*
*Nor did he allow his realm to grow sluggish in heavy lethargy.*

<margin>Proverb: This is a very emphatic progression, which would be suited to a matter of greater importance.</margin>

Thus, they do not ordinarily exalt the worthy and virtuous, because it seems to them that those men have no occasion to return as many thanks as...

Certainly, if the empire of Fortune corresponded and were equal to the empire of her most noble spirit and genius, it would be necessary for this great Amphitrite <note>A sea goddess in Greek mythology, used here as a metaphor for the ocean surrounding Britain.</note> to open her fringes and enlarge her circumference so much that, just as she encompasses a Britain and an Ireland, she might be given another entire globe that would equal the universal mass; so that with a fuller significance her powerful hand might sustain the globe of a general and entire monarchy.

You have no reason to speak of such a mature, discreet, and provident Council, with which that heroic soul for twenty-five years and more—with but a nod of her eyes in the center of the gales of a sea of adversity—has made peace and quiet triumph; she has remained firm amidst such vigorous floods and swelling waves of various storms, with which this proud and mad Ocean that surrounds her on all sides has struck her with all its might. men: who, by design for wealth or favor, reduce themselves to shelter under the wings of the great; and these for the most part are not taken from their own homes, and without indignity follow their Milords <note>The Italian text uses "Milordi," referring to English noblemen</note>, being esteemed and favored by them. And if he who encounters them should be a foreigner: let him give them as much room as he likes, for they want him to know by any means how well they can play the Caesar, the Hannibal, the Hector, and even a charging ox. They do not act only like the donkey which (especially when it is loaded) contents itself with its straight path along the line, where if you do not move, he will not move either, and it will be necessary that either you to him, or he to you, gives a jolt: but so do these who carry water; for if you do not keep your wits about you, they will make you feel the point of that iron nose <note>The metal spout of the water-carrier's vessel</note> that sits at the mouth of the jar. So also do those who carry beer and ale <note>original: "hala"</note>, who, following their course, if by their inadvertence they should rush upon you, will make you feel the impetus of the load they carry; and that they are not only powerful enough to carry on their shoulders, but also to knock a house down, and pull (if it were a cart) as well. These individuals, by the authority they hold in the case of carrying a burden, are worthy of excuse, because they have more of the horse, mule, and donkey than of the man: but I accuse all the others...

Theophilo. It is true that there are also many who are not gentlemen of anything but their lineage, who, for their own convenience and ours, it is well that they are neither understood nor even seen.

For Copernicus, it was not enough to say merely that the earth moves; but he also protests and confirms it, writing to the Pope <note>referring to the dedication of 'De revolutionibus' to Pope Paul III</note>, and saying that the opinions of philosophers are very far from those of the common people, [which are] worthy of being shunned as contrary to truth and righteousness. And many other express indications [support this] sentence: notwithstanding that at the end it seems that in a certain way [he appeals to the] judgment as much of those who understand this philosophy as of the others who are pure mathematicians, that if by apparent inconveniences such a supposition should not please them: it is fitting that he also be granted the liberty to posit the motion of the earth to make firmer demonstrations than those made by the ancients, who were free to feign so many sorts and models of circles to demonstrate the phenomena of the stars. From which words one cannot gather that he doubts what he has so constantly confessed, and will sufficiently prove in the first book by responding to some arguments of those who estimate the contrary: where he not only performs the office of a mathematician who supposes, but also of a physicist who demonstrates the motion of the earth.

But certainly, little is added to the Nolan <note>Giordano Bruno, who was from Nola</note> by the fact that Copernicus, Nicetas of Syracuse the Pythagorean, Philolaus, Heraclides of Pontus, Ecphantus the Pythagorean, Plato in the *Timaeus* (though timidly and inconstantly, because he held it more by faith than by science), and the divine Cusanus <note>Nicholas of Cusa</note> in the second book of his *On Learned Ignorance*, and other rare subjects in every way, have said, taught, and confirmed it before: because he <note>the Nolan</note> holds it by other proper and firmer principles, through which—not by authority, but by living sense and reason—he holds this as certain as any other thing that can be held for certain.

**Smith.** That is all well; but pray, what argument is that which this "preliminary" <note>Referring to the anonymous preface to Copernicus's *De revolutionibus*, actually written by Andreas Osiander, which claimed the theory was merely a mathematical hypothesis rather than physical reality.</note> of Copernicus brings forward? For it seems to him to have more than a little verisimilitude (if indeed it is not true) that the star of Venus ought to have as much variety in its size as it has in its distance?

**Theophilo.** This fool, who fears and is anxious that some might go mad with the doctrine of Copernicus, I do not know if in a time of need he could have brought forward more inconveniences than that one; which, having been brought forward with such solemnity, he deems sufficient to demonstrate that to think such a thing is the mark of one too ignorant of Optics and Geometry. I would like to know what Optics and Geometry this beast <note>A common Brunian insult for his academic opponents.</note> understands, for he shows all too well how ignorant he and those from whom he learned are of true Optics and Geometry.

I would like to know how, from the size of luminous bodies, one can infer the ratio of their proximity and distance? And conversely, how from the distance and proximity of such bodies, one can infer some proportional variety of size? I would like to know by what principle of perspective or optics we can definitely conclude the exact distance, or the greater or lesser difference, from every variation of diameter? I would desire to understand if we are in error when we pose this conclusion: From the appearance of the quantity of a luminous body, we cannot infer the truth of its size, nor of its distance; because just as there is not the same ratio for an opaque body and a luminous body, so there is not the same ratio for a less luminous body, another more luminous, and another most luminous, so that we might judge their size or their distance. The mass of a man's head cannot be seen at two miles; yet that of a lamp, which is much smaller, or some similar thing of flame, will be seen without much difference (if indeed with any difference) at a distance of sixty miles; just as from Otranto in Puglia one often sees the candles of Avellona <note>Modern Vlorë, Albania; Bruno uses this to illustrate how light travels across the Ionian Sea.</note>, between which lands lies a great stretch of the Ionian Sea. Everyone who has sense and reason knows that if the lamps were of a light twice as clear, just as they are now seen at a distance of seventy miles without varying in size, they would be seen at a distance of one hundred and forty miles. At a triple ratio, two hundred and ten; at a quadruple ratio, two hundred and eighty; likewise always judging in other additions of proportions and degrees. Because it is rather from the quality and intense power of the light, than from the quantity of the ignited body, that the ratio of the same diameter and mass of the body is usually maintained. Do you wish then, O wise opticians and shrewd perspectivists, that...

If I see a light one hundred <term>stades<note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note></term> away that appears to have a diameter of four inches, would it be logical that at a distance of fifty stades it must have eight; at a distance of twenty-five, sixteen; at twelve and a half, thirty-two? **Smith.** So much so that, according to what you say, although it may be false, the opinion of **Heraclitus of Ephesus** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his doctrine of change.</note>—who said the sun is exactly the size it appears to the eyes—cannot be disproven by geometric arguments. **Epicurus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who founded a highly influential school of atomism.</note> subscribed to this, as appears in his letter to Sophocles; and in the eleventh book of *On Nature* (as **Diogenes Laertius** <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> reports), he says that (as far as he can judge) the size of the sun, the moon, and other stars is exactly as large as it appears to our senses. For he says that if they lost their size due to distance, they would have even more reason to lose their color; and certainly, he says, we should not judge those lights differently than those which are near us.

**Prudenzio.** The Epicurean **Lucretius** <note>A Roman poet and philosopher who popularized Epicureanism in Latin.</note> also bears witness to that in the fifth book of *On Nature*:

The wheel of the sun cannot be much larger, nor its heat much less,
Than it appears to be to our senses.
For from whatever distances fires can fling their light
And breathe a warm vapor upon our limbs,
Those intervals take nothing away from the body
Of the flames; the fire is not narrowed in appearance.
And the moon, whether she moves with a borrowed light illuminating the world,
Or throws out her own light from her own body,
Whatever that may be, she is carried with a shape no larger than it seems.
Finally, all the fires of the ether that you see from here,
As long as their flickering is clear and their glow is perceived,
One may know that they can be only a very tiny bit smaller,
Or larger by only a small and brief amount,
Since whatever fires we perceive on earth,
Seem sometimes to change their size only by a very little bit
In either direction, when they are further away.

**Theophilus.** To Nundinio, and indeed to all those who profess to understand, it is never possible to find even a semi-probable reason why there should be a margin <note>a boundary or limit</note> to this physical universe; and consequently, why the spaces it contains should be finite in number; and furthermore, why there should be a naturally determined center and middle of it.

**Smith.** Now, did Nundinio add anything to this? Did he bring forward any argument or likelihood to infer, first, that the universe is finite; second, that it has the Earth as its center; and third, that this center is entirely and in every way immobile in terms of local motion?

**Theophilus.** Nundinio—like one who says what he says out of faith and habit, and denies what he denies out of lack of habit and the novelty of it (as is common for those who reflect little and are not masters of their own actions, whether rational or natural)—remained stunned and astonished, like one to whom a new phantom <note>original: "phantasma"; a sudden, strange apparition or idea</note> suddenly appears. Then, as he was somewhat more discreet and less boastful and malicious than his companion, he kept silent and did not add words where he could not add reasons.

**Prudenzio.** <note>The text uses "Frv." likely for "Fru." or "Prudenzio," the pedantic character</note> It is not so with Doctor Torquato, who, whether by right or wrong, by God or by the devil, always wants to fight; when he has lost the shield to defend himself and the sword to offend—I mean when he has no more answers or arguments—he leaps into the kicks of rage, sharpens the claws of detraction, grinds the teeth of insults, and flings wide the throat of clamor, so that the opposing reasons cannot be spoken and do not reach the ears of the bystanders. Or so I have heard said.

**Smith.** So he said nothing more?

**Theophilus.** He said nothing more on that subject, but entered into another proposal.

### Fourth Proposal of Nundinio

Because the Nolan <note>Giordano Bruno himself, named after his birthplace, Nola</note> said in passing that there are innumerable earths similar to this one, Doctor Nundinio—like a "good" debater who has nothing to add to the point—begins to ask questions off the point. Moving away from what we were saying about the mobility or immobility of this globe, he asks about the quality of the other globes, and wants to know of what matter those bodies were made which are esteemed to be of the <term>quintessence</term> <note>the "fifth element" (aether), which Aristotelian physics claimed made up the incorruptible heavens</note>: an unalterable and incorruptible matter, of which the densest parts are the stars.

**Prudenzio.** This questioning seems off the point to me, though I do not understand logic.

**Theophilus.** The Nolan, out of courtesy, did not wish to reproach him for this.

# The Ash Wednesday Supper

But after having told him that he would have liked Nundinio to follow the main subject, or to ask questions concerning it, he <note>The Nolan (Giordano Bruno)</note> replied to him that the other globes which are earths are not different in any respect from this one in species, only in being larger or smaller, just as inequality occurs in other species of animals due to individual differences. But those spheres which are fire, such as the sun, he believes (for now) differ in species as the hot and the cold, or that which is lucid by itself and that which is lucid by another <note>Self-luminous vs. reflecting light</note>.

**Smith:** Why did he say he believed this "for now," and did not affirm it absolutely?

**Theophilus:** Fearing that Nundinio might again leave the question he had newly taken up, and seize and attach himself to this one. I leave aside that the earth being an animal <note>Bruno viewed the Earth as a living, ensouled organism</note>, and consequently a dissimilar body, it should not be judged a cold body because of some parts—mostly external ones ventilated by the air—when by other members, which are greater in number and size, it must be believed to be both hot and very hot. I leave aside also that by disputing while supposing in part the principles of the adversary (who wishes to be esteemed and makes profession of being a Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle</note>), and in another part his own principles (which are not granted, but proven), the earth would come to be as hot as the sun in some comparison.

**Smith:** How is that?

**Theophilus:** Because (according to what we have said) from the vanishing of the dark and opaque parts of the globe, and from the union of the crystalline and lucid parts, light comes to be diffused more and more into the more and more distant regions. Now, if light is the cause of heat (as many others affirm along with Aristotle himself, who maintain that even the moon and other stars are more or less hot according to a greater or lesser participation in light; whence, when some planets are called "cold," they want it understood by a certain comparison and respect), it will happen that the earth, with the rays that she sends to the distant parts of the ethereal region, according to the power of the light, comes to communicate just as much power of heat. But it is not established for us that a thing is hot just because it is lucid, because we see many lucid things near us that are not hot. Now, to return to Nundinio: behold, he begins to show his teeth, widen his jaws, squint his eyes, wrinkle his brows, flare his nostrils, and send a capon’s croak through his windpipe; so that by this laughter the bystanders might judge that he understood well, that he was right, and that the other was saying ridiculous things.

<summary>Theophilus explains Bruno's theory that the Earth is a living, warm organism and discusses the relationship between reflected light and heat, while mocking Nundinio's arrogant and dismissive behavior during the debate.</summary>

**Frulla:** And to show that it is true; did you see how he was laughing at it?
**Theophilus:** This is what happens to one who gives sweets to swine <note>A variation of the biblical "pearls before swine."</note>. When asked why he laughed, he replied that this talk and imagining that there are other worlds <note>original: "terre" (earths), referring to other planets or celestial bodies</note> which have the same properties and accidents was taken from the true narratives of Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century satirist who wrote "A True Story," a parody of travel tales involving a trip to the moon.</note>.

The Nolan replied that if Lucian, when he said the moon was another earth inhabited and cultivated like this one, meant to say it to mock those philosophers who affirmed there are many worlds (and particularly the moon, whose similarity to our globe is all the more sensible as it is closer to us), he was not right. Instead, he showed himself to be in common ignorance and blindness. For if we consider well, we will find the earth and so many other bodies called stars to be the principal members of the universe. Just as they give life and nourishment to things—which take matter from them and restore it to them—so, and much more greatly, they have life within themselves. By this life, with an ordered and natural will from an intrinsic principle, they move toward things and through spaces appropriate to them.

And there are no other extrinsic movers <note>External forces or spirits traditionally thought to push the planets.</note> who, by moving fantastic spheres, transport these bodies as if they were nailed into them. If that were true, the motion would be violent, outside the nature of the moving body; the mover would be more imperfect, and the motion and the mover would be anxious and laborious, and many other inconveniences would be added. Consider then that just as the male moves toward the female, and the female toward the male; every herb and animal, some more and some less expressly, moves toward its vital principle, such as the sun and other stars. The magnet <term>calamita: a natural magnet or lodestone</term> moves toward iron, straw toward amber, and finally every thing goes to find its like and flees its contrary. All this happens from a sufficient interior principle by which it is naturally stirred, and not from an exterior principle as we always see happen to those things moved either against or outside their own nature.

The earth and the other stars move, therefore, according to their own local differences from an intrinsic principle which is their own soul. "Do you believe," said Nundinio, "that this soul is sensitive <note>Capable of sensation or feeling.</note>?" "Not only sensitive," replied the Nolan, "but also intellectual; not only intellectual like ours, but perhaps even more so." At this, Nundinio fell silent and did not laugh.

**Prudentio:** It seems to me that if the earth is animated, it must feel no pleasure when these caves and caverns are made in its back, just as we feel pain and displeasure when a tooth is planted there or our flesh is pierced.

**Theophilus:** Nundinio did not have so much of Prudentio's <note>A play on the name "Prudentio," implying a lack of even basic cautious reasoning.</note> wit that he could even estimate...

this argument was worthy of being produced, even if it had occurred to him, because he is not so ignorant a philosopher <note>original: "philosofo"</note> as not to know that if she [the Earth] has sense, she does not have it similar to ours; if she has limbs, she does not have them similar to ours; if she has flesh, blood, nerves, bones, and veins, they are not similar to ours; if she has a heart, she does not have it similar to our own. So it is with all the other parts, which have a proportion to the members of various others that we call animals, and are commonly esteemed to be the only animals. Prudentio is not so good, nor so bad a physician, as not to know that to the great mass of the earth these are the most insensible accidents, which to our own imbecility <note>meaning our physical weakness or limited perception</note> are so sensible. And I believe he understands that no differently than in the animals which we recognize as animals, their parts are in continual alteration and motion, and have a certain flow and ebb, always gathering something from the outside and sending something out from the inside. Whence the nails grow; the fur, wool, and hair are nourished; the skin is healed; the hides are hardened. So the earth receives the outflow and inflow of parts, through which many animals (manifest to us as such) expressly show us their life. As it is more than likely (given that everything participates in life) that many and innumerable individuals live not only in us, but in all composite things. And when we see something that is said to die, we should not believe it dies so much as that it changes, and that accidental composition and harmony ceases, while the things that concur in it remain always immortal—more so those called spiritual than those called corporal and material, as we will show at another time.

If I dispute with you with civility <note>original: "ciuilita"</note> and respect, you should do at least as much for me, whom I know to be of such wit that if I wished to defend as truth the aforementioned narrations of Lucian, you would not be sufficient to destroy them. **Theophilus.** Finally, he <note>Referring to the character Nundinio, who represents the traditional Aristotelian view.</note> produced that argument of which all the pamphlets are full: that if it were true that the Earth moves toward the side we call the East, it would be necessary for the clouds in the air to always appear to travel toward the West, by reason of the extremely swift and rapid motion of this globe, which in the space of twenty-four hours must have completed such a vast circuit. To this, the Nolan <note>Giordano Bruno himself, often referred to as "The Nolan" because he was from Nola, Italy.</note> replied that this air through which the clouds and winds travel is part of the Earth. For he intends (and it must be so for this purpose) that under the name "Earth" one should understand the entire machine and the whole entire living being <note>Bruno viewed the Earth as a living organism or "animal."</note> which consists of its dissimilar parts. Thus the rivers, the stones, the seas, and all the vaporous and turbulent air which is enclosed within the highest mountains, belong to the Earth as a member of it, or even as the air that is in the lungs and other cavities of animals through which they breathe, their arteries dilate, and other effects necessary for life are fulfilled. The clouds, therefore, move by the accidents <note>In a philosophical sense, "accidents" are non-essential properties or events occurring within a substance.</note> that are within the body of the Earth, and are as if in its bowels, just as the waters are. Aristotle understood this in the first book of the *Meteorology*, where he says that this air which is around the Earth—moist and hot due to its exhalations—has above it another air, which is hot and dry, and there no clouds are found. And this air is outside the circumference of the Earth and that surface which defines it so that it becomes perfectly round; and that the generation of winds does not occur except in the bowels and places of the Earth. Therefore, above the high mountains, neither clouds nor winds appear; and there the air moves regularly in a circle, like the universal body. This is perhaps what Plato meant when he said that we inhabit the cavities and dark parts of the Earth, and that we have the same proportion to the animals that live above the Earth as the fish have to us, inhabiting a thicker fluid. He means to say that, in a certain way, this vaporous air is water; and the pure air that contains more fortunate animals is above the Earth, where just as this Amphitrite <note>A Greek sea goddess, here used as a poetic term for the sea.</note> is water to us, so this air of ours is water to them. Here, then, is how one can respond to the argument reported by Nundinio; because just as the sea is not on the surface, but in the bowels of the Earth, as the liver—the source of humors—is within us, this turbulent air is not outside, but is as if in the lungs of animals.

**Smith.** Now, how does it happen that we see the entire hemisphere, given that we inhabit the bowels of the Earth?

**Theophilus.** From the mass of the globose Earth, not only on the outermost surface but also on those which are interior, it happens that to the sight...

Because of this, point **M** is not so hindered that it cannot see the hemisphere; for the highest mountains do not come to interpose themselves at point **M** like the line **M B** (which I believe would happen if the surface of the earth were flat), but like the line **M C** or **M D**, which does not cause such an impediment, as is seen by virtue of the circumferential arc. In this way, they come to comprise more, and many artificial horizons, in which the accidents of one cannot cause alteration to the others. However, by "highest mountains" we do not mean the likes of the Alps and the Pyrenees and such; but rather like all of France, which lies between two seas—the Northern Ocean <note>The Atlantic/English Channel</note> and the Southern Mediterranean. From these seas toward Auvergne <note>A mountainous region in central France</note> one is always ascending, just as one also does from the Alps and the Pyrenees...

If this were not true, it would follow that when the ship runs through the sea, no one could ever pull something in a straight line from one side of it to the other, and it would not be possible for one to make a jump and return with his feet to the same place from which he took them. # The Ash Wednesday Supper

if something were thrown toward the Earth from a location outside of it, it would lose its straightness of motion due to the Earth's movement. This is apparent in the case of ship **A. B.** which, while passing along a river, if someone located on the bank **C.** were to throw a stone straight <note>original: "per dritto"</note>, his aim would fail by as much as the velocity of the ship's course accounts for. But if someone were placed atop the mast of said ship, no matter how fast it runs, he will not miss his mark at all; so that the stone or other heavy thing thrown will fall in a straight line from point **E**, which is at the top of the mast or in the crow's nest, to point **D**, which is at the foot of the mast, or another part of the belly and body of said ship. Likewise, if someone inside the ship throws a stone straight up from point **D** to point **E**, it will return downward along the same line, no matter how much the ship moves, provided it does not tilt.

**Smi.** From the consideration of this difference, the door is opened to many and most important secrets of nature and profound philosophy. For it is a very frequent thing, yet little considered, how great a difference there is between one who treats <note>The Italian "medica" here implies self-administration or self-care, used as an analogy for internal vs. external forces.</note> himself and one who is treated by another. It is quite manifest to us that we take greater pleasure and satisfaction if we come to feed ourselves by our own hand than by the arms of another. Children, as soon as they can use their own instruments <note>meaning their own hands/limbs</note> to take food, do not willingly use those of others; as if nature in a certain way makes them learn that just as there is not as much pleasure, there is also not as much profit. Do you see how infants who suckle cling with their hand to the breast? And I have never been so terrified by a robbery as by one committed by a domestic servant. Because I know not what shadow and portent a familiar person brings with them more than a stranger, because it reflects a kind of evil genius and a formidable omen.

**The.** Now to return to the point. If, then, there are two people, one of whom is inside the moving ship and the other outside of it; and both have their hands at approximately the same point in the air; and from that same place at the same time, each lets a stone drop without giving it any push: the stone of the first, without losing a point or deviating from its line, will reach the fixed place; and that of the second will find itself left behind. This proceeds from nothing else except that the stone leaving the hand of the one supported by the ship—and consequently moving according to its motion—has such an impressed virtue <note>term: "impressed virtue" (virtù impressa) refers to the pre-Newtonian concept of momentum or impetus carried by an object.</note> which the other does not have, which comes from the hand of the one who is outside, even though the stones have the same gravity <note>weight</note>, the same...

# The Ash Wednesday Supper

Whether one calls the earth a great or small **luminary** <note>original: "luminare"; a source of light</note>, and says the same of the **sun** and the **moon**, this was well and truly said according to its degree. This is because one must make oneself understood according to common words and feelings, and not act like a fool or a madman who misuses knowledge and wisdom. To speak in terms of **truth** where it is not required, and to wish that the common folk and the foolish multitude—from whom only practical action is required—should have specific scientific understanding, would be like wanting the hand to have an eye. Nature did not make the hand for seeing, but for working and consenting to what the sight perceives. 

Thus, even if he <note>referring to Moses or a divine legislator</note> understood the nature of **spiritual substances**, to what end should he have treated them, except insofar as some of them have a friendliness and ministry toward men when they act as **ambassadors** <note>original: "ambasciatrici"; referring to angels or messengers</note>? Even if he had known that the moon and other worldly bodies—both those that are seen and those invisible to us—possess everything that belongs to our own world, or at least something similar; do you think it would have been the office of a **legislator** to take up and give these burdens to the people? What does the practice of our laws and the exercise of our virtues have to do with those other worlds? 

Therefore, where divine men speak by presupposing the commonly received sense of natural things, they should not serve as an **authority**. Rather, we should look to the words of divine men where they speak indifferently, and where the common people have no fixed opinion. In such cases, I also want regard to be given to the **enthusiasms** <note>divine inspirations</note> of **Poets**, who have spoken with a superior light. One must not take as a **metaphor** what was not said as a metaphor, nor, on the contrary, take as **truth** what was said as a **similitude** <note>a comparison or parable</note>. 

But this distinction between the metaphorical and the true is not for everyone to grasp, just as it is not given to everyone to be able to understand it. Now, if we wish to turn the eye of consideration to a book that is contemplative, natural, moral, and divine, we shall find this **philosophy** <note>referring to the Copernican/Brunian infinite universe</note> very much favored and supported. I speak of the **Book of Job**, which is one of the most singular that can be read, full of all good **theology**, **natural science**, and **morality**, and filled with most wise discourses, which **Moses** joined as a **sacrament** <note>a sacred mystery or addition</note> to the books of his law. 

In that book, one of the characters, wishing to describe the **providential power of God**, said that He forms peace among His eminent ones—that is, His sublime sons, which are the **stars**, the **Gods**. Of these, some are fires and others are waters (just as we say some are **suns** and others are **earths**). These agree with one another because, however much they may be contraries, nevertheless one lives, is nourished, and flourishes by the other; provided they do not crowd together, but move around one another at certain distances. Thus the **universe** is distinguished into fire and...

**Theophil.** Now, no one among those standing around was so ignorant that they did not show, by their face and gestures, that they understood this man was a great big sheep <note>original: "pecoraccia," a derogatory term for a stupid person</note> of the golden order.

**Theophil.** Yet, to get the business moving, they prayed the Nolano <note>Giordano Bruno, who was from Nola.</note> to explain what he wished to defend, so that the aforementioned Doctor Torquato might argue against it. The Nolano replied that he had already explained himself too much; and that if the arguments of his adversaries were scarce, this did not proceed from a lack of subject matter, as must be manifest even to the blind. Yet he confirmed to them once again that the universe is infinite. And that it consists of an immense ethereal region. It is truly a heaven which is called space and a bosom, in which there are so many stars fixed, no differently than the earth is. And thus the moon, the sun, and other innumerable bodies are in this ethereal region, just as we see the earth to be. And that one should not believe in any other firmament, any other base, or any other foundation where these great animals <note>Bruno refers to planets and stars as "heavenly animals" because he believed they possessed a vital principle or soul that guided their movement.</note> might lean, which concur in the constitution of the world. This is the true subject and infinite matter of the infinite divine actual power: as both regulated reason and discourse have made us understand, as well as the divine revelations which say there is no number to the ministers of the Most High, whom thousands of thousands assist, and ten hundreds of thousands administer unto him. These are the great animals, many of which are sensible to us from every side by the clear light they diffuse from their bodies. Of these, some are effectively hot, like the sun and other innumerable fires; others are cold, like the earth, the moon, Venus, and other innumerable earths. These, in order to communicate with one another and participate in one another's vital principle, at certain spaces and certain distances, complete their circuits around one another, as is manifest in these seven <note>The seven known planets of the traditional system, though Bruno reclassifies them.</note> which turn around the sun, of which the earth is one. The earth, by moving in the space of 24 hours from the side called the West toward the East, causes the appearance of that motion of the universe around it, which is called the mundane and diurnal motion. Which imagination is entirely false, contrary to nature, and impossible; it being possible, convenient, true, and necessary that the earth moves around its own center to participate in light and darkness, day and night, heat and cold. Around the sun for the participation in Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter. Toward the so-called poles and opposite hemispheric points for the renewal of ages and the changing of its face; to the end that where there was sea, there shall be dry land; where it was torrid, it shall be cold; where the tropic was, there shall be the equinox—

It is, therefore, a thing fitting to the convenience of the things that exist, and to the effect of the most perfect cause, that this motion be natural from an internal principle and its own impulse, without resistance. bodies that move without the sensible contact of any other pushing or pulling force. Therefore, those who say that the **lodestone** <note>A naturally magnetized mineral; a magnet.</note> pulls the iron, the amber pulls the straw, the jet pulls the feather, or the sun pulls the heliotrope <note>A plant that turns toward the sun.</note>, understand it in reverse. From this consideration—that nothing moves locally by an extrinsic principle without a contact more vigorous than the resistance of the object—it follows how solemn a foolishness it is, and a thing impossible to persuade to a regulated sense: that the moon moves the waters of the sea, causing the tide, or that it makes the humors <note>Bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament.</note> increase, fecundates the fish, fills the oysters, and produces other effects. For the moon is properly the **sign** of all these things, and not the **cause**. I say sign and indication because seeing these things occur with certain dispositions of the moon—and other contrary and diverse things with contrary and diverse dispositions—proceeds from the order and correspondence of things, and the laws of one change which are conformable and corresponding to the laws of the other.

**Smith.** From the ignorance of this distinction, it follows that many notebooks are full of similar errors, teaching us so many strange philosophies where things that are signs, circumstances, and accidents are called causes. Among these ineptitudes, one of the "queens" is the claim that perpendicular and straight rays are the cause of greater heat, and acute and oblique rays the cause of greater cold. This, however, is an accident of the sun; the true cause of this is when it persists more or less above the earth. Reflected and direct rays; acute and obtuse angles; perpendicular, incident, and plane lines; greater and lesser arcs; this or that aspect—these are **mathematical circumstances** and not **natural causes**. It is one thing to play with geometry, another to verify with nature. It is not lines and angles that make fire heat more or less, but the near or distant positions, and the long or short durations.

**Theophilus.** You understand it very well; see how one truth clarifies another. Just as if water or vapor found itself in the region of fire, or a place similar to it, it would flee with greater speed than an exhalation <note>In Aristotelian physics, an "exhalation" is a dry or moist vapor rising from the earth</note> which possesses a certain participation and greater natural affinity with fire than it does contrariety or difference. Let it suffice for you to hold this: because regarding the intention of the Nolan <note>Giordano Bruno, born in Nola</note>, I find no fixed determination concerning the motion or rest of the sun. That motion, therefore, which we see in the flame that is held and contained within the cavities of furnaces, proceeds from the fact that the power of the fire pursues, ignites, alters, and transmutes the vaporous air, upon which it wishes to increase and nourish itself; and that other [the air] retreats and flees the enemy of its being and its correction.

**Smith:** You have said "vaporous air": what would you say of pure and simple air?

**Theophilus:** That is no more | subject to heat than to cold; it is no more a capable vessel and recipient of moisture when it is thickened by the cold, than of vapor and exhalation when water is thinned by the heat.

**Smith:** Since in nature there is nothing without providence and without a final cause: I would like to know from you again (because from what you have said, this can be perfectly understood) for what cause is the local motion of the earth?

**Theophilus:** The cause of such motion is the renewal and rebirth of this body, which according to the same disposition cannot be perpetual. Just as things that cannot be perpetual in number (to speak according to common usage) are made perpetual according to their species; so substances that cannot perpetuate themselves under the same face are continually changing their face. Because the matter and substance of things is incorruptible, and since it must be the subject of all forms in all its parts—so that in all its parts (as far as it is capable) it may become everything and be everything—if not at one and the same time and instant of eternity, at least in different times and various instants of eternity, successively and vicisitudinally <note>meaning: through a cycle of changes or "vicissitudes"</note>. For although all matter is capable of all forms together, nevertheless every part of matter cannot be capable of all those forms together. Therefore, since death and dissolution are not fitting for this entire mass of which this globe consists, and since annihilation is impossible for all of nature: from time to time, | one [part] taking the place of all the others; because otherwise these bodies, which are dissolvable, would at times actually dissolve, as happens to us particular and lesser animals. But to these...

It was said by the First Principle (as Plato believes in the *Timaeus* <note>A Socratic dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of the physical world and human beings</note>, and as we also believe): **You are dissoluble, but you shall not be dissolved.** It happens, therefore, that there is no part in the center or middle of the star that does not eventually move to the circumference or outside of it; and there is no portion in that outermost and external part that must not, at some time, become innermost and internal. Our daily experience demonstrates this to us: within the womb and bowels of the earth, some things are gathered together, while others are sent out from them. We ourselves, and the things that belong to us, come and go; we pass away and return; and there is nothing of ours that does not become foreign, and nothing foreign that does not become ours. There is nothing of which we are composed that must not at some time be ours <note>meaning part of our individual possession or identity</note>, just as there is nothing which is ours of which we must not at some time be composed. This is true if the matter of things is one, within a single genus; or if there are two matters, within two genera. For I do not yet determine whether the substance and matter we call "spiritual" changes into that which we call "corporeal," and vice versa, or truly not.

Thus, all things in their own kind have a total vicissitude <note>term: vicissitude; the natural change or mutation of things from one state to another</note> of dominion and servitude, happiness and unhappiness, of that state called life and that called death, of light and darkness, of good and evil. And there is nothing to which it naturally belongs to be eternal, except for the substance which is matter; to which it no less belongs to be in continual mutation. I do not speak at present of the "supersubstantial" substance <note>original: "sustanza soprasustantiale"; likely referring to the Divine or the One which exists beyond physical matter</note>, but return to speak particularly of this great individual who is our perpetual nurse and mother <note>The Earth</note>, about whom you asked: for what reason does local motion exist?

And I say that the cause of local motion, as much for the whole as for each of its parts, is the goal of vicissitude—not only so that the whole may find itself in all places, but also so that by such means the whole may have all dispositions and forms. For this reason, local motion has most worthily been esteemed the principle of every other mutation and form; and if this were taken away, no other could exist. Aristotle was able to perceive the mutation according to the dispositions and qualities found in all parts of the earth, but he did not understand that local motion which is the principle of those changes. Yet, at the end of the first book of his *Meteorology* <note>original: "Metheora"; Aristotle's treatise on earth sciences</note>, he spoke like one who prophesies and divines; for although he himself sometimes does not understand his own meaning—limping along, as it were, and always mixing something of his own error with the divine fury <note>A state of inspired revelation or poetic madness</note>—he says, for the most part and in the main, the truth. Now let us bring forward what he says that is both true and worthy of consideration, and then we shall add the causes of it, which he was unable to know. "Not always," he says, "do the same..."

<summary>The author argues that all matter is in a state of constant flux and "vicissitude," where parts of the earth move from the center to the surface. # The Ash Wednesday Supper

<page-num>190</page-num>

The same places on the earth are not always moist or dry, but change according to the generation and failure of rivers. Therefore, that which was and is sea has not always been, nor will it always be, sea; and that which will be and has been land is not, nor was it always, land. Instead, with a certain <term>vicissitude</term><note>A regular change or succession of states; a cyclical turning.</note>, a determined circle, and order, one must believe that where one is, the other shall be; and where the other is, the other shall be. And if you ask Aristotle for the principle and cause of this, he responds that the interior parts of the earth, like the bodies of plants and animals, have their period of perfection and then grow old.

116 | But there is a difference between the earth and the other aforementioned bodies; because those, as whole entities, experience progress, perfection, and decline—what he calls their "prime" and "old age"—at one and the same time in all their parts. But in the earth, this happens successively, part by part, with the succession of cold and heat, which causes increase and diminution. This follows the sun and its circuit, through which the parts of the earth acquire different <term>complexions</term><note>In Renaissance thought, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body.</note> and virtues. From this, watery places remain so for a certain time; then they dry up again and grow old, while others are revived and become flooded in certain parts. Hence we see springs vanish, and rivers that were once small become large, and then from large become small and finally dry. And because the rivers fail, it follows by necessary consequence that pools are removed and the seas are changed.

However, because this happens successively across the earth over very long and slow periods of time, our lives and the lives of our fathers can hardly judge it. This is because the age and memory of all peoples fail sooner, and great corruptions and mutations occur—through desolations, wildernesses, wars, pestilences, and floods; alterations of languages and writings, migrations, and the sterility of places—so that we cannot remember these things from beginning to end through such long, varied, and most turbulent centuries.

These great mutations are shown to us clearly enough in the antiquities of Egypt: in the regions of the Nile, all of which (except for the <term>Canopic mouth</term><note>The westernmost branch of the Nile Delta.</note>) were made by the work of human hands; and in the dwellings of the city of Memphis, where the lower places were inhabited after the higher ones. And in Argos and Mycenae, of which at the time of the Trojans the former region was marshy and very few lived there, while Mycenae, being more fertile, was much more honored. In our own times, the opposite is true: for Mycenae is entirely dry, and Argos has become temperate and quite fertile. Now, as happens in these small places, we must think the same regarding great places and entire regions. Therefore, just as we see that many places which were formerly watery are now continents, so too has the sea overtaken many others. We see these mutations happening little by little.

<summary>The text explains the Aristotelian theory of the Earth's cyclical transformation, arguing that land and sea swap places over vast periods of time due to climatic changes. It cites historical examples like the Nile Delta and ancient Greek cities to show how environmental shifts outlast human memory and records.</summary>

At that time, in no place was it suitable for vines; and now it sends forth wines as delicious as other parts of the world; and from the northernmost lands of that region, the fruits of the vineyards are gathered.

And this year I have also eaten grapes from the gardens of London, not indeed as perfect as the worst of France: but yet such as they affirm have never been produced similarly in English soil. From this, then—that the Mediterranean Sea, leaving France and parts of Italy (which I have seen with my own eyes) drier and warmer, goes inclining toward the Balance <note>The zodiac sign Libra, here referring to a shift in the Earth's orientation or celestial influence</note>—it follows that as Italy and France become warmer and warmer, and Britain becomes more temperate, we must judge that generally the conditions of the regions are changing, in that the cold disposition is diminishing toward the Arctic pole.

Ask Aristotle: whence does this happen? He answers: from the sun, and from the circular motion. Not so much confusedly and obscurely, as it was also divinely, loftily, and most truly said by him. But how? Perhaps as by a philosopher? No, but rather as by a diviner; or perhaps by one who understood and did not dare to speak; perhaps like one who sees, and does not believe what he sees, and even if he believes it, hesitates to affirm it, fearing that someone might come to constrain him to provide that reason which he does not have. He reports it, but in a manner by which he shuts the mouth of anyone who would wish to know further. Or perhaps it is a way of speaking taken from the ancient philosophers.

He says, then, that heat and cold, dryness and moisture, increase and decrease over all parts of the earth; in which everything has its renewal, consistency, old age, and diminution: and wishing to provide the cause of this, he says: *Because of the Sun and the Circulation* <note>original Latin: "Propter Solem Et Circvmlationem"</note>. First, then, for its own life and that of the things contained within it—and to provide something like a respiration and inspiration with the diurnal <note>daily</note> heat and cold, light and darkness—in the space of twenty-four equal hours, the Earth moves around its own center, exposing its entire back to the sun as much as possible.

Second, for the regeneration of the things that live and dissolve upon its back, it circles the lucid body of the sun with its center in three hundred and sixty-five days and about a quarter; where, from four points of the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path</note>, it marks the cry <note>the announcement or beginning</note> of the generation, the youth, the maturity, and the decline of its things.

Third, for the renewal of the ages, it participates in another motion by which that relation which this upper hemisphere of the Earth has to the universe comes to be obtained by the lower hemisphere, and the latter succeeds the former.

The first motion is measured from a point on the Earth's equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note>; so that it returns either to the same point, or nearly the same. The second motion is measured from an imaginary point on the ecliptic (which is the path of the Earth around the sun) until it returns to the same, or nearly the same. The third motion is measured by the orientation held by a hemispheric line of the Earth, which serves as the horizon; with its differences relative to the universe, until that same line, or one proportional to it, returns to the same orientation. The fourth motion is measured by the progress of a polar point of the Earth, which, passing through the line of some meridian through the other pole, returns to the same, or nearly the same, aspect where it was before. And

regarding this, it should be considered that although we say there are four motions; nevertheless, they all concur in one composite motion. Consider that of these four motions: The first is taken from that which, in a natural day, makes everything appear to move around the Earth above the poles of the world, as they say. The second is taken from that which makes it appear that the sun in a year circles the entire zodiac, moving every day—according to Ptolemy in the third book of the *Almagest*—fifty-nine minutes, eight seconds, 17 thirds, 13 fourths, 12 fifths, 31 sixths. According to Alfonso <note>Referring to the Alfonsine Tables, 13th-century astronomical tables</note>: Fifty-nine minutes, 8 seconds, 11 thirds, 37 fourths, 19 fifths, 13 sesti, 56 sevenths.

According to Copernicus: fifty-nine minutes, 8 seconds, 11 thirds. The third motion is taken from that which makes the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note> appear to move—according to the order of the signs, contrary to the diurnal motion, above the poles of the zodiac—so slowly that in two hundred years it does not move more than one degree and 28 minutes: so that in forty-nine thousand years it comes to complete the circle; the beginning of which motion they attribute to a ninth sphere. The fourth motion is taken from the trepidation <note>A discarded theory of the oscillation of the equinoxes</note>, access and recess, which they say the eighth sphere makes upon two equal circles, which they imagine in the concavity of the ninth sphere, above the beginnings of Aries and Libra of its zodiac. It is taken from what they see to be necessary: that the ecliptic of the eighth sphere is not always understood to intersect the equinoctial at the same points; but sometimes it is at the head of Aries, sometimes beyond it on one side or the other of the ecliptic. From what they see, the greatest declinations of the zodiac are not always the same: whence it necessarily follows that the equinoxes and solstices continually vary, as has actually been seen for a long time. Consider that although we say these motions are four; nevertheless, it should be noted that they all concur in one composite. Third, returning little by little, and advancing in its path and speed of rotation, or losing and diminishing speed (as happens to a ball that, rising upward, moves more slowly than it did at first, and does the opposite when returning downward, and in a moderate proportion in the middle distances through which it ascends and descends); according to the <term>disposition</term><note>original: "habitudine" - the physical state or orientation</note> held by this half of the circumference, which is marked 1, 2, 3, 4, that other half which is at 5, 6, 7, 8 will follow. You, Frulla, keep our discourses secret; and see to it that they do not reach the ears of those whom we have rebuked, lest they become angry with us and come to give us new occasions to treat them worse and receive a better punishment. You, Master Prudentio, make the conclusion and a moral epilogue only of our four-part dialogue <term>tetralogue: a conversation between four people</term>; because the speculative occasion, taken from the Ash Wednesday Supper, is already concluded.

# The Ash Wednesday Supper

1 to do you service, or pleasure, or favor, should come to spend the night in your
houses: see to it that he is defended by you from such encounters. And
having to return to his lodging through the dark sky: if you do not
wish to have him accompanied by fifty or a hundred torches (which, even
5 if he were to march at midday, would not be lacking if he happened
to die in a Roman Catholic land <note>A jab at the elaborate funeral processions in Catholic countries</note>) at least have him accompanied
by one of them. Or indeed, if this seems too much to you: lend him a
lantern, with a tallow candle inside; so that we may have eloquent
matter to speak of his safe arrival from your houses, of
10 which we have not spoken now.

I adjure you, O Doctors Nundinio and Torquato <note>The two English pedants Bruno debated at the supper</note>, by the feast of
the Cannibals <note>original: "Antropophagi"</note>, by the mortar of the Cynic Anaxarchus <note>Anaxarchus was a philosopher reportedly pounded to death in a mortar</note>, by the immeasurable
serpents of Laocoön, and by the trembling plague-sore of Saint Roch:
that you recall (even if he were in the deep abyss, or were to be there until the
15 Day of Judgment) that rustic and uncivilized pedagogue of ours who 128
gave you your upbringing, and that other Arch-ass and ignoramus who taught you
how to dispute; to the end that they may refund you for your ill-spent expenses, and the interest on the
time and brains they have made you lose. I adjure you, London
boatmen, who with your oars beat the waves of the proud Thames,
20 by the honor of Evenus and Tiberinus, for whom two famous
rivers are named; and by the celebrated and spacious tomb of Palinurus <note>Aeneas's pilot who fell into the sea</note>: that for
our money you guide us to the port. And you other savage Thrasos <note>Braggart soldiers</note> and
fierce followers of Mars <note>original: "Mauortii"</note> among the common people: you are conjured by the caresses that
the Thracian women <note>original: "Strimonie"</note> gave to Orpheus <note>They tore him to pieces</note>. By the last service that the
25 horses gave to Diomedes <note>They ate him</note>, and to the brother of Semele <note>Actaeon, torn by his dogs</note>, and by the power of the stone-turning
shield of Cepheus <note>The Aegis/Medusa's head</note>: that when you see and encounter foreigners and
travelers, if you will not abstain from those grim and Fury-like <note>original: "Erinnici"</note> faces, at
least let abstinence from those shoves and jolts be recommended to you. I return to con-
jure you all together: some by the shield and spear of Minerva; others
30 by the noble offspring of the Trojan Horse; others by the venerable
beard of Aesculapius; others by the trident of Neptune; others by the
kisses that the mares gave to Glaucus <note>Glaucus was devoured by his mares</note>: that another time, with better
dialogues, you may let us perform an anatomy of your deeds; or at least keep silent.

# On the Cause, Principle, and One

### Introductory Epistle,
->written to the most illustrious Lord Michel de Castelnau,<-
->Lord of Mauvissière, Concressault, and Joinville.<-
->Knight of the Order of the Most Christian King,<-
->Member of his Private Council,<-
->Captain of fifty men-at-arms,<-
->and Ambassador to the Most Serene Queen of England.<-

Most illustrious and unique knight, if I turn the eyes of consideration to gaze upon your long-suffering <note>original: *longanimitá*; implying great patience and endurance</note>, perseverance, and solicitude, with which—adding duty to duty and benefit to benefit—you have conquered, bound, and constrained me. You are accustomed to overcoming every difficulty, escaping from any danger whatsoever, and bringing all your most honorable designs to completion; I come to perceive how appropriately that noble device <note>original: *diuisa*; a heraldic motto or emblem</note> suits you, with which you adorn your formidable crest. There, that liquid humor <note>water</note> which wounds gently, while it drips continuously and frequently, by force of perseverance softens, hollows out, tames, breaks, and levels a certain dense, sharp, hard, and rugged stone. <note>A reference to the Latin proverb *Gutta cavat lapidem*—the drop hollows the stone.</note>

If, on the other hand, I call to mind how (leaving aside your other honored deeds) by divine ordinance, high providence, and predestination, you are a sufficient and steadfast defender for me against the unjust outrages I suffer. Here, a truly heroic soul was needed so as not to drop one's arms, despair, and surrender to such a rapid torrent of criminal slanders, with which—at full strength—I have been attacked by the envy of the ignorant, the presumption of sophists <term>sophists: those who use clever but fallacious arguments</term>, the detraction of the malevolent, the murmuring of servants, the whispers of mercenaries, the contradictions of household members, the suspicions of the stupid, the scruples of tale-bearers, the zeal of hypocrites, the hatred of barbarians, the fury of the plebeians, the rages of the common folk, the laments of those struck back, and the cries of those punished. Where nothing else was lacking but a discourteous, mad, and malicious feminine disdain, whose false tears are usually more powerful than any swollen waves and rigid storms of presumption, envy, and...

<meta>This page continues the introductory dedication of Giordano Bruno's "On the Cause, Principle, and One," following his previous works published in London. The tone is defiant and highly metaphorical, typical of Bruno's "Nolano" persona.</meta>

# On the Cause, Principle, and One

...detractions, murmurs, betrayals, angers, indignations, hatreds, and furies <note>original: "furori"</note>; behold, I see you as a solid, firm, and constant rock. Rising and showing your head out of the swollen sea, you are not chipped, moved, or shaken by the angry sky, nor by the horror of winter, nor by the violent shocks of tumid <note>original: "tumide," meaning swollen or rising</note> waves, nor by shrieking aerial storms <note>original: "aerie procelle"</note>, nor by the violent breath of the North Winds. Instead, you grow ever more green, and with similar substance, you are hardened and reclothed. You, therefore, are endowed with a double virtue, through which gentle and pleasant droplets are most powerful, and rigid, tempestuous waves are most vain; through which the fortunate stone renders itself weak against the drops, and the troubled rock rises so powerful against the floods. You are he who provides a safe and tranquil port to the true Muses, and a ruinous reef upon which the false fortifications of the impetuous designs of their enemy sails come to vanish. I, therefore—whom no one could ever accuse of being ungrateful, whom none could reproach as discourteous, and of whom there is no one who can justly complain—I, hated by fools, despised by the vile, blamed by the ignoble, vituperated by rogues, and persecuted by beastly spirits; I, loved by the wise, admired by the learned, magnified by the great, esteemed by the powerful, and favored by the Gods.

I, having been already received, nourished <note>original: "nodrito"</note>, defended, liberated, kept safe, and maintained in port by such great favor from you—as one escaped through your help from a perilous and great tempest—to you I consecrate this anchor, these ropes, these broken sails, and these goods, which are most dear to me and shall be most precious to the future world, so that by your favor they are not submerged by the iniquitous, turbulent Ocean that is my enemy. These, hung in the sacred temple of Fame, just as they will be powerful against the insolence <note>original: "proternia"</note> of ignorance and the voracity of time, so shall they render eternal testimony of your invincible favor. This is so the world may know that this generous and divine offspring—inspired by high intelligence, conceived by regulated sense, and brought forth by the Nolan Muse—has not died in its swaddling clothes because of you, and promises itself life hereafter, so long as this earth with its living back continues turning toward the eternal sight of the other flashing <note>original: "lampeggianti"</note> stars.

Behold that species of philosophy in which is certainly and truly found that which is sought in vain in contrary and diverse systems. And first, with utmost brevity, I offer you through five dialogues everything that seems relevant to the real contemplation of the **Cause, Principle, and One**.

## Argument of the First Dialogue

Wherein in the first dialogue you have an apology, or something of that sort <note>original: "qualch' altro non só che," literally "some other I-know-not-what"</note>, concerning the five dialogues regarding *The Ash Wednesday Supper*, etc.
