In the second Dialogue you have, first, the reason for the difficulty of such knowledge: in order to know how far the object of knowledge is removed from the cognitive power <note>The "cognitive power" refers to the human intellect's ability to perceive and understand truth.</note>.

Second, in what manner and to what extent the principle and cause are clarified by that which is caused and originated. Third, how much the knowledge of the substance of the universe contributes to the notice of that upon which it depends. Fourth, by what means and path we particularly attempt to know the first principle. Fifth, the difference and agreement, identity and diversity, between the meaning of this term (**Cause**) and this term (**Principle**). Sixth, what the cause is which is distinguished into efficient, formal, and final: and in how many ways the efficient cause is named, and with how many reasons it is conceived. How this efficient cause is in a certain way internal to natural things, being nature itself; and how it is in a certain way external to them. How the formal cause is joined to the efficient, and is that through which the efficient operates; and how the same is raised by the efficient from the womb of matter. How the principle, the efficient, and the form coincide in one subject; and how one cause is distinct from the other. Seventh, the difference between the universal formal cause, which is a single [8] soul—through which the infinite universe (as infinite) is not a living being <term>animale: a living creature or ensouled being</term> positively, but negatively—and the particular formal cause which is multipliable, and multiplied unto infinity, which is more perfect the more it exists in a more general and superior subject: whence the great living beings such as the stars must be esteemed, by great comparison, more divine, that is, more intelligent without error, and operators without defect.

Eighth, that the first and principal natural form, formal principle, and efficient nature, is the soul of the universe: which is the principle of life, vegetation, and sense in all things that live, vegetate, and feel. And it is held by way of conclusion, that it is a thing unworthy of a rational subject to be able to believe that the universe and its other principal bodies are inanimate; seeing that from their parts and excrements derive the animals that we call most perfect. Ninth, that there is nothing so lacking, broken, diminished, and imperfect, that—by that which has a formal principle—does not likewise have a soul, although it does not have the act of a "supposit" <note>original: "supposito" - a technical term for an individual substance or self-subsisting person</note> which we call an animal. And it concludes with Pythagoras and others who have not opened their eyes in vain, how an immense spirit, according to diverse reasons and orders, fills and contains the whole. Tenth, it proceeds to make understood that since this spirit is persistent together with matter, which...

<meta>This page continues the summary of the philosophical arguments regarding the nature of substance and the unity of the universe, following the critique of Aristotelian physics.</meta>

<page-num>206</page-num>
-># On Cause, Principle, and the One<-

produced and brought forth by the efficient cause (which can also be indistinct from the substance according to its being). These things have no less a claim to actuality in their sensible and unfolded being, except according to an accidental subsistence. This is because everything that is seen and made manifest through accidents <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not belong to the essence of a thing, such as its color or size.</note> based on dimensions is pure accident; meanwhile, the individual substance remains forever the same, coinciding with individual matter. Hence it is clearly seen that from this "unfolding" or manifestation, we can grasp nothing but accidents; so much so that the "substantial differences" remain hidden, as Aristotle was forced by the truth to admit. In such a way that, if we wish to consider well, we can infer from this that there is but one **omniform substance** <note>original: "omniforme sustanza"; meaning a single substance that can take all possible forms.</note>, one true Being and Entity, which appears according to innumerable circumstances and individuals, showing itself in so many and such diverse subjects.

Sixth, it is shown how far from all reason is that which Aristotle and others like him intend regarding matter "being in potency" <note>The state of being "potentially" something else, which Bruno argues is misunderstood by the Aristotelians.</note>, which for them is certainly nothing. For according to these same men, matter is so permanently fixed that it never changes or varies its being, but rather all variety and mutation happens *around* it; and that which exists after it "could have been" is, even according to them, always the composite <note>The combination of matter and form.</note>. Seventh, the "appetite" of matter is determined, showing how vainly it is defined by those who do not depart from the reasoning taken from the principles and suppositions of those very men who proclaim it to be the "daughter of privation" and similar to the "irreparable greed of a wanton woman" <note>A reference to the Aristotelian metaphor comparing matter's desire for form to a female's desire for a male.</note>.

->## Argument of the Fifth Dialogue<-

In the fifth Dialogue, dealing specifically with **The One**, the foundation of the edifice of all natural and divine knowledge is completed. First, the proposition of the coincidence of matter and form, and of potency and act, is brought forward: so that Being, which is logically divided into "that which is" and "that which can be," is physically undivided, indistinct, and one. And this One is simultaneously infinite, immobile, and indivisible, without difference between whole and part, or between principle and that which is principled. Second, that in the One, a century is not different from a year, nor a year from a moment; a palm's breadth is not different from a stadium <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance.</note>, nor a stadium from a parasang <note>An ancient Persian unit of distance, roughly 3.5 miles.</note>. In its essence, this or that specific being is not one thing and then another; and therefore in the universe there is no number, and therefore the universe is **One**. Third, that in the infinite, the point is not different from the body: because potency is not one thing and act another. There, if the point can move in length, the line in width, and the surface in depth, then the one is long, the other is wide, the other is deep; and every thing is long, wide, and deep.

<summary>This page outlines the concluding arguments of the treatise, asserting that all physical variety is merely "accidental" while the underlying substance remains a single, infinite, and indivisible "One." It critiques Aristotelian views on matter and introduces the concept of the coincidence of opposites in the infinite universe.</summary>

<keywords>substance, accident, potency, act, infinity, the One, Aristotle, matter and form, unity of the universe, physical dimensions</keywords>

# On the Cause, Principle, and Unity.

## To Time.
[21]
Slow old man, and yet swift: closing and releasing:
Should anyone call you good, or call you evil?
You are generous, and you are stingy: the gifts you offer, you take away:
And you who were present as a parent, are present as a slayer:
What was brought forth from your bowels, you hide back within your bowels,
You, who are permitted to seize with your throat what is ready in your lap.
Since you make all things, and since you destroy all things, for this
Could I not call you good? Could I not call you evil?
Furthermore, where you shall be frustrated in your rabid, dire strike,
Threatening with your scythe, refrain from stretching your hands there,
Where no traces of dark Chaos appear pressed down,
Lest you seem good, lest you seem evil.
<note>original: "Lente senex... Chaos atri". This Latin poem personifies Time as Saturn/Cronus, the deity who both births and devours his children, representing the cyclical nature of the material world.</note>

## On Love.
[22]
Love, through whom I discern the truth so high,
Who opens the gates of diamond and of black,
Through the eyes enters my divinity, and through seeing
He is born, lives, is nourished, and has an eternal kingdom.
He makes one perceive all that heaven, earth, and hell hold,
He makes true images of the absent present,
He regains strength, and drawing straight, he strikes,
And always wounds the heart, uncovering every interior.
Therefore, vile commoners, attend to the truth,
Lend your ear to my speech which is not fallacious,
Open, open (if you can) your insane and squinting eyes.
You believe him a child because you understand little.
Because you change so quickly, he seems fleeting to you:
Because you are sightless, you call him blind.
<note>Bruno here reinterprets the "blind" Cupid of courtly love as a divine intellectual force that allows the philosopher to see the underlying unity of the universe.</note>

## Cause, principle, and eternal one,
[23]
From whom being, life, and motion depend:
And which extends in length, in breadth, and in depth
As far as is spoken of in heaven, earth, and hell.
With sense, with reason, with mind I discern
That act, measure, and count do not comprehend
That vigor, mass, and number, which extends
Beyond every inferior, middle, and superior thing.
Blind error, greedy time, wicked fortune,
Deaf envy, vile rage, iniquitous zeal,
<note>The poem breaks off here, listing the worldly obstacles—envy and ignorance—that oppose the philosopher's vision of the Infinite One.</note>

# On Cause, Principle, and Unity

...who say that you take on the voice of a rabid and infuriated dog, besides the fact that sometimes you play the monkey, sometimes the wolf, sometimes the magpie, sometimes the parrot, sometimes one animal, then another: mixing grave and serious subjects—moral and natural, ignoble and noble, philosophical and comic?

**Philotheus:** Do not be surprised, brother, because that was nothing other than a supper <note>Referring to Bruno's previous book, *The Ash Wednesday Supper* (La Cena de le Ceneri)</note> where brains are governed by the affections, which are offered to them by the potency of the flavors and the vapors of the drinks and foods. Therefore, just as the material and corporal supper is, so consequently follows the verbal and spiritual one. Thus, this dialogue has its various and diverse parts, just as that other supper usually has its own; no differently, this one has its own conditions, circumstances, and means, just as that one might have its own.

**Armesso:** Please, make yourself understood.

**Philotheus:** There (as is ordinary and proper) one usually finds things for the salad, for the main course, for fruit, for everyday use, from the kitchen, from the spice-shop; things for the healthy and for the sick. Cold and hot, raw and cooked, from the water and from the earth, domestic and wild, roasted and boiled, ripe and unripe. And things for nourishment alone and for taste, substantial and light, salty and bland, sour and sweet, bitter and pleasant. So here, by a certain consequence, there appeared to you its contradictions and diversities, accommodated to contrary and diverse stomachs and tastes, which might find pleasure in presenting themselves at our symbolic symposium <note>original: "typico symposio"</note>; to the end that there be no one who complains of having arrived in vain, and whoever does not like this part, may take from that other.

**Armesso:** That is true; but what will you say if, in addition, there appear in your banquet—in our supper—things that are good neither for salad nor for the main course, neither for fruit nor for everyday use, neither cold nor hot, raw nor cooked, nor of any value for appetite | or for hunger, nor good for the healthy or the sick; and which clearly do not come from the hands of a cook or an apothecary <note>original: "speciale"</note>?

**Philotheus:** You will see that in this, too, our supper is no different from any other that could exist. Just as there, in the best part of the eating, either some too-hot morsel burns you—so that you must spit it out anew—or, weeping and tearing up, you must send it wandering through the palate until you can give it that cursed shove down the gullet <note>original: "gargazzuolo"</note>; or perhaps a tooth is numbed; or your tongue is intercepted and bitten along with the bread; or some little stone happens to break and lodge itself <note>original: "incalcinarsi"</note> between the teeth, making you reject the whole mouthful; or some fur or hair...

<summary>Philotheus defends the chaotic and "animalistic" style of his philosophical dialogues by comparing them to a real banquet, where diverse tastes and even unpleasant accidents are natural and necessary. He argues that a spiritual or intellectual "supper" must mirror the variety and contradictions of a physical one.</summary>

...of the cook sticks to your palate, making you almost vomit; or some fish bone gets stuck in your windpipe, making you cough gently; or some little bone gets lodged sideways in your throat, putting you in danger of suffocating: so in our dinner (to our common misfortune), things were found corresponding and proportional to those. All of which happens because of the sin of our ancient <term>protoplast<note>From the Greek 'protoplastos,' meaning the first-formed; a reference to Adam as the first human.</note></term> Adam, through whom perverse human nature is condemned to always have distastes joined to tastes.

**Arminio.** Piously and holily spoken. Now, how do you respond to those who say that you are a rabid <term>Cynic<note>The Cynics were a school of ancient Greek philosophers known for their rejection of social conventions and their biting, "dog-like" criticism of others.</note></term>?
**Teofilo.** <note>The text uses 'Phil.' for Philotheus/Teofilo, the author's mouthpiece.</note> I will easily concede, if not all, at least part of this.
**Arminio.** | But you know that it is not as much a disgrace for a man to receive outrages as it is to commit them.

**Teofilo.** It is enough that mine are called "vengeances," and those of others are called "offenses."
**Arminio.** Even the gods are subject to receiving injuries, suffering infamy, and enduring blame; but to blame, to defame, and to injure is the property of the vile, the ignoble, the worthless, and the wicked.
**Teofilo.** This is true; however, we do not injure, but rather we repel the injuries that are done—not so much to us as to despised philosophy—acting in such a way that other displeasures are not added to those already received.

**Arminio.** Do you wish, then, to appear as a biting dog, so that everyone does not dare to molest you?
**Teofilo.** So it is, because I desire quiet, and displeasure displeases me.
**Arminio.** Yes, but they judge that you proceed too rigorously.
**Teofilo.** So that they do not return a second time, and so others may learn not to come and dispute with me, or with anyone else, using such <term>half-measures<note>Original: "mezzi termini." Refers to weak or evasive arguments.</note></term> regarding these conclusions.

**Arminio.** The offense was private; the vengeance is public.
**Teofilo.** It is not unjust for that reason: because many errors are committed in private that are justly punished in public.
**Arminio.** But with this you come to ruin your reputation, and you make yourself more blameworthy than they; because it will be said publicly that you are impatient, whimsical, bizarre, and a scatterbrain.
**Teofilo.** I do not care: as long as they or others are not troublesome to me further. For this reason, I show the Cynic's staff, so that they leave me to my own affairs in peace; and if they do not wish to show me affection, let them at least not come to exercise their incivility upon me.
**Arminio.** Now, does it seem to you that it belongs to a philosopher to stand upon vengeance?

# On Cause, Principle, and Unity. <page-num>215</page-num>

**Philotheo.** If those who harass me were a single Socrates <note>Socrates is invoked here as the ideal, rational interlocutor, contrasting with the "multitude" of ignorant critics.</note>.
**Armesso.** Do you not know that long-suffering and patience befit everyone, through which they come to be like the heroes and eminent gods; who, according to some, take vengeance slowly, and according to others, neither take vengeance nor become angry?
**Philotheo.** You are mistaken in thinking that I was intent on vengeance.
**Armesso.** And what then?
**Philotheo.** I was intent on correction; in the exercise of which we are also like the gods. You know that poor Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and smithing.</note> was granted permission by Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus, king of the gods.</note> to work even on feast days, and that cursed anvil never tires or grows weary of enduring the shocks of so many and such fierce hammers—for no sooner is one raised than the other is lowered—to ensure that the righteous thunderbolts (with which the delinquent and guilty are punished) do not fail.
**Armesso.** There is a difference between you and the blacksmith of Jove and husband of the Cyprian goddess <note>Venus (Aphrodite), who was famously unfaithful to Vulcan.</note>.
**Philotheo.** It is enough that I am perhaps not unlike them in the patience and long-suffering which I have exercised in this matter, not entirely loosening the reins of disdain, nor touching anger with a sharper spur.

**Armesso.** It is not for everyone to be a corrector, especially of the multitude.
**Philotheo.** Say rather: especially when it does not concern them.
**Armesso.** It is said that you should not be meddlesome in a foreign land.
**Philotheo.** And I say two things: First, that one must not kill a foreign physician because he attempts to perform those cures which the locals do not. Second, I say that to the true philosopher, every land is his homeland.
**Armesso.** But what if they accept you neither as a philosopher, nor as a physician, nor as a fellow countryman?
**Philotheo.** That will not stop me from being so.
**Armesso.** Who gives you credit for it?
**Philotheo.** The deities who placed me here, I who find myself here, and those who have eyes and see me here.
**Armesso.** You have very few and little-known witnesses.
**Philotheo.** Very few and little-known are the true physicians; almost all are truly sick. I say again, that they have no right—some to act, others to permit such treatment to be dealt to those who offer honorable wares, whether they be foreigners or not.
**Armesso.** Few recognize these wares.

**Teofilo:** Let us therefore praise antiquity in its own kind, when philosophers were such that they were promoted from that rank to be lawmakers, counselors, and kings. Such were the counselors and kings, who from that state rose to be priests. In these times, the greatest part of priests are such that they themselves are despised, and through them the divine laws are despised; almost all those we see as philosophers are such that they are held in contempt, and through them the sciences come to be held in contempt. **Elitropio:** These other philosophers have not discovered as much, they do not have as much to guard, and they do not have as much to defend. They themselves can easily hold in low esteem that philosophy which is worth nothing, or another that is worth little, or that which they do not know. Since the water is drawn from these three fountains to make beer and ale <term>ceruosa: an archaic term for grain-based beer</term> (of which water even the oxen and horses do not fail to drink), it follows that there is no person who, having stayed less than three or four days in those studies and colleges, does not come to be soaked <note>original: "imbibito," literally saturated or drunk</note> not only by the fountain of Aristotle, but also by those of Pythagoras and Plato.

**Armesso**: Alas, you speak only too much the truth. From this it follows, O **Theophilo**, that doctors <note>original: "dottori"; referring to university professors or those holding doctorates</note> go as cheaply as sardines; for just as they are created, found, and fished out with little effort, so too are they bought for a small price. Now, therefore, such being the common crowd of doctors among us in this age—saving, however, the reputation of some celebrated for their eloquence, their learning, and their civil courtesy, such as a **Tobie Matthew**, a **Culpepper**, and others whom I cannot name—it happens that it is so far from the case that a man, by calling himself "doctor," should be esteemed to have a new degree of nobility, that he is rather suspected of the contrary nature and condition, unless he be personally known. Hence it happens that those who are noble by lineage or other circumstance, even if they add the principal part of nobility, which is learning, are ashamed to take degrees and have themselves called doctors, it being enough for them to be learned. And of these you will find a greater number in the courts than there are pedants to be found in the universities.

**Theophilo**: Do not complain, **Armesso**, because in all places where there are doctors and priests, one finds both kinds of seed; where those who are truly learned and truly priests, though promoted from a low condition, cannot help but be refined <note>original: "incuiuliti"; to be made civil or courtly</note> and ennobled, because science is a most exquisite path to making the human soul heroic. But those others show themselves to be all the more expressly rustic, the more they seem to want to thunder from on high <note>original: "altitonare"; a Latinism for thundering like a god</note> either with a "Divine Father" or like the giant **Salmoneus** <note>In Greek mythology, Salmoneus was a king who tried to imitate Zeus's thunder and lightning</note>, as they strut about like a purple-clad satyr or faun with that terrifying and imperial pretension <note>original: "prosopopeia"</note>; after having determined from the regent's chair to which declination *this*, *that*, and *this nothing* <note>original: "hic, et haec, et hoc nihil"; a satirical play on Latin grammar drills</note> belong.

Here "Rhadamanthus calls the ghosts of the silent" <note>original: "Radamanto umbras uocat ille silentum" — a reference to the judge of the underworld in Virgil's Aeneid.</note>; here Minos, King of Crete, "shakes the urn" <note>original: "urnam mouet" — another Virgilian reference to the judging of souls.</note>. They call the orations to examination and hold discussions on phrases, saying: "These taste of the poet, these of the comic actor; this is grave, this is light; that is the sublime, and that other the humble style of speaking <note>original: "humile dicendi genus"</note>. This oration is harsh; it would be smooth if it were formed thus. This is an infant writer, little studious of antiquity; he does not smell of the man from Arpinum <note>original: "non redolet Arpinatem" — referring to Cicero, who was born in Arpinum.</note>; he lacks the flavor of Latium <note>original: "desipit Latium" — meaning his Latin is not authentic.</note>." This word is not Tuscan; it is not used by Boccaccio, Petrarch, or other approved authors. One does not write *homo* [man], but *omo*; not *honore* [honor], but *onore*; not *Polihimnio*, but *Poliinnio*. With this he triumphs, he is content with himself, and his own deeds please him more than anything else. He is a Jove who looks down from his high watchtower and considers the lives of other men subject to so many errors, calamities, miseries, and useless labors; he alone is happy, he alone lives a celestial life, when he contemplates his own divinity in the mirror of a collection of excerpts, a dictionary, a Calepino, a lexicon, a *Cornucopia*, or a Nizolio <note>These refer to famous Renaissance reference books and dictionaries, such as those by Ambrogio Calepino or Mario Nizolio.</note>. # On the Cause, Principle, and One.
### October 2, 1583

If he laments, he calls himself Heraclitus <note>The "weeping philosopher" of Ephesus</note>; if he disputes, he is called Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher famous for his logic</note>; if he discourses, he is named Aristotle; if he creates chimeras, he is titled Plato; if he bellows a little sermon, he entitles himself Demosthenes; if he construes Virgil, he is Maro <note>Virgil's cognomen</note> himself. Here he corrects Achilles, approves of Aeneas, reproves Hector, exclaims against Pyrrhus, condoles with Priam, argues with Turnus, excuses Dido, commends Achates, and finally, while he **renders word for word** <note>original Latin: "verbum verbo reddit"</note> and strings together a **row of wild synonyms**, he **thinks nothing divine is foreign to him** <note>original Latin: "nihil divinum a se alienum putat" — a play on Terence's famous line about being human</note>. And so, haughtily dismounting from his professor's chair, like one who has arranged the heavens, regulated senates, tamed armies, and reformed worlds, it is certain that were it not for the injury of time, he would achieve with effects what he achieves with opinion. **O times, o customs!** <note>original Latin: "O tempora, o mores"</note> How rare are those who understand the nature of participles, adverbs, and conjunctions! How much time has passed since the reason and true cause was found for why the adjective must agree with the substantive, why the relative must **couple** <note>original Latin: "coire"</note> with the antecedent, and by what rule it is placed now before, now after the speech; and with what measures and in what orders those interjections of **grieving** or **rejoicing** <note>original Latin: "dolentis, gaudentis"</note> are interspersed—*heu, oh, ahi, ah, hem, ohe, hui*—and other seasonings, without which the whole discourse is utterly insipid?

**Et.** <note>The character Elpino</note> Say what you will, and understand it as you please, I say that for the happiness of life it is better to consider oneself Croesus <note>A king of Lydia legendary for his wealth</note> and be poor, than to consider oneself poor and be Croesus. Is it not more conducive to bliss to have a Gourd that seems beautiful to you and satisfies you, than a Leda or a Helen who bothers you and brings you disgust? What does it matter then to these men that they are ignorant and ignobly occupied, if they are all the happier the more they please only themselves? Thus fresh grass is as good to the donkey, and barley to the horse, as **puccia-bread** <note>A coarse, rustic bread</note> and partridge are to you. Thus the pig is as satisfied with acorns and swill as a Jove with ambrosia and nectar. Do you perhaps wish to take these men away from that sweet madness? For such a cure they would soon break your head. I leave aside the question of who knows if this is madness, or that? A Pyrrhonist <note>A follower of the skeptic philosopher Pyrrho</note> said: who knows if our state is death, and that of those we call deceased is life? Likewise, who knows if all happiness and true bliss consists in the proper couplings and positions of the members of speeches?

**Ar.** <note>The character Armesso</note> Thus the world is disposed: we play the Democritus <note>The "laughing philosopher"</note> over the pedants and grammarians; the busy courtiers play the Democritus over us; the carefree monks and priests **act the Democritus** over everyone; and reciprocally the pedants mock us, we mock the courtiers, and everyone mocks the monks; and in conclusion, while one is mad...

# On Cause, Principle, and Unity

...but demonstrating it is difficult. It is a most easy thing to arrange the causes, circumstances, and methods of doctrines; but then our methodologists and analysts execute poorly their "organs" <note>The *Organon* or instruments of logic</note>, principles of methods, and the "art of arts" <note>A traditional term for logic or philosophy</note>.

**Gervasio:** Like those who know how to make such beautiful swords, but do not know how to use them.

**Poliinnio:** Stop there.

**Gervasio:** May your eyes be stopped, so that you may never open them.

**Teofilo:** I say, however, that it is not required of the natural philosopher to bring forth all causes and principles, but only the physical ones, and of these, the principal and proper ones. Therefore, although things are said to have that Cause and that Principle because they depend on the First Principle and Cause, nevertheless there is not such a necessary relationship that from the knowledge of the one, the knowledge of the other is inferred. And thus, it is not required that they be ordered within the same discipline.

**Dixon:** How is this?

**Teofilo:** Because from the knowledge of all dependent things, we cannot infer any other notice of the First Principle and Cause except by way of a most faint "vestige" <note>original: *vestigio*; a trace or footprint left by God in creation</note>. This is because everything derives from His will or goodness, which is the principle of His operation, from which the universal effect proceeds. This same thing can be considered in artificial things, insofar as he who sees the statue does not see the sculptor; he who sees the portrait of Helen does not see Apelles <note>A famous painter of ancient Greece</note>. Instead, he sees the effect of the operation, which comes from the excellence of Apelles' genius (all of which is an effect of the accidents and circumstances of the substance of that man, who, as for his absolute being, is not known at all).

**Dixon:** So much so that to know the universe is like knowing nothing of the being and substance of the First Principle, because it is like knowing the "accidents of accidents" <note>In Aristotelian terms, accidents are non-essential properties; Dixon suggests we are two steps removed from the true Essence</note>.

**Teofilo:** Just so; but I would not want you to imagine that I mean there are accidents in God, or that He can be known as if by His own accidents.

**Dixon:** I do not attribute such a dull wit to you, and I know that it is one thing to say there *are* accidents, another to say they are *His* accidents, and another to say that everything foreign to the divine nature is *like* His accidents. In this last way, I believe you mean the effects of the divine operation; which, although they are the substance of things—indeed, the very natural substances themselves—nevertheless, they are like most remote accidents for the purpose of letting us reach a comprehensive knowledge of the divine supernatural essence.

**Teofilo:** You speak well.

<summary>Teofilo explains that natural philosophy focuses on physical causes rather than the divine essence, arguing that the universe is merely a "trace" or "vestige" of God, much like a painting reveals the skill but not the person of the artist.</summary>

# On the Cause, Principle, and Unity
<page-num>229</page-num>

**Dictionio:** Here then is the situation: regarding the divine substance—both because it is infinite and because it is most distant from those effects which are the final limit of our discursive faculty's path—we can know nothing of it except by way of a "trace" as the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato who emphasized the spiritual over the material.</note> say; of a "remote effect" as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching.</note> say; of "garments" as the Cabalists <note>Practitioners of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note> say; of "shoulders" or "back parts" as the Talmudists <note>Scholars of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> say; and of a "mirror, shadow, and enigma" as the Apocalyptic writers say.

**Teofilo:** Indeed, even more so; because we do not perfectly see this universe—whose substance and principle are so difficult to comprehend—it follows that we know the first principle and cause through its effect with far less certainty than Apelles <note>The most renowned painter of ancient Greece.</note> might be known through his finished statues. For we can see those statues in their entirety and examine them part by part; but we cannot do so with the great and infinite effect of divine power. Therefore, that similarity must be understood without any proportional comparison.

**Dictionio:** So it is, and so I understand it.

**Teofilo:** It will be well, then, to abstain from speaking of such a high matter.

**Dictionio:** I agree, because it is sufficient, morally and theologically, to know the first principle insofar as the supernal gods have revealed it and divine men have declared it. Furthermore, not only every law and theology, but also all reformed philosophies conclude that it is the mark of a profane and turbulent spirit to want to rush headlong into demanding reasons and seeking to define those things which are above the sphere of our intelligence.

**Teofilo:** Well said. But those people are not so much worthy of blame as those others are most worthy of praise: those who exert themselves toward the knowledge of this principle and cause, in order to apprehend its greatness as much as possible by discoursing with the eyes of regulated senses <note>Reasoned observation of the physical world.</note> regarding these magnificent stars and flashing bodies. These are so many inhabited worlds, and great living beings, and most excellent divinities, which seem to be—and are—innumerable worlds not much dissimilar to this one which contains us. Since it is impossible that they have their being from themselves (given that they are composed and dissoluble, though they are not for that reason worthy of being dissolved, as was well said in the *Timaeus* <note>A dialogue by Plato regarding the creation of the world.</note>), it is necessary that they acknowledge a principle and cause. Consequently, by the greatness of their being, living, and acting, they demonstrate and preach in an infinite space, with innumerable voices, the infinite excellence and majesty of their first principle and cause. Leaving aside then (as you say) that consideration insofar as it is superior to every sense and intellect, let us consider the principle and cause insofar as it is a "trace" in nature, or is nature itself.

itself, or rather shines within the scope and bosom of that [nature]. Therefore, ask me in order, if you wish for me to respond to you in order.

**Dixon:** I shall do so. But first, because you are accustomed to saying "cause" and "principle," I would like to know if these are taken by you as synonymous names?

**Theophilus:** No.

**Dixon:** Now then, what difference is there between one term and the other?

**Theophilus:** I respond that when we say God is the first principle and first cause, we mean one and the same thing through different <term>reasons</term><note>original: "raggioni"; here meaning logical perspectives or modes of understanding</note>; when we speak of principles and causes in nature, we speak of different things with their own different reasons. We call God the first principle insofar as all things come after him according to a certain order of prior and posterior, whether according to nature, according to duration, or according to dignity. We call God the first cause insofar as all things are distinct from him as the effect is from the <term>efficient</term><note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being, like a carpenter making a chair.</note>, or the thing produced from the producer. And these two reasons are different, because not everything that is prior and more worthy is the cause of that which is posterior and less worthy; and not everything that is a cause is prior and more worthy than that which is caused, as is quite clear to anyone who reasons well.

**Dixon:** Now tell me, regarding natural subjects, what is the difference between cause and principle?

**Theophilus:** Although at times one is usurped for the other, nevertheless, speaking properly, not everything that is a principle is a cause. For the point is the principle of the line, but it is not the cause of it; the instant is the principle of the operation; the "starting point" is the principle of motion, but not the cause of motion; the premises are the principle of the argumentation, but they are not the cause of it. Therefore, "principle" is a more general term than "cause."

**Dixon:** Therefore, narrowing these two terms to certain proper significations, according to the custom of those who speak more <term>reformedly</term><note>meaning with greater precision or according to the "reformed" philosophical rigor of the era</note>, I believe you mean that a **principle** is that which intrinsically concurs in the constitution of a thing and remains in the effect—such as they say of **matter** and **form**, which remain in the composite, or even the elements from which the thing comes to be composed and into which it is resolved. **Cause**, you call that which concurs in the production of things from the outside, and has its being outside of the composition—such as the **efficient** [cause] and the **end** <note>The "final cause" or purpose for which a thing exists.</note> toward which the produced thing is ordained.

**Theophilus:** Very well.

**Dixon:** Now that we are resolved on the difference between these things, I first desire that you report our intention regarding the causes, and then regarding the principles. And as for the causes, first I would like to know...

...of the first efficient cause, of the formal cause—which you say is joined to the efficient—and furthermore of the final cause, which is understood to be the motivator of the latter.

**T.** I am very pleased with your order of presentation. Now, regarding the effective cause <note>original: "causa effattrice"</note>, I say that the universal physical efficient cause is the **universal intellect**. This is the first and principal faculty of the **soul of the world**, which is the universal form of that soul.

**Di.** You seem to me not only to conform to the opinion of Empedocles <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed the four elements and the forces of Love and Strife.</note>, but to be more certain, more distinct, and more explicit—furthermore (as far as the preceding text shows me) more profound. **T.** The universal intellect is the innermost, most real, and proper faculty and potential part of the soul of the world. This is one and the same thing that fills the whole, illuminates the universe, and directs nature to produce its species in the appropriate way; and so it relates to the production of natural things just as our own intellect relates to the congruent production of rational ideas. This is called by the **Pythagoreans** the mover and agitator of the universe, as the poet explained when he said: *Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the entire mass and mingles itself with the whole body.* <note>original Latin: "Totamque infusa per artus, Mens agitat molem, et toto se corpore miscet." A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, VI.726-727, used here to describe the World Soul.</note> This is named by the **Platonists** the "world-smith" <note>original: "fabro del mondo," referring to the Demiurge or divine craftsman.</note>. This craftsman (they say) proceeds from the higher world (which is entirely one) to this sensible world which is divided into many, where not only friendship but also discord reigns due to the distance between the parts. This intellect, by infusing and extending something of its own into matter—while remaining itself quiet and immobile—produces everything. It is called by the **Magi** <note>Refers to the practitioners of "natural magic" or the Hermetic tradition.</note> the "most fecund of seeds," or even the "sower"; for it is that which impregnates matter with all forms and, according to their reason and condition, comes to figure, form, and weave them with such admirable orders that they cannot be attributed to chance, nor to any other principle that does not know how to distinguish and order. **Orpheus** calls it the "eye of the world," because it sees all natural things within and without, to the end that everything—not only intrinsically but also extrinsically—comes to be produced and maintained in its proper symmetry.

By **Empedocles** it is called the "distinguisher," as one who never tires of unfolding the forms confused within the womb of matter, and of arousing the generation of one thing from the corruption of another. **Plotinus** <note>The founder of Neoplatonism.</note> calls it "father and progenitor," because it distributes the seeds in the field of nature and is the immediate dispenser of forms. By us, it is called the **internal artificer**, because it forms the matter and the figure from within, just as from within the seed or root it sends out and unfolds the trunk.

<summary>This page defines the Universal Intellect as the internal efficient cause of the universe, acting as a "world-smith" that organizes matter from within. It synthesizes various philosophical traditions—Pythagorean, Platonist, Hermetic, and Orphic—to describe how this intellect directs the growth and symmetry of all natural things.</summary>

# On Cause, Principle, and the One

From within the trunk it drives out the branches; from within the branches, the formed boughs; from within these, it unfolds the buds; from within, it forms, shapes, and weaves—as if from nerves—the leaves, the flowers, and the fruits. And from within, at certain times, it recalls its humors from the leaves and fruits back to the boughs, from the boughs to the branches, from the branches to the trunk, and from the trunk to the root. Similarly, in animals, unfolding its labor from the seed first and from the center of the heart to the external members, and from those finally folding the unfolded faculties back toward the heart, it acts as if it were re-gathering the once-extended threads. 

Now, if we believe that a work is not produced without reason and intellect—even a "dead" work <note>The author refers to inanimate art, like sculpture, as "dead" compared to living nature.</note> which we know how to fashion with a certain order and imitation upon the surface of matter, as when by stripping and carving a piece of wood we make the image of a horse appear—how much greater should we believe that artisan intellect to be? That which, from the interior of the seminal matter, hardens the bones, extends the cartilages, hollows out the arteries, breathes into the pores, weaves the fibers, branches the nerves, and with such admirable mastery disposes the whole? How much greater (I say) is this craftsman, who is not attached to only one part of matter, but works continually as a whole in the whole? There are three sorts of intellect: the Divine, which is everything; this Worldly Intellect <note>The *Intellectus Universalis* or World Soul.</note>, which makes everything; and the other particular intellects, which become everything. For it is necessary that between the extremes this middle be found, which is the true efficient cause—not only extrinsic, but also intrinsic—of all natural things.

**Dixon:** I would like to see you distinguish how you understand it as an extrinsic cause, and how as an intrinsic one?

**Teofilo:** I call it an extrinsic cause because, as the efficient cause, it is not a part of the composite things and the products. It is an intrinsic cause insofar as it does not work *upon* matter and outside of it, but as was just said; <margin>whence it is an extrinsic cause</margin> because its being is distinct from the substance and essence of the effects, and because its being is not like that of things that can be generated and corrupted (though it concerns itself with them); it is an intrinsic cause regarding the act of its operation.

**Dixon:** It seems to me you have spoken enough of the efficient cause; now I would like to understand what that thing is which you claim to be the formal cause joined to the efficient? Is it perhaps the "ideal reason" <term>Ideal Reason: The conceptual blueprint or "Idea" in the mind of the creator</term>? For every agent that works according to an intellectual rule does not seek to effect anything except according to some intention; and this is not without the apprehension of something; and this is nothing other than the form of the thing that is to be produced. And therefore, this intellect, which has the faculty to produce all species and to drive them out with such beautiful architecture from potency...

<margin>1</margin> the book entitled *The Fountain of Life* <note>original: "Fonte di uita"; referring to the *Fons Vitae* by the 11th-century philosopher Solomon ibn Gabirol (Avicebron).</note>; these same thinkers, along with the Cyrenaics, Cynics, and Stoics, contend that forms are nothing more than certain accidental arrangements of matter. For a long time, I was a strong adherent to this opinion, solely because it has foundations more <margin>5</margin> in line with nature than those of Aristotle. However, after having considered it more maturely, and having regard for more things, we find <margin>64</margin> that it is necessary to recognize two kinds of substance in nature: one which is **form**, and the other which is **matter**. For there must be a most substantial **act** <note>In philosophy, "act" or "actuality" refers to the realization of a thing's potential.</note>, in which the active power of everything resides, <margin>10</margin> and also a **potential**, and a subject, in which there is no less a passive power for everything. In the former is the power to do; in the latter is the power to be made.

*D.* <note>Dixin, a character representing a thoughtful student of philosophy.</note> It is a manifest thing to anyone who considers carefully that it is impossible for something to always be able to make everything, unless there is always something <margin>15</margin> that can be made into everything. How could the **soul of the world** (I mean every form), which is indivisible, be a shaper without a subject of dimensions or quantity—which is matter? And how could matter be shaped? Perhaps by itself? It seems we could say that matter is shaped by itself, if we choose to consider the <margin>20</margin> entire formed body to be matter—to call it "matter," just as we might call an animal with all its faculties "matter," distinguishing it not from its form, but only from the "efficient cause" <note>The "efficient cause" is the external agent or force that brings about a change or produces an object.</note>.

*T.* <note>Teofilo, the speaker representing Bruno’s own philosophical views.</note> No one can stop you from using the name "matter" in your own way, just as many sects have given various <margin>25</margin> meanings to it. But this way of considering things that you describe—I know it cannot sit well except with a mechanic or a physician who relies on practice, such as one who divides the universal body into **Mercury**, **Salt**, and **Sulfur** <note>These are the "tria prima" or three primary substances in Paracelsian alchemy.</note>. To speak thus does not show so much a divine medical wit | as it might show a most foolish person <margin>65</margin> <margin>30</margin> who wished to be called a philosopher. The philosopher's goal is not to arrive only at that distinction of principles which is physically achieved through the separation produced by the power of fire <note>The "power of fire" refers to chemical or alchemical distillation.</note>; but also at that distinction of principles which no material agent can reach. For the soul, inseparable from Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt, is a **formal principle**. It is not subject to material qualities, but is entirely the master of matter; it is untouched by the work of chemists, whose division ends at the three aforementioned things. They know another kind of soul than this "soul of the world" which we must define.

<margin>1</margin> ignorance, as do Pythagoras, Empedocles, and your Nolan <note>Giordano Bruno often refers to himself as "il Nolano" (the Nolan), as he was born in Nola, Italy.</note>, whose opinions
you touched upon yesterday.
*T.* This is what the Nolan maintains: that there is one intellect that gives being
to every thing, called by the Pythagoreans and in the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato discussing the origin of the universe.</note> the "giver of forms";
<margin>5</margin> one soul and formal principle which becomes and informs <note>To "inform" here means to give internal shape or essence to something.</note> every thing, <margin>74</margin>
called by these same people the "source of forms"; and one matter from which
every thing is made and formed, called by all the "receptacle of forms."
*D.* This doctrine (since it seems to lack nothing at
all) pleases me greatly; and truly it is necessary that just as
<margin>10</margin> we can posit a constant and eternal material principle, we should posit
a similarly eternal formal principle. We see that all natural forms
cease to exist in matter and newly enter into matter;
wherefore it seems that nothing is really constant, firm, eternal, and worthy
of being regarded as a "principle," except for matter. Furthermore,
<margin>15</margin> forms do not have being without matter; they are generated
and corrupted within it; they emerge from its bosom and are gathered back into it.
Therefore, matter—which always remains the same and fertile—must
have the principal prerogative of being known as the sole substantial prin-
ciple: that which is, and which always remains. All forms
<margin>20</margin> together should be understood only as various dispositions of
matter that come and go, some ceasing and others renewing themselves;
hence, they do not all have the reputation of being a principle. Therefore, there have been
those who, having well considered the nature of natural forms
as could be gathered from Aristotle and others like him, have con-
<margin>25</margin> cluded at last that forms are nothing but accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities, like the color of a shirt, which can change without the thing itself ceasing to be what it is.</note> and circumstances of
matter; and therefore the prerogative of "act" and "perfection" should be referred
to matter and not to things of which we can truly say <margin>75</margin>
they are not substance, nor nature, but "things of substance" and "things
of nature." This nature, they say, is matter, which for them is a
<margin>30</margin> necessary, eternal, and divine principle—like that Moor, Avicebron <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol, a Jewish philosopher and poet in Spain known in Latin as Avicebron; Bruno refers to him here as "the Moor" because he lived in Islamic Al-Andalus.</note>, who
calls it "God who is in all things."
*T.* Those people have been led into this error by not knowing
any form other than the accidental one. And this Moor, although he had
accepted "substantial form" from the Peripatetic <note>The Peripatetic school refers to the followers of Aristotle.</note> doctrine
<margin>34</margin> in which he was raised, nevertheless considered it a
<margin>35</margin> corruptible thing—not only changeable in relation to matter, but
as something that is given birth and does not give birth; is founded and does not
found; is rejected and does not reject. He disregarded it, and held it in
contempt in comparison to matter, which is stable, eternal,
the progenitress, the mother. And certainly, this happens to those who do
<margin>40</margin> not know what we know.

*Dic.* This has been very well considered: but it is time that <margin>1</margin>
we return from the digression to our purpose. We know now how to

matter, one could allow that other way and manner of philosophizing

understand it as a divine thing; and not as something so purely
formless that it does not form and clothe itself. <margin>10</margin>
**76** *T.* Not easily, | because nothing operates absolutely upon itself,
and there is always some distinction between that which is the agent and
that which is made, or that upon which the action and operation occur: wherefore
it is well to distinguish matter from the soul in the body of nature; and
in the soul to distinguish that principle of the species. Thus we say that in <margin>15</margin>
this body there are three things: First, the universal intellect indwelling in things;
Second, the soul that gives life to the whole; Third, the subject. But we
will not for this reason deny that he is a philosopher who takes as the
genus of his philosophizing this formed body, or (as we might call it) this
rational animal, and begins to take as first principles in some <margin>20</margin>
way the members of this body—such as, for instance, air, earth, fire;
or the ethereal region and the stars; or spirit and body; or the <term>vacuum</term>
and the plenum <note>The "plenum" refers to a space entirely filled with matter, while the "vacuum" is empty space; Bruno argued for an infinite universe containing both, unlike Aristotle.</note>: understanding the vacuum, however, not as Aristotle
took it, but in another appropriate way. That philosophy will not
seem to me worthy of being rejected, especially when, upon whatever <margin>25</margin>
foundation it presupposes, or whatever form of building it proposes,
it comes to achieve the perfection of <term>speculative science</term> <note>This refers to the theoretical study of nature and the search for underlying truths through reason rather than just practical application.</note> and the
knowledge of natural things, as has indeed been done by many more
ancient philosophers. Because it is the mark of an ambitious and presumptuous,
vain, and envious mind to wish to persuade others that there is only one <margin>30</margin>
way to investigate and arrive at the knowledge of nature; and it is the
mark of a fool and a man without reason to convince himself of this.
**77** Although, | then, the more constant, firm, contemplative, and
distinct way, and the higher mode of consideration, should always be
preferred, honored, and sought after more; nevertheless, that other <margin>35</margin>
way is not to be blamed, which is not without good fruit, even if it
is not from the same tree.
*D.* Then you approve of the study of diverse philosophies?
*T.* Greatly, for those who have an abundance of time and talent; to others, I
approve the study of the best, if the gods will that they find it. <margin>40</margin>

<summary>Theophilo argues that while matter and form (soul) are distinct in nature, various philosophical systems—even those focusing on physical elements—are valid if they lead to an understanding of nature. He emphasizes that there is no single "correct" path to scientific truth and warns against intellectual arrogance.</summary>

<margin>1</margin> *D.* I am certain, however, that you do not approve of all philosophies, but only the good and the best ones.
*T.* So it is. Just as in the various systems of medicine, I do not reject that which is done magically through the application of roots, the hanging of <margin>5</margin> stones, and the murmuring of incantations—if the rigor of the theologians allows me to speak as a pure naturalist <note>original: "puro naturale"; Theophilo is distancing himself from religious dogma to speak strictly as a scientist or philosopher of nature.</note>. I approve of what is done physically, proceeding by apothecary recipes, by which one pursues or expels <term>choler</term>, <term>blood</term>, <term>phlegm</term>, and <term>melancholy</term> <note>These are the "four humors" of ancient medicine, believed to control health and temperament.</note>. I accept that other method which is done chemically, which extracts the <term>quintessences</term> and, through the work <margin>10</margin> of fire, makes <term>Mercury</term> fly from all those compounds, <term>Salt</term> settle, and <term>Sulfur</term> flare or dissolve <note>original: "Mercurio, sale, solfro"; these are the three principles of Paracelsian alchemy.</note>. But yet, regarding medicine, I do not wish to determine among so many good ways which might be the best; because the epileptic, upon whom the physician and the chemist have wasted their time, if he is cured by the mage, will approve—not without <margin>15</margin> reason—of this one more than that or the other doctor. Similarly, you may reason through the other species of knowledge: none of which shall be less good than another, if both one and the others come to effect the **60\*** end they propose. In the end, that doctor is better for me who heals me, than the others who would kill or torment me.
<margin>20</margin> *G.* Why does it happen that these sects of doctors are such enemies to one another?
*T.* From greed, from envy, from ambition, and from ignorance. Commonly, they barely understand their own method of healing, so much so that they are far from being able to judge that of others. Besides, <margin>25</margin> the majority, being unable to rise to honor and profit by their own virtues, study how to prefer themselves by lowering others, making a show of despising that which they cannot acquire. But among these, the best and true one is he who is not so much a "physician" <note>In this context, a "physician" refers to one trained in traditional Galenic medicine.</note> that he is not also a chemist and a mathematician. Now, to come to our point: among the species <margin>30</margin> of philosophy, that one is the best which most conveniently and loftily effects the perfection of the human intellect, and is most corresponding to the truth of nature, and as much as possible is a cooperator with her. This is done either by divining (I mean by natural order and the reason of <term>vicissitude</term> <note>original: "uicissitudine"; the constant cycle of change and transformation in the universe.</note>; not by animal instinct like the beasts and those who are like them; <margin>35</margin> nor by the inspiration of good or evil demons, as the prophets do; nor by melancholic enthusiasm, as the poets and other contemplatives do), or by ordaining laws and reforming customs, or by healing, or even by knowing and living a more blessed and more divine life. Behold, then, how there is no kind of philosophy that has been ordained by a regulated <margin>40</margin> sentiment | which does not contain within itself some good property. **79**

**Theophilo.** Certainly, this principle which is called matter can be considered <insert>81</insert> in two ways: First as a power <note>The Italian *potenza* refers to "potency" or "potential"—the capacity for something to become something else.</note>, and second as a subject. <margin>15</margin> active, through which the subject of that power can operate; and into passive, through which it can be, or can receive, or can have, or can be the subject of an efficient cause <note>An "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being, like a carpenter making a chair.</note> in some manner. Not speaking of active power at present, I say that the power which signifies in a passive way (though it is not always passive) can be considered either relatively 
<margin>20</margin> or absolutely; and thus there is nothing of which one can speak of "being" of which one does not also speak of the "possibility of being." This corresponds to active power in such a way that the one is never without the other in any way; thus, if there has always been the power to make, to produce, and to create, there has always been the power to be made, produced, and created; because 
<margin>25</margin> one power implies the other; I mean that by being posited, it <insert>82</insert> necessarily posits the other. This power, because it does not imply weakness in that of which it is spoken but rather confirms virtue and efficacy—indeed, in the end, it is found to be all one and the very same thing as active power—there is no philosopher or theologian who doubts attributing it 
<margin>30</margin> to the first supernatural principle <note>The "first supernatural principle" refers to God or the Absolute.</note>. Because the absolute possibility by which things that are in act <note>The state of "act" or "actuality" means something fully realized or currently existing.</note> can exist is not prior to actuality, nor even after it; furthermore, the "being able to be" exists alongside "being in act" and does not precede it; for if that which can 
<margin>34</margin> exist made itself, it would exist before it was made. Now contemplate 
<margin>35</margin> the first and best principle, which is all that it can be: and it itself would not be everything if it could not be everything; in him, therefore, act and power are the same thing. It is not so in other things, which, although they are what they can be, could perhaps not be; and certainly they could be other, or otherwise than

Man is what he can be, but he is not everything he can be.
A stone is not everything it can be, because it is not lime, it

other than a shadow of the first act and first power, and for that reason, within it <margin>20</margin>

be according to an unfolded, dispersed, and distinct mode. Its Principle 
is so unitedly and indifferently; because everything is everything, and the same <margin>25</margin>

the whole—that which can be, and is in act, everything that is in potency?
**84 T.** These things are not act and power; but are defect and <margin>30</margin>
impotence <note>The lack of power or ability.</note>, which are found in unfolded things, because they are not everything 
they can be, and they struggle toward what they could be. 
Therefore, not being able to be so many things at once and in a single moment, 
they lose one being to have another: and sometimes they confuse 
one being with another, and sometimes they are diminished, lacking, and <margin>35</margin>
crippled, because of the incompatibility of this being and that, and the 
occupation of matter in this and that. Now returning to the point, 
the first absolute principle is greatness; it is magnitude: and it is such 
magnitude and greatness that it is everything it can be. It is not great 
with a greatness that could be greater, nor could it be smaller... <margin>40</margin>

# On Cause, Principle, and the One.
<page-num>259</page-num>
<header>On Cause, Principle, and the One.</header>

<margin>1</margin> [smaller] <note>The text continues from "minore" (smaller) on the previous page.</note>, nor can it be divided, like any other magnitude that is not 
everything it can be; therefore, it is the maximum, minimum, and infinite magnitude, 
indivisible, and the source of every measure. It is not greater, for it is the minimum; 
it is not the minimum, because it is that same maximum. It is beyond all equa-
<margin>5</margin> lity, because it is everything that it can be. What I say of 
magnitude, you must understand for everything else that can be said, because it is similarly 
goodness which is every goodness that can be; it is beauty which is all the 
beauty that can be; and there is no other beauty that is everything it 
can be, except this One. The One is that which is everything and can 
<margin>10</margin> be everything absolutely. In natural things we see nothing 
else that is other than what it is in act <note>In Aristotelian terms, "act" or "actuality" refers to what a thing currently is, while "potency" refers to what it has the potential to become.</note>, according to which it is what 
it can be by having a certain kind of actuality; <gloss>85</gloss> nevertheless, in 
this unique specific being, no particular thing is ever everything it can be. 
Behold the sun: it is not everything that the sun can be; 
<margin>15</margin> it is not everywhere the sun can be, because when it is at the eastern horizon 
to the earth, it is not at the west, nor the meridian, nor at any other aspect. 
Now, if we wish to show the way in which God is the sun, we will say 
(because He is all that He can be) that He is simultaneously east, west, 
meridian, midnight <note>original: *merinottiale*; referring to the point of the sun at midnight.</note>, and every one of all the points of the cur-
<margin>20</margin> vature of the earth. Therefore, if we wish to understand that this sun moves 
and changes location (either by its own revolution or 
that of the earth), it is because it is not actually in one point without the potency of being in all 
the others, and therefore it has the capacity to be there. If, then, it is all that 
it can be, and possesses all that it is capable of possessing, it will be 
<margin>25</margin> simultaneously everywhere and in everything. It is so perfectly "most mobile" and "most 
swift" that it is also "most stable" and "most immobile." Therefore, among the divine 
discourses we find it said that He is stable in eternity, and most swift, running 
from end to end <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 7:24, describing the Spirit of God or Wisdom as both perfectly still and swifter than any motion.</note>; because that which, in the very same 
instant, departs from the point of the East and has returned to the point 
<margin>30</margin> of the East, is understood to be immobile. Furthermore, it is seen no less in the East than in the West,

For this reason, Protagoras, <note>A famous Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher.</note> when asked why he had given his daughter to an enemy, replied that he could do nothing worse to him than give him a wife. Furthermore, a good Frenchman will not make me a liar; when he (like all others suffering a most dangerous storm at sea) was commanded by Cicala, the master of the ship, to throw the heaviest things <margin>95</margin> | into the sea, he was the first to throw in his wife.

**Gervasio:** Do you not report, on the contrary, so many other examples of those who have considered themselves most fortunate because of their women? What will you say of his noble daughter, who has barely seen the sun for a lustrum and a year? <note>A "lustrum" is five years; the daughter, Catherine-Marie, is six years old here.</note> By her speech, you could not judge if she is from Italy, France, or England. By her hand upon musical instruments, you could not tell if she is a corporeal or incorporeal substance. By the mature goodness of her manners, you would doubt whether she descended from heaven or sprang from the earth. Everyone sees that in her, for the formation of such a beautiful body, the blood of both parents has met, just as the virtues of their heroic souls have met for the building of her singular spirit.

<margin>15</margin> This was also understood in part by <term>Plotinus</term><note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism.</note>, the prince of the Platonic sect. But this [inferior] matter, through a certain <term>vicissitude</term><note>The constant change or shifting of states.</note> of its parts, becomes everything; at different times, it becomes one thing and then another, though <margin>20</margin> always under the conditions of diversity, alteration, and motion. But nature makes everything from its matter by way of separation, of birth, of efflux, as the Pythagoreans understood, as Anaxagoras and Democritus grasped, and as the Sages of Babylon confirmed. To these Moses also subscribed, who, in describing the generation of things commanded by the universal efficient [cause], uses this way of speaking: 30 **Let the earth produce its animals, let the waters produce living souls.** It is as if he said "let matter produce them": because, according to him, the material principle of things is water. Thus he says that the efficient intellect (which he calls "spirit") brooded over the waters; that is, he gave them procreative power, and from them produced the natural species, which 35 all then are called by him, in substance, "waters." Whence, speaking of the separation of the lower and upper bodies, he says that the mind separated the waters from the waters, from the midst of which he suggests the dry land appeared. All, then, by way of separation, maintain that things come from matter, and not by way of addition and reception. Therefore, 40 one should rather say that matter contains the forms and includes them, than thinking...

<margin>25</margin> one does not desire what one already possesses). Indeed, she abominates more powerfully than she desires, seeing as she eternally rejects that specific form which she held for only a short time.
<margin>30</margin> Therefore, if you will remember that for as many as she takes, she rejects just as many, you must allow me to say she feels disgust for them, just as I will let you say she feels desire.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Fifth Dialogue. # On Cause, Principle, and the One.
## Fifth Dialogue.

<margin>1</margin> **Teofilo.** The universe is, therefore, one, infinite, and immobile. One, I say, is the <term>absolute possibility</term><note>The total potential for anything to exist or happen.</note>, and one is the <term>act</term><note>The actual realization or existence of things.</note>. One is the form or soul; one is the matter or body. One is the thing; one is the <term>being</term><note>The Latinate term "ente" refers to the fundamental state of existing.</note>. One is the greatest and
<margin>5</margin> best: which must be beyond comprehension, and therefore unlimitable and interminable; and for that reason infinite and unbounded; and consequently immobile. It does not move locally, because it has nothing outside of itself to which it might be transported, seeing as it is the whole. It is not generated, because there is no other being that it could desire or expect, seeing as
<margin>10</margin><margin>117</margin> it possesses | all being. It does not perish, because there is no other thing into which it could change, seeing as it is everything. It cannot diminish or grow, seeing as it is infinite; just as nothing can be added to it, so nothing can be subtracted from it: because the infinite has no proportional parts. It cannot be altered into any other disposition, because it has no
<margin>15</margin> external force by which it might suffer or be affected. Moreover, by comprising all <term>contraries</term><note>The idea that opposing forces (like hot and cold, or beginning and end) are unified within the infinite whole.</note> in its being, in unity and harmony, and having no inclination toward any other or new way of being, or even toward another mode of being, it cannot be the subject of change according to any quality, nor can it have a contrary or
<margin>20</margin> diverse force that alters it: because in it, everything is in agreement. It is not matter, because it is neither shaped nor shapeable, neither bounded nor boundable. It is not form, because it does not inform or give shape to anything else, seeing as it is everything, it is the greatest, it is one, it is the universe. It is not measurable, nor is it a measure. It does not contain itself, because it is not greater than itself. It is not
<margin>25</margin> contained, because it is not smaller than itself. It is not equaled, because it is not "this" and "that" separately, but one and the same. Being the same and one, it does not have different types of being; and because it does not have different types of being, it does not have different parts; and because it has no parts, it is not a composite. This is a boundary such that it is not a boundary; it is form in such a way that it is not
<margin>30</margin><margin>118</margin> form; it is matter in such a way that it is not matter; it is soul in such a way that it is not soul: because it is everything indifferently, and | therefore it is one; the universe is one. # On Cause, Principle, and the One.

<margin>1</margin> If you wish to speak of a "part" of the infinite, you must call it infinite; for if it is infinite, it coincides in a single being with the whole. Thus, the universe is one, infinite, and indivisible. And if within the infinite no difference is found, such as between the whole and a part, or between one thing and another, then certainly the infinite is one. Under the
<margin>5</margin> comprehension of the infinite, there is no "larger" part and "smaller" part; because no part, however large it may be, is any closer to the proportion of the infinite than any other part, however small. Therefore, in infinite duration, the hour does not differ from the day, the day from the year, the year from the century, or the century from the moment; for there are no more
<margin>10</margin> moments and hours than there are centuries, and the former have no less a proportion than the latter to eternity. <meta>This page continues the Fifth Dialogue of Giordano Bruno's "On Cause, Principle, and the One." # On Cause, Principle, and the One.

<margin>1</margin> because of this, Being is not more than one: but many-moded, many-formed,
and many-shaped. However, by considering deeply with the 
<term>natural philosophers</term><note>The "Physici," those who study nature (physis) rather than just abstract logic.</note>,

<term>Solomon</term><note>The biblical king; Bruno refers to the book of Ecclesiastes.</note> who says there is nothing new under the sun: but that which is, was

<margin>15</margin> everything concurs in a perfect unity. Behold how we should not 
trouble our spirit; behold how there is nothing for which we

<margin>1</margin> On the contrary, the quadrangle is resolved into triangles) and therefore the triangle is the first foundation of every bounded and shaped thing. Leaving aside the comparison between different types of figures, I speak of triangles compared to other triangles: and taking angle for angle, all (however large or small) are equal, as appears in this **137** <margin>15</margin> square which is divided by the diameter into so many triangles. There, one sees that not only are the right angles of the three squares A, B, and C equal, but also all the acute angles that result from the division of said diameter, which constitutes twice as many triangles, all with equal angles. | Hence, by a <margin>20</margin> very clear analogy, one sees how the one infinite substance can be entirely in all things, although in some it is finite <note>original: "finita"</note>, and in others infinitely; in some with a smaller measure, and in others with a larger measure. Join <margin>25</margin> to this (to see further how in this "one" and "infinite," the opposites coincide) the fact that the acute angle and the obtuse angle are two opposites. Do you not see how they arise <margin>30</margin> from one, individual <note>Meaning "indivisible" in this context.</note>, and the same principle? That is, from a tilt made by the perpendicular line M, which joins the horizontal line BD at point C? This perpendicular line, upon that point, with a simple tilt toward point D—after it had previously formed two identical right angles—now comes to make a <margin>35</margin> much greater difference between the acute and obtuse angle the closer it approaches the point C. Once it is joined and united with the base line, it creates an "indifference" between acute and obtuse; both are similarly nullified, because they are one in the potentiality of the same line. Just as that line was able to unite and <margin>40</margin> become indifferent with the line BD, so it can disunite and become different from it, arising from the same, one, and individual principle.

**139 |** As for the proofs, then: who does not first know, regarding the primary active qualities of corporeal nature, that the principle of heat is indivisible, and therefore separate from all heat; for the principle must not be any of the things it principles? <note>In Aristotelian and Neoplatonic logic, the "principle" or source of a quality cannot itself be defined by that quality; the source of heat is not "hot" in the way a heated object is.</note> If this is so, <margin>10</margin> who should hesitate to affirm that the principle is neither hot nor cold, but one and the same for both heat and cold? From this it follows that one contrary is the principle of the other, and that therefore transmutations are circular; for what <margin>15</margin> reason, if not because there is one subject, one principle, one term, one continuation, and a meeting point of both? From the limit of maximum heat, does not the principle of motion toward cold begin? Hence it is clear that not only do the two maximums sometimes coincide in resistance, and the two minimums in agreement; but even the maximum and the minimum meet through the cycle of transformation. Thus, not without cause do doctors usually fear in the best of health, and the prudent are most timid in the <margin>25</margin> supreme degree of happiness. <note>Bruno suggests that reaching a peak or extreme is the very moment one begins to slide toward the opposite state.</note> Who does not see that there is one principle for corruption and generation? Is not the end of the corrupted the beginning of the generated? Do we not say that as one is removed, the other is placed: "that was, this is"? Certainly (if we measure well) we see that corruption is nothing but a <margin>30</margin> generation, and generation is nothing but a corruption. Love is a hate, and hate is a love in the end. The hatred of the contrary is the love of the convenient; <margin>32</margin> **140** the love of this is the hatred of that. From where does the physician more conveniently seek the antidote than from the <margin>35</margin> poison? In the greatest poisons are the best medicines. Is not a single power directed toward two contrary objects? # On Cause, Principle, and the One.

II dela

*Pol.* Excellent. <note>original Latin: *Optimé*</note> <margin>1</margin>
*Ge.* Here I am, made wise; for just as he who does not understand the "One" understands nothing: so he who truly understands the "One" understands everything; and he who draws nearer to the intelligence of the "One," approaches closer to the apprehension of the whole. <note>In Bruno's philosophy, "the One" refers to the singular, divine substance that constitutes the entire universe, regardless of how many different forms we see on the surface.</note> <margin>5</margin>

*Th.* Praised be the gods, and magnified by all living things be the infinite, most simple, most unified, most high, and most absolute Cause, Principle, and One. <margin>10</margin>
