If I (O most illustrious Knight) handled the plow, grazed a flock, cultivated a garden, or mended a garment: no one would watch me, few would observe me, by rare men would I be rebuked, and <margin>10</margin> I could easily please everyone. But for being a delineator of the field of nature, solicitous regarding the pasture of the soul, desirous of the cultivation of the wit, and a Daedalus <note>In Greek mythology, Daedalus was a master craftsman and inventor; Bruno uses this to describe his intricate work on the structures of the mind.</note> regarding the habits of the intellect: behold, one <margin>[4]</margin> eyes and threatens me, one observes and | attacks me, one reaches and bites me, one seizes and devours me; it is not one, it is not a few, they are many, <margin>15</margin> they are almost all. If you wish to understand why this is; I tell you that the cause is the general crowd which displeases me, the common rabble I hate, the multitude that does not content me, and the One <note>original: "una". In Italian, this is feminine, referring to Truth (La Verità) or Wisdom (La Sapienza).</note> with whom I am in love. She is the one for whom I am free in subjection, content in pain, rich in necessity, and alive in death; she is the one for whom I do not envy those who are <margin>20</margin> slaves in liberty, have pain in pleasures, are poor in riches, and dead in life; because in their bodies they have the chain that binds them, in their spirit the hell that depresses them, in their soul the error that sickens them, and in their mind the lethargy that kills them: there being no magnanimity that might liberate them, no perseverance that might lift them, no splendor that might <margin>25</margin> enlighten them, nor science that might give them life. Hence it happens that I do not pull back my foot as one weary from the arduous path, nor as one lazy do I lower my arms from the work that presents itself, nor as one desperate do I turn my back to the enemy who opposes me, nor as one dazzled do I divert my eyes from the divine object: while for the most part I feel myself reputed a sophist, <note>A term of abuse in Bruno's time for someone who uses clever but false arguments. Bruno's critics accused him of being more interested in sounding smart than being truthful.</note> more <margin>30</margin> studious of appearing subtle than of being truthful; an ambitious man who studies more...

This shall be manifested by the demonstrative arguments which depend upon lively reasons, which derive from regulated sense, which comes informed by no false appearances, which like true ambassadors set out from the subjects of nature; making themselves present to those who seek them, open to <margin>20</margin> those who gaze upon them, clear to him who learns them, certain to him who comprehends them. Now behold, I offer you my contemplation concerning the infinite universe and innumerable worlds.

### Argument of the First Dialogue.

You have then in the first dialogue: first, that the inconstancy of the <margin>25</margin> sense shows that it is not the principle of certainty, and it achieves certainty only through a definite comparison and conference of one object of sense <insert>[6]</insert> to another, and one sense to another, and it is inferred how the truth resides in different subjects.

Second, one begins to demonstrate the infinity of the universe, and <margin>30</margin> the first argument is taken from the fact that those who, by the work of the imagination <term>Phantasia: the mental faculty that allows humans to visualize concepts, which Bruno argues can be misled by finite boundaries.</term>, wish to build walls for the world, do not know how to end it.

Third, the second argument is taken from how it is inappropriate to say that the world is finite and that it is within itself: because this belongs to the Immense <note>In Bruno's philosophy, "the Immense" usually refers to the infinite nature of God or the Universe itself.</note> alone. Next, the third argument is taken from the <margin>35</margin> inappropriate and impossible imagining of the world as being in no place; because in any case it would follow that it has no being: since everything, whether corporeal or incorporeal; is either corporeally or incorporeally in a place. The fourth argument is taken from a very urgent demonstration or question posed by the Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus, who argued for an infinite universe and the existence of "atoms and the void."</note>.

Therefore, it possesses "act" <term>atto</term>, because no potentiality is eternal without <margin>25</margin> act; and thus it has its act eternally joined to it. Indeed, if we consider it well, the senses themselves present it as infinite: because we always see one thing bounded by another, and we never perceive, with either external or internal sense, any thing that is not bounded by something else or something similar.

In the second part of this dialogue, what is demonstrated by the passive power of the universe is shown by the active power of the efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is a philosophical term for the agent or force that brings something into being; here, Bruno refers to God.</note>, with several reasons, of which the first is taken from the fact<margin>10</margin> that divine efficacy should not be idle: and all the more so when placing an effect outside its own substance (if indeed anything can be outside it) and that He is no less idle and envious <note>In this context, "envious" (original: *invidiosa*) carries the Platonic sense of "begrudging" or "withholding" goodness by not creating to His full potential.</note> in producing a finite effect than in producing nothing. And the difference between the "infinite whole" and the "totally infinite" is provided. <note>Bruno argues that the Universe is an "infinite whole" because it is unbounded in size, but only God is "totally infinite" because He is infinite in every attribute and in every part of Himself.</note> The fourth: that no less for lack of will than for lack of power, omnipotence is blamed for having made the world<margin>20</margin> finite, and for being an infinite agent acting upon a finite subject. The sixth is the inverse of the tenth of the first part, and the cause is provided for why the theologians defend the contrary, not without expedient reason: and of the friendship between these scholars and the learned philosophers.

## Argument of the Second Dialogue.

The second dialogue pursues the same conclusion. First, it brings
<margin>5</margin> forth four reasons, the first of which is taken from the fact that all the attributes of divinity are as one <note>This refers to the theological concept of "divine simplicity," where God's attributes—like power, goodness, and infinity—are identical with His essence rather than being separate parts.</note>. The second, that our imagination should not be able to extend further than divine action. The third, from the indifference <note>In this context, "indifference" means that the divine intellect does not distinguish between creating something finite or infinite in terms of effort or capacity; both are equally possible for God.</note> of the divine intellect and action: and from the fact that He understands the infinite no less than the finite. The fourth, from the fact that if
<margin>10</margin> corporeal quality has infinite active power—that is, the quality sensible to us—then what will become of the whole, which resides in the absolute active and passive power? Second, it shows that a corporeal thing cannot be bounded by an incorporeal thing; but only by a vacuum or by a plenum <note>A "plenum" is a space completely filled with matter, the opposite of a vacuum.</note>: and in every case, beyond the world there is space, which in the end is nothing other than matter
<margin>15</margin> and the same passive power <note>By "passive power," Bruno refers to the capacity of matter to be shaped or to receive action, as opposed to the "active power" of the creator.</note>, where the non-envious and non-idle active power must realize itself in action. And it demonstrates the vanity of Aristotle's argument regarding the impossibility of dimensions. Third, it teaches the difference between the world and the universe, because whoever calls the universe "one and infinite" necessarily distinguishes between these two terms <note>Bruno distinguishes between the "world" (a single planetary system) and the "Universe" (the infinite whole containing many worlds).</note>. | Fourth **[13]**
<margin>20</margin> it brings forth the contrary reasons for which the universe is judged to be finite: where Elpino reports all the opinions of Aristotle, and Philotheo goes about examining them. Some of these are taken from the nature of simple bodies, others from the nature of composite bodies: and it shows the vanity of six arguments taken from the definition of motions that cannot be
<margin>25</margin> infinite, and from other similar propositions, which are without purpose or foundation: as is seen by our reasons, which more naturally will reveal the logic of the differences and the limits of motion: and as far as the occasion and place allow, they show the most real knowledge of the impulse of heavy and light things <note>Referring to the concepts of gravity and levity (buoyancy) as understood in Renaissance physics.</note>: because through these we
<margin>30</margin> show how the infinite body is neither heavy nor light, and how the finite body receives such differences, and how it does not. And from this, the vanity of the arguments of Aristotle becomes clear, who, arguing against those who posit an infinite world, assumes a center and a circumference, and insists that in the finite or infinite, the earth must occupy the center. In conclu-
<margin>35</margin>sion, there is no argument, great or small, that this philosopher has brought to destroy the infinity of the world—whether from the first book of *On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "cielo et mondo"; refers to Aristotle’s *De Caelo*.</note> or from the third of the *Physics* <note>original: "physica ascoltatione"; refers to Aristotle’s *Physica*.</note>—concerning which there is not more than enough discussion.

<margin>1</margin> ...regarding the shape, the spheres, and the diversity of the heavens. It is affirmed that there is only one heaven, which is a general space that embraces infinite worlds, although we do not deny—indeed we affirm—infinite heavens, taking this word <note>The word "heaven" or "cielo" was traditionally used to refer to the solid crystalline spheres. Bruno redefines it as the local region of space surrounding any given star or planet.</note> in a different sense: for just as this earth has its own <margin>5</margin> heaven, which is its region in which it moves and through which it travels, so does every one of all the other innumerable worlds. It becomes clear from where the imagination of so many such moving deferents <note>In the old Ptolemaic system, a "deferent" was the large circular path along which a planet's smaller orbital circle (epicycle) moved. Bruno rejects these as mathematical fictions.</note> arose—spheres shaped so as to have two external surfaces and one internal cavity, and other recipes and medicines that cause nausea and horror even to <margin>10</margin> those who order and execute them, and to the wretched souls who must swallow them.

->Secondly, it is noted that the general motion, and that of the said<-
eccentrics, and as many as can be referred to the said firmament, are all imaginary. They really depend on a motion that the Earth makes with its center along the ecliptic, and four other variations of motion that it <margin>15</margin> makes around the center of its own mass. From this it follows that the proper motion of each star is derived from the difference that can be verified subjectively within itself as something moving on its own through the spacious field. This consideration makes us understand that all the reasons for an <margin>20</margin> infinite mover and infinite motion are vain, being founded on ignorance of the motion of this globe of ours. Thirdly, it is proposed that there is no star that does not move as this one [the Earth] does, and others which, being near to us, allow us to sensibly perceive the local differences of their motions. However, the suns—which are bodies where fire predominates—move in one way; <margin>25</margin> while the earths—in which water is predominant—move in another <note>Bruno classified celestial bodies into two types: "suns" (stars) which produce their own light and heat, and "earths" (planets) which are cold and reflect light.</note>. And from this it becomes clear where the light diffused by the stars proceeds from, some of which shine by themselves, while others shine by reflection from another.

->Fourthly, in what manner bodies very distant from the sun can<-
equally participate in the heat as those closer to it. Here, the opinion attributed to Epicurus—that one sun is sufficient <margin>30</margin> for the infinite universe—is rejected <note>Epicurus was an ancient Greek philosopher. Bruno argues that one sun couldn't possibly light an infinite space; there must be infinite suns.</note>. The true difference is provided between those stars that twinkle and those that do not. Fifthly, the opinion of Cusanus <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a German philosopher and cardinal who also suggested the universe might be infinite and that the Earth moves.</note> is examined concerning the matter and habitability of worlds, and concerning the nature of light. Sixthly, it is shown how, although some bodies are in themselves bright and <margin>35</margin> hot, the sun does not shine for the sun, nor the earth for the same earth, nor water for the same water; rather, light always proceeds from the opposite star. We see this sensibly when the whole sea appears bright from high places, such as mountains; yet when we are on the sea, or in that same field, we do not see it shine, except <margin>40</margin> for the light of the sun and the moon across a certain small dimension...

### Argument of the Fourth Dialogue.

In the following dialogue, first, what has been said at other times is repeated:

### Argument of the Fifth Dialogue.

At the beginning of the fifth dialogue, someone endowed with a more fortunate intellect is presented, who, although raised in a contrary doctrine, by having the power to judge what he has heard and seen, can <margin>25</margin> distinguish between one discipline and another, and easily yields and <insert>[21]</insert> corrects himself. It is said who those people are to whom Aristotle seems a miracle of nature, given that those who understand him poorly and have a base intellect hold him in high esteem. For we should pity such people and flee their disputes, because <margin>30</margin> with them there is nothing to be gained but loss.
Here Albertino, a new interlocutor, brings forward twelve arguments, in which consists the entire persuasion against the plurality and multitude of worlds. The third from the places of mobile bodies. The fourth from the distance of horizons from the center. The fifth from the contiguity of multiple spherical worlds. The sixth from the triangular spaces caused by their contact. The seventh from the fact that actual infinity <margin>40</margin> does not exist; and from a determined number, which is no more reasonable than another. The eighth argument comes from the determination of natural things: and from the **passive power** <note>the capacity of matter to be acted upon or transformed</note> of things, which does not correspond to the divine efficacy and **active power**. <margin>5</margin> But here it must be considered that it is a most unfitting thing that the First and Highest <note>referring to God</note> should be like one who has the skill to <term>play the lyre <note>original: "cytharizare"</note></term>, but for lack of a lyre, does not play; <insert>[22]</insert> and should be one who can act, | but does not; because that thing which he can do cannot be done by him: which poses a more than obvious contradiction, which cannot fail to be recognized except by <margin>10</margin> those who know nothing. <margin>15</margin> These are those doubts and motives, in the solution of which consists so much doctrine as is sufficient alone to discover the intimate and radical errors of **common philosophy** <note>the standard Aristotelian scholasticism taught in universities at the time</note>, and the weight and importance of our own. Here is the reason why we should not fear that anything might flow away, that any particular particle might either be lost, or truly vanish, <margin>20</margin> or be spread into a vacuum that would dismember it into annihilation. Here is the reason for the <term>vicissitudinal change <note>the constant, cyclical transformation of matter from one form to another</note></term> of the whole; by which there is no evil from which one does not escape, and no good which one does not encounter: while through the infinite field, through perpetual mutation, the whole substance remains the same and one. From which contemplation (if we <margin>25</margin> are attentive) it will happen that no strange accident will cast us down through grief or fear, and no fortune will exalt us through pleasure or hope: whence we shall have the true path to **true morality**; we shall be magnanimous, <insert>[23]</insert> despisers of | that which childish thoughts esteem, and we shall certainly become greater than those gods whom the blind commoners adore, because <margin>30</margin> we shall become true contemplators of the **history of nature** which is written within ourselves, and orderly executors of the divine laws which are engraved in the center of our hearts. We shall know that there is no other flying from here to heaven than from heaven to here: no other ascending from there to here, than from here to there: nor is there any other descending from one or the other <margin>35</margin> boundary. We are no more on the circumference to them <note>other celestial bodies</note> than they are to us; they are no more a center to us than we are to them: we tread upon the star, and are encompassed by the heavens, no differently than they are.

Behold us, then, free from envy; behold us free from vain anxiety and the foolish care of craving from afar that great good which we possess nearby <margin>40</margin> and joined to us. Behold us freer from the great fear that they <note>the stars/worlds</note> might fall upon us...

But while we consider more deeply the being and substance of that in which we are immutable, we will find that there is no death—not only for us, but for no substance; since nothing is substantially diminished, but everything, wandering through infinite space, changes its face. And because we all are subject to a most excellent <term>efficient cause <note>the primary source of change or creation; for Bruno, this is the divine intellect</note></term>; we must not believe, estimate, or hope for anything else, except that as everything is from good; so everything is good, by good, and for good; from well, through well, to well. The contrary of this does not appear except to him who perceives nothing but the present being; just as the beauty of a building is not manifest to him who sees only a tiny part of it, like a stone, a piece of cement, or half a wall: but especially to him who can see the whole, and who has the faculty to compare part to part. Let us not fear that what is accumulated | in this world, by the violence of some [25]
wandering spirit, or by the wrath of some <term>thundering Jove <note>original: "fulmineo Gioue," referring to Jupiter, the king of the gods</term></note> should be dispersed outside this tomb, or dome of the heaven; or be shaken and flow out like dust outside this starry mantle: and the nature of things can no more come to be emptied in substance, than to the appearance of our eyes that air which was contained within the hollow of a bubble vanishes: for we know a world in which thing always succeeds thing; without there being an ultimate depth, from whence, as from the hand of a blacksmith, they irreparably flow into nothingness. There are no ends, boundaries, margins, or walls that defraud and subtract from us the infinite abundance of things. Thence the earth and its sea are fertile; thence the flame of the sun is perpetual: eternally supplying itself with fuel...

<margin>10</margin>We know that so great an Emperor <note>referring to God</note> does not have so narrow a seat, so wretched a throne, so cramped a tribunal, so small a court, so tiny and weak an image: something that a phantom might give birth to, a dream might shatter, a mania might repair, a chimera might disperse, a misfortune might diminish, a crime might take away, or a thought might restore; which with a breath is filled, and with a sip is emptied. we have sufficient evidence from our senses, for they are unable to contradict the truth; furthermore, the senses clearly admit their own weakness and insufficiency by creating an appearance of finitude caused by the horizon—and in forming this horizon, we see how inconsistent they are. Now, since experience shows that the senses deceive us regarding the surface of this globe on which we find ourselves, we should be much more suspicious regarding that boundary which the senses make us perceive in the star-filled concavity <note>The "star-filled concavity" refers to the traditional view of the sky as a solid sphere or dome containing the stars.</note>.

<margin>4 |</margin> *Philotheo.* I shall do so. If the world is finite, and outside the world is nothing: I ask you, where is the world? Where is the universe? Aristotle replies: it is in itself. The convex surface of the first heaven is the universal place <note>original: "loco uniuersale"</note>, and that, as the first container, is not within another container. For <term>place</term> <note>original: "luogo." In Aristotelian physics, "place" is defined strictly as the inner surface of a containing body. If you say there is nothing, then the heaven and the world will certainly not be in any place at all.
*Fracastorio.* Therefore the world will be nowhere. Everything will be in nothingness. <note>original: "Nullibi ergo erit mundus. Omne erit in nihilo."</note>
*Philotheo.* The world would be something that cannot be found. If you say (as it seems you wish to say something to avoid the "void" and "nothingness") that outside the world is an intellectual and divine being, such that God comes to be the "place" of all things, you will find yourself in great difficulty trying to explain how an incorporeal, intelligible thing without dimensions could be the "place" of a dimensioned thing. If you say He contains it as a form, or in the way the soul contains the body, you do not answer the question of what is "outside," nor the inquiry into what is found beyond and outside the universe. And if you want to excuse yourself by saying that where there is nothing and where there is no thing, there is also no place, no "beyond," and no "outside," this does not [satisfy me]...

<margin>15</margin> *Philotheo.* I add to this that there is no mind that does not perceive this Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked around the "peripatos" or colonnades of the Lyceum while teaching.</note> statement as a tangled contradiction. Aristotle defined "place" not as a containing body, nor as a certain space, but as the surface of a containing body; and yet the first, principal, and greatest place is that to which such a definition applies the least—or not at all. That is the convex surface of the first heaven <note>In ancient cosmology, the outermost sphere that holds the stars and bounds the universe.</note>, which is the surface of a body: and of such a body which only contains and is not contained. Now, to make that surface a "place," it is not required that it belong to a contained body, but that it belong to a <margin>25</margin> containing body. If it is the surface of a containing body and is not joined and continued to a contained body, it is a place without anything placed <margin>6</margin> <note>original: "locato"</note>, considering that it is not fitting for the first heaven to be a place except through its concave <note>The "concave" surface is the inner side of a sphere, curving inward like the inside of a bowl.</note> surface, which touches the convex surface of the second [sphere]. See then how that definition is vain, confused, and self-destructive; which confusion arises from having that inconvenient premise, which wants nothing to be placed beyond the heavens.
*Elpino.* The Peripatetics will say that the first heaven is a containing body through its concave surface and not through the convex one, and according to the former, it is a place.

...he cannot escape making two out of one, because that which is the container and that which is the contained are always distinct from one another. <margin>1</margin> And they are so distinct that (according to him [Aristotle] himself) the container is incorporeal and the contained is a body; the container is immobile, the contained is mobile; the container is mathematical, the contained is physical. Now, whatever one wishes to say <margin>5</margin> about that surface, I will constantly ask: what is beyond it?
<margin>7</margin> If it is answered that there is nothing, I will say this is the vacuum; this is the void. And such a vacuum and such a void have no measure, nor any further limit. It is, however, bounded on its inner side, and this is more difficult to imagine than the thought that the universe is infinite and immense. <margin>10</margin> Because we cannot escape the vacuum if we wish to posit a finite universe. Let us see now if it is fitting that there be such a space in which there is nothing. In this infinite space this universe is found (whether by chance, or by necessity, or by providence—for now I will not involve myself in that); <margin>15</margin> I ask whether this space which contains the world has a greater aptitude <term>aptitude</term> <note>In this context, 'aptitude' refers to the inherent capacity or suitability of space to hold or receive matter.</note> for containing a world than the other space that lies beyond?

*Fracastoro.* It certainly seems to me that it does not; because where there is nothing, there is no difference at all; where there is no difference, there is no variation in aptitude; <margin>18</margin> and perhaps there is even less aptitude where there is nothing at all.

*Elpino.* Nor any lack of aptitude <note>Original: "ineptia."</note> either. And of the two, the former is more likely than the latter. <margin>20</margin>

*Philotheo.* You speak well. Thus I say that just as the vacuum and the void (which is necessarily posited by this Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> discourse) has no aptitude to receive, it must have even less reason to reject the world. But of these two aptitudes, we see one in actuality, and the other we cannot see at all, except with the eye of <margin>25</margin> reason. Just as this world is in this space equal to the size of the world <margin>8</margin> (which by the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato; Bruno refers here to the Platonic idea that space or 'chora' acts as a kind of substrate for matter.</note> is called matter), so another world can be in that space, and in innumerable spaces beyond this one, equal to this one. <margin>30</margin>

*Elpino.* I understand. Now continue with your point. <margin>1</margin>

<margin>1</margin> **Fr.** I complete and arrange a pair of syllogisms <note>A syllogism is a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two shared premises.</note> in this manner. The First Efficient <note>original: "primo efficiente"; This refers to the "First Efficient Cause," a philosophical term for God as the primary agent who brings the universe into being.</note> if He wished to do other than what He wishes to do, He could do other than what He does; but He cannot wish to do other than what He wishes to do; therefore He cannot do other than what He does. <margin>10</margin> **Phi.** These, if not simple, are demonstrative syllogisms. Nonetheless, I praise certain worthy theologians for not admitting them: because, considering prudently, they know that the crude and ignorant common people, faced with this necessity, would come to be unable to conceive how free choice <note>original: "elettione"; literally "election," meaning the capacity to choose between good and evil.</note> and dignity, and the merits of justice, can stand. <margin>15</margin> despairing under a certain fate, they are necessarily most wicked. <margin>20</margin> similar premises. Therefore, stating the opposite among the wise is not so scandalous, nor does it detract from the divine greatness and excellence; whereas what is true is pernicious to civil discourse, and contrary to the purpose of | laws—not for being true, but for being misunderstood, both by those who treat it maliciously, and by those who
<margin>25</margin> are not capable of understanding it without the loss of morals.

<margin>30</margin> cessity and immutability in God, do not place any less emphasis on moral liberty and the faculty of our choice: because they know well and can understand how that divine necessity and this human liberty are compatible. However, some of the true fathers and pastors of peoples perhaps remove this saying and others like it so as not to give an opening to the wicked and seductive enemies
<margin>35</margin> of civility and the general profit, who draw troublesome conclusions by abusing the simplicity and ignorance of those who can only with difficulty understand the truth and are most readily inclined to evil. <margin>40</margin> its author—propositions which are not proposed by us to the common folk, but...

# On the infinite universe and worlds. 321

...always remains most stable. Similarly, regarding its motion around the center—where there is its East *I*, its South *V*, its West *K*, and its North <note>original: "merinottio," a term for the midnight point or North</note> *O*—each of these points revolves by virtue of an infinite impulse. Therefore, each of them has simultaneously departed and returned; consequently, each is always fixed and remains where it was. So much so that, in conclusion, for these bodies to be moved by infinite power is the same as not being moved at all, because to move in an instant and not to move are one and the same thing. There remains, therefore, the other active principle <margin>27</margin> of motion, which comes from intrinsic power <note>This refers to the internal "soul" or nature of an object that allows it to move through space over time, rather than the instantaneous movement of the divine.</note> and consequently occurs within time and a certain succession; and this motion is distinct from rest. Here, then, is how we can say God moves the whole, and how we must understand that He grants the power of movement to everything that moves.

**Elp.** Now that you have so deeply and effectively removed and resolved this difficulty for me, I yield completely to your judgment, and I hope always to receive similar resolutions from you. For although I have practiced and attempted little in this area until now, I have nonetheless received and conceived a great deal; and I hope for much more advantage, because although I do not fully see your mind, from the radiance it diffuses I perceive that within is enclosed either a sun or an even greater light. From today forward—not with the hope of surpassing your proficiency, but with the intent of providing occasion for your elucidations—I will return to propose questions to you, if you will deign to meet for as many days at the same hour in this place as shall be enough for me to hear and understand until my mind is completely at peace.

**Phi.** So I shall do.
**Fra.** You will be most welcome, and we will be very attentive listeners.
**Bur.** And I, though having little understanding—if I do not understand the meanings, I will listen to the words; if I do not listen to the words, I will hear the voice. Farewell.

Certainly, to say that the infinite exists only in potentiality, and in a certain <margin>30</margin> succession but not in act, necessarily implies that the active power can put this into successive act but not into a completed act. Since the infinite cannot be completed, it would follow that the First Cause does not have an active power that is simple, absolute, and one. Instead, it would have one active power to which an infinite <margin>35</margin> successive possibility responds, and another to which a possibility responds that is indistinguishable from the act itself. ### ->On the Infinite Universe and Worlds.<-

Thus, even the same thing, following the same motion, can be said to go upward or downward depending on the perspective of different observers. Determined bodies, then, <margin>25</margin> do not have infinite motion, but finite and determined motion within their own boundaries; but regarding the indeterminate and the infinite, there is neither finite nor infinite motion, and there is no difference of place nor of time. Just as there can be infinite other earths or bodies of similar condition, there are infinite other suns or fires of similar nature. All of these move from the surrounding places to their own container as to their center. From this, it would follow that there are infinite <margin>25</margin> heavy bodies according to their number; however, this does not result in an "infinite gravity" within a single subject in an intensive sense, but rather as existing in innumerable subjects in an extensive sense. ...infinite, [there are] infinite finite weights: <margin>1</margin> seeing as this infinity is not like that of a continuum, but like that of discrete things <note>A "continuum" is a single, unbroken thing (like a line), while "discrete" things are separate, individual items (like a handful of marbles).</note>: which are in an infinite continuum, which is the space, the place, and the dimension capable of holding them all. It is, therefore, not inconvenient that there should be infinite discrete heavy bodies, which do not <margin>5</margin> [together] form a single [infinite] heavy body. Just as infinite waters do not form a single <margin>51</margin> infinite body of water, and infinite parts of earth do not make one infinite earth: so that there are bodies infinite in multitude which physically do not compose a single body of infinite size. And this makes the greatest difference; as is seen proportionally in the towing of a ship, which is pulled by ten men joined together, but will never be pulled by thousands who are disconnected and acting individually.

*Elpino.* With this and other arguments, you have resolved a thousand times over what [Aristotle] proposes as the fourth reason; which says that if one understands an infinite body, it must be understood as infinite in all dimensions: so that no part of anything can exist outside of it: therefore <margin>15</margin> it is not possible that in an infinite body there are several dissimilar parts, each of which is infinite.

*Teofilo.* All this is true and does not contradict us, for we have said so many times that there are many finite dissimilar things within one infinite, and we have considered how this might be. Perhaps it is proportional to <margin>20</margin> someone saying there are several continuous things together; for example, and as a likeness, in liquid mud <note>original: "luto"</note>, where always and in every part water is joined to water, and earth to earth; where, because of the imperceptibility of the meeting of the smallest parts of earth and the smallest parts of water, they will not be called discrete, nor many continuous things: but one continuum, which is not water, and is not earth, but is mud: where another person might just as easily choose to say that water is not properly joined to <margin>52</margin> water, and earth to earth, but water to earth, and earth to water. And similarly, a third person might come along and, denying both ways of speaking, say that mud is joined to mud. And according to <margin>30</margin> these reasons, the infinite universe can be taken as one continuum, in which the <term>ether</term> <note>The subtle, fluid substance Bruno believed filled all space between the planets and stars.</note> interposed between such great bodies creates no more of a gap than the air that is placed and interposed between the parts of water and dry earth in mud. The difference lies only in the smallness of the parts and the tininess and imperceptibility found in the mud, versus the greatness, majority, and perceptibility of the parts that are in the universe; so that the contrary and diverse moving bodies concur in the constitution of one immobile continuum, in which the contraries <margin>35</margin> concur toward the constitution of one thing, and belong to one order, and finally are one. It would certainly be inconvenient and impossible... <margin>40</margin>

He uses the metaphor of mud—a mixture of earth and water—to explain how different elements and planetary bodies form a single, unified, and infinite cosmic whole.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical demonstration regarding the nature of an infinite body. On the previous page, Teofilo argued that an infinite universe cannot possess weight or lightness as a whole, as these qualities require a center and a circumference to define "up" and "down." Here, he transitions into a geometric and physical proof—frequently used to counter Aristotelian physics—to show that interaction between the finite and the infinite is impossible because they share no common ratio.</meta>

### ## On the Infinite Universe and Worlds.

<margin>1</margin> H, as is the ratio of B to AZ; B, however, in the same time G, would be a perfect agent <note>original: "agente" — the entity performing an action or movement</note> in both a finite thing and an infinite thing: that is, in AZ, which is a part of the infinite, and in A, which is the infinite itself. This is impossible; therefore, an infinite body can be neither an agent nor a patient <note>original: "patiente" — the entity receiving an action or being moved</note>. This is because two <margin>5</margin> equal patients are acted upon equally in the same amount of time by the same agent; a smaller patient is acted upon by the same agent in a shorter time, and a larger patient in a longer time. Furthermore, when there are different agents acting in an equal amount of time and their action is completed, there will be a ratio of agent to agent just as there is a ratio of <margin>10</margin> patient to patient. Furthermore, every agent works upon a patient in a finite time (I speak of that agent which reaches the end of its action, not of that whose motion is continuous, as can only be the case with the motion of **55** <term>translation: local motion from one place to another</term>), because it is impossible for a finite action to take place in infinite time. Thus, it is first made clear how the finite cannot <margin>15</margin> have a completed action upon the infinite.

->G. time.<-
->A. infinite patient. B. larger finite agent.<-
->A. part of the infinite. Z.<-
->H. finite patient. D. smaller finite agent.<-

<margin>20</margin> Second, it is similarly shown that the infinite cannot be an agent acting upon a finite thing. Let the infinite agent be A, and the finite patient be B, and let us pose that the infinite A is the agent acting upon the finite B in a finite time G. Next, let the finite body D be the agent acting upon a part of B, that is, BZ, in the same time G. Certainly, there will be a ratio of the patient BZ to <margin>24</margin> the whole patient B, just as there is a ratio of the agent D to the other finite agent H. And the ratio being changed from agent D to patient BZ, just as the ratio of agent H is to the whole of B, it follows that B will be moved by H in the same time in which BZ is moved by D; **56** that is, in time G, in which time B is moved by the infinite agent <margin>30</margin> A. This is impossible. This impossibility follows from what we have already said: namely, that if an infinite thing works in a finite time, the action must not be within time at all, because there is no ratio between the finite and the infinite. Therefore, if we pose two different agents which have the same action upon the same patient, necessarily the action of <margin>35</margin> those two will occur in two different times; and there will be a ratio of time to time, just as there is of agent to agent. But if we pose two agents, of which one is infinite and the other finite, having the same action upon the same patient, it will be necessary to say one of two things: either that the action of the infinite occurs in an instant, or that the action of the finite agent occurs in <margin>40</margin> infinite time. Both are impossible.

### ## On the Infinite Universe and Worlds.

<margin>1</margin>a greater part, and a smaller part, and a part that has a greater or lesser proportion to it: for you are no closer to the infinite by a hundredfold than by a triad <note>original: "ternario" — a group of three; here used to mean the number three</note>, because an infinite number consists of no fewer infinite triads than of infinite hundreds. In the same way, a thousand years are not a part of eternity, because they have no proportion to the whole: but they are indeed parts of some measure of time, such as ten thousand years, or a hundred thousand centuries.

<margin>15</margin>*Elpino.* Now, then, help me understand. What would you say are the parts of infinite duration?

*Philotheus.* The proportional parts of duration are those which have a proportion within duration and time: but certainly not within infinite duration and infinite time; because in that, the greatest time—that is, the <margin>20</margin>largest proportional part of duration—ends up being equivalent to the smallest, considering that there are no more infinite centuries than there are <margin>60</margin>infinite hours. I say that in infinite duration, which is eternity, there are no more hours than there are centuries: so that everything which is called a part of the infinite, insofar as it is a part of the infinite, is infinite—both in infinite duration and in infinite mass. From this doctrine, <margin>25</margin>you may consider how circumspect <note>Philotheus is being ironic here, highlighting Aristotle's lack of care in his logical premises</note> Aristotle is in his suppositions when he takes finite parts of the infinite, and how strong the arguments of certain theologians are when, from the eternity of time, they wish to infer the absurdity of so many infinites being greater than one another, just as there can be different species of numbers. From this doctrine, <margin>30</margin>I say, you have the means to extricate yourself from innumerable labyrinths.

*Elpino.* Particularly from the one that concerns our subject regarding the infinite steps and infinite miles that would result in one smaller infinite and another larger infinite within the immensity of the universe. Now continue. <margin>35</margin>

*Philotheus.* Secondly, Aristotle does not proceed demonstratively in his inference. Because from the fact that the universe is infinite, and that within it (I do not say *of* it, because it is one thing to speak of parts *in* the infinite, and another to speak of parts *of* the infinite) there are infinite parts which all have action and passion <note>original: "attione et passione" — the capacity to act upon something and to be acted upon</note>, and consequently transmutation among themselves: he wishes to infer either that the <margin>40</margin>infinite has action or passion in the finite, or from the finite, or that the infinite...

->22 *<-

<margin>1</margin> [that the] infinite <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion of infinite proportions.</note> acts upon the infinite, and that the latter is acted upon and transformed by the former. We say that this inference is not valid in a physical sense, although it is logically true; for even if by using our reason we find infinite parts that are active and infinite <margin>61</margin> <margin>5</margin> parts that are passive, and we take the one as one contrary and the other as another contrary: yet in nature, because these parts are disjointed and separate, and divided by specific boundaries, as we see, they do not force or incline us to say that the infinite as a whole is an agent or a patient <note>In Renaissance philosophy, an "agent" is the thing doing the action, and a "patient" is the thing receiving the action or being changed.</note>. Rather, within the infinite, innumerable finite parts experience action <margin>10</margin> and passion <term>passion: here used in the Scholastic sense of "passio," meaning the capacity of a body to be acted upon or altered by an external force</term>. It is granted, therefore, not that the infinite as a whole is mobile and alterable, but that within it there are infinite mobile and alterable things. It is not that the finite is acted upon by the infinite, nor the infinite by the finite, nor the infinite by the infinite according to a physical and natural infinity; but according to that which proceeds from a logical and rational aggregation, which computes <margin>15</margin> all heavy things as one "heavy thing," even though all heavy things are not a single heavy thing. The infinite and the whole remaining thus immobile, unalterable, and incorruptible, there can be within it—and there are indeed—innumerable and infinite motions and alterations that are perfect and complete. Add to what has been said that, even if there were <margin>20</margin> two bodies that were infinite on one side but bounded on the other where they meet, it would not follow—as Aristotle thinks necessarily follows—that the action and passion would be infinite. This is because if one of these two bodies acts upon the other, it will not act according to its entire dimension and size; for it is not near, proximal, joined, or <margin>25</margin> continuous to the other according to its whole self, nor according to all its parts. For let us suppose the case that there are <margin>62</margin> two infinite bodies, A and B, which are continuous or joined together at the line or surface F-G. Certainly, they will not come to exert power against each other according to their whole virtue <note>original: "virtú" — in this context, it refers to the inherent power or physical force of a body</note>, because they are not near one <margin>30</margin> another in all their parts, since the contact or continuation can only exist at some finite boundary. And I say further that even if we suppose that surface or line to be infinite, it will not follow from this that the bodies joined there cause infinite action and passion; for these forces are not intensive <note>concentrated at a single point</note> but extensive <note>spread out over an area</note>, just as the parts themselves are extensive. Wherefore it happens that in no part does the infinite work <margin>35</margin> according to its whole power, but extensively, part by part, discretely and separately.

For the parts of those two bodies cannot be <margin>5</margin> altered beyond a certain, determined distance; therefore, M and 10, N and 20, O and 30, P and 40, have no capacity to alter each other. See then, **63** how if two infinite bodies were positioned, an infinite action would not follow. | I say further still, that even if it were assumed and conceded that these two infinite bodies could act against one another intensively, and refer to one another according to their entire power; <margin>10</margin> even so, no effect of action or **passion** <term>passion: from the Latin "passio," meaning the capacity of a body to be acted upon or changed by an external force; the counterpart to "action."</term> would follow. This is because the one is no less capable in repugnance and resistance than the other is in attacking and persisting; therefore, no alteration whatsoever would follow. Behold then, how from two opposed infinite contraries, <margin>15</margin> either a finite alteration follows, or none follows at all.

*Elp.* Now what will you say to the supposition of one contrary body being finite, and the other infinite; as if the Earth were a cold body, and the heaven were fire, and all the stars were fires, and the heaven was immense, and the stars innumerable? Do you wish for that which Aristotle infers <margin>20</margin> to follow: that the finite would be absorbed by the infinite?

*Philo.* Certainly not, as can be gathered from what we have said; for since the physical power is spread through the dimensions of an infinite body, it would not be effective against the finite with infinite vigor and power, but only with that which can be diffused from the finite parts, <margin>25</margin> and according to a certain distance removed. For it is impossible that it operates according to all its parts, but only according to the nearest ones, as is seen in the preceding demonstration, where we presuppose A and B to be two infinite bodies, which are not capable of transmuting one another except by the parts **64** | that are within the distance between 10, 20, 30, 40, and <margin>30</margin> M, N, O, P. Therefore, it matters not at all for making a greater and more vigorous action, even if the body B should run on and increase to infinity while the body A remains finite. Behold then, how from two opposed contraries a finite action and a finite alteration always follow; no less when assuming one to be infinite and the other finite, than when <margin>35</margin> assuming both to be infinite.

*Elp.* You have satisfied me greatly, so that it seems to me a redundant thing to bring up those other crude arguments with which he <note>Aristotle.</note> wishes to demonstrate that there is no infinite body outside the heavens; such as the one that says: "Every body that is in a **place** <note>original: "loco." ### ## On the Infinite Universe and Worlds.

<margin>1</margin>...in a place; outside the heaven there is no place, therefore there is no body. Indeed, there is not even an "outside" <note>original: "extra." Philotheus is quoting the Aristotelian view that there is no space or "extra" void beyond the final celestial sphere.</note>; because "outside" implies a difference in place, and of a sensible <note>Meaning "perceptible by the senses."</note> place—not a spiritual or intelligible body, as someone might say: if it is sensible, it is finite.
<margin>5</margin>*Phi.* I believe and understand that beyond and further beyond that imagined boundary of the heaven, there is always an ethereal region, and worldly bodies, stars, earths, suns—all of them absolutely sensible, both in themselves and to those who are either within them or near them, even though they are not sensible to us because of their great distance and remoteness. In the meantime, consider what a foun-
<margin>10</margin>dation this man <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or his followers.</note> builds upon: that because we do not perceive a sensible body beyond the imagined circumference, he concludes that no body exists at all. And therefore, he | stopped at believing in no other body but the **eighth sphere**, **65** beyond which the Astronomers of his time had not perceived any other heaven. And because they always attributed the apparent rotation of the world around the earth
<margin>15</margin>to a **prime mover** <term>prime mover: the "primum mobile," which in ancient astronomy was the outermost moving sphere that pushed all the internal spheres (the planets and stars) around the Earth.</term> above all the others, they laid down such foundations that they have gone on endlessly adding sphere upon sphere, finding others without stars and, consequently, without sensible bodies—to such an extent that even astronomical theories and imaginings condemn this opinion. It is much more 
<margin>20</margin>condemned by those who better understand how the bodies said to belong to the eighth heaven <note>The sphere of the "fixed stars."</note> have no less a distinction among themselves of greater and lesser distance from the surface of the earth than do the other seven <note>The spheres of the Sun, Moon, and the five planets known in antiquity.</note>; for the reasoning behind their equidistance depends only on the completely false assumption of the **fixity of the earth** <note>original: "fission de la terra." Bruno is arguing against the Geocentric model where the Earth is the unmoving center.</note>, against which 
<margin>25</margin>all nature cries out, every reason proclaims, and every regulated and well-informed intellect finally judges. However it may be, it is said against all reason that the universe ends and terminates where the reach of our senses concludes; for our ability to sense is a reason to infer that bodies *exist*, but the negation of that sense—which may 
<margin>30</margin>be due to a defect in the sensing power and not a lack of the sensible object—is not sufficient even for a slight suspicion that the bodies do not exist. <margin>1</margin> the sun. Likewise, Venus, Mercury, and the others, which are also other earths, make their circuits around the same father of life <note>original: "padre de uita" — Bruno refers to the Sun as a source of vital heat and motion for the planets.</note>.

*Elpino.* The proper motions of each are those which are seen beyond this <margin>5</margin> so-called "worldly" motion <note>This refers to the apparent daily rotation of the entire sky, which Bruno attributes to the Earth's rotation.</note>, as well as those proper to the so-called fixed stars (both of which must be attributed to the Earth). Such motions are of more various types than there are bodies; so much so that one will never see two stars agree in the same order and measure of motion, if motion were to be seen in all of them. These stars show no variation <margin>10</margin> at all because of the great distance they have from us. Although they make their turns around the solar fire, and rotate around their own centers through the participation of vital heat, the differences in their approaching and receding cannot be understood by us.
*Philotheo.* So it is.
<margin>15</margin> *Elpino.* There are, therefore, innumerable suns; there are infinite earths which similarly circle those suns, just as we see these seven <note>The "seven" refers to the traditional planets known at the time: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon. *Elpino.* Why is it, then, that around other lights which are suns, we do not <margin>20</margin> see other lights circling which are earths? Why is it that beyond these we cannot perceive any motion, and all other worldly bodies (except for those called comets) are always seen in the same arrangement and distance?
*Philotheo.* The reason is that we see the suns, which are the largest—indeed, the greatest—bodies; but we do not see <margin>73</margin> the earths, <margin>25</margin> which, being much smaller bodies, are invisible. Likewise, it is not against reason that there are other earths which revolve around this sun, yet are not manifest to us, either because of their greater distance, or their smaller size, or because they do not have much water surface, or <margin>30</margin> simply because they do not have that surface turned toward us and opposite the sun—the surface by which, like a crystal mirror, they catch the luminous rays and make themselves visible. Hence, it is no wonder, nor a thing against nature, that we often hear of the sun being somewhat eclipsed without the moon coming between it and our sight. Besides <margin>35</margin> the visible ones, there may also be innumerable "aqueous lights" (that is, earths of which waters are a part) that circle the sun; but the difference in their circuit is imperceptible because of the great distance. Thus, in that extremely slow motion which is perceived in those stars visible above or beyond Saturn, no difference is seen between the motion of one and the motion <margin>40</margin> of another, nor any rule in the motion of all of them around the center—whether we place the Earth at the center, or we place the Sun at the center.

# On the Infinite Universe and Worlds.

*Elpino.* How then did you intend that all those bodies, however far they may be from the center—that is, from the sun—could reasonably share in its vital heat? <note>Bruno views "vital heat" not just as physical temperature, but as a life-giving force necessary for a world to be inhabited.</note>

*Philotheo.* By this: that the further they are away, the larger the circle they describe; the larger the circle they make, the more slowly they move around the sun; and the more slowly they move, the longer they withstand <margin>74</margin> its hot and fiery | rays.

*Elpino.* You intended, then, that although those bodies were so far from the sun, they could nonetheless partake in enough heat; because by turning more quickly around their own center, and more slowly around the sun, they can not only partake in as much heat, but even more if necessary? This is because, through the faster motion around its own center, the same part of the earth’s surface <note>original: "conuesso de la terra" — literally the "convexity of the earth."</note> that was not heated as much returns more quickly to be restored; and by the slower motion around the fiery center, staying more fixed under its influence, it comes to receive the flaming rays more vigorously.

*Philotheo.* So it is.

*Elpino.* Therefore, you mean that if the stars beyond Saturn are truly immobile, as they appear to be, they would then be innumerable suns or fires, more or less perceptible to us, around which circle nearby earths that are imperceptible to us. <note>Bruno is proposing that every "fixed star" we see is actually a sun like our own, with its own planets (earths) that we cannot see because they are too small and dark.</note>

*Philotheo.* One would have to say so, since all earths are worthy of having the same logic applied to them, and all suns the same.

*Elpino.* Do you mean by this that all of those are suns?

*Philotheo.* No, because I do not know if all or the majority are immobile, or if some of them turn around others; for no one has observed it, and furthermore, it is not easy to observe. Just as one does not easily see the motion and progress of a distant object, which over a great distance is not easily seen to have changed place—as happens when watching ships far out at sea. But let it be as it will: since <margin>75</margin> the universe is | infinite, there must ultimately be many suns. For it is impossible that the heat and light of one particular sun could spread through the immense void, as Epicurus <note>Epicurus (c. 341–270 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher who argued for an infinite universe of atoms, though he held different views on the nature of the sun.</note> may have imagined, if what others report of him is true. Therefore, it is also required that there be suns that are also innumerable, many of which are visible to us in the form of small bodies; but such a star will appear as a minor star even though it may be much larger than the one that seems largest to us.

*Elpino.* All this must at least be judged possible and appropriate.

*Philotheo.* Around those suns there may revolve earths of greater or smaller mass than this one.

77 | *Phi.* Up to this point he speaks divinely; but continue by bringing forward what he adds next.
*El.* From what he adds, it can be understood that this Earth may be another sun, and that all the stars are likewise suns. And the moon does not appear similarly bright because perhaps we are located toward the more middle, or (as he says) central parts of its circumference—that is, in its humid and watery region. And therefore, although it has its own light, it nonetheless does not appear; and we only see that which is caused on the watery surface by the reflection of the solar light."
*Phi.* This gentleman <note>Referring to Nicholas of Cusa.</note> has known and seen much, and he is truly one of the most singular geniuses to have breathed under this air. But regarding the apprehension of truth, he acted like a swimmer in tempestuous waves, now tossed high, now low; for he did not see the light continuously, openly, and clearly, and he did not swim as if on flat and tranquil water, but interruptedly and with certain intervals. The reason for this is that he had not purged all those false principles with which he was imbued by the common doctrine <note>The prevailing Aristotelian and Ptolemaic views taught in medieval universities.</note> from which he had departed; so that perhaps, by design, the title 78 given to | his book, *Of Learned Ignorance* <note>original: "della dotta ignoranza" — referring to Cusa's famous work *De Docta Ignorantia* (1440), which argues that the finite mind cannot fully grasp the infinite God except through an awareness of its own ignorance.</note>, or *Of Ignorant Doctrine*, fits him very well.
*Elp.* What is that principle which he did not purge and ought to have been purged?
*Phi.* That the element of fire is like the air, worn down <note>original: "attrito" — referring to the Aristotelian idea that fire is generated by the friction of celestial spheres.</note> by the motion of the heaven; and that fire is an extremely thin body—contrary to 그 reality and truth which is made manifest to us through what we consider for other purposes and in our own proper discourses. There, we conclude it necessary that there be a solid and consistent material principle of heat, just as there is for a cold body; and that the ethereal region cannot be made of fire, nor be fire itself, but rather be set on fire and ignited by a nearby solid and dense body, such as the sun. So, where we can speak naturally, there is no need to resort to mathematical fantasies <note>Bruno often used "mathematical fantasies" to describe abstract geometric models that lacked a physical or "real" basis in nature.</note>. We see that the Earth has parts which of themselves are not bright; we see that some can shine because of something else, such as its water and its vaporous air, which gather heat and light from the sun and can transmit both to the surrounding regions. Therefore, it is necessary that there be a primary body to which it belongs to be at once—

<meta>This page continues the Third Dialogue of Giordano Bruno’s "On the Infinite Universe and Worlds." Philotheo is expanding on his cosmology, arguing that celestial bodies like the Sun and Earth are not made of a "fifth element" (quintessence) as Aristotle claimed, but are composed of the same four elements—earth, water, air, and fire—in different proportions. He is specifically addressing how heat, light, and life exist on these seemingly opposite worlds.</meta>

# On the Infinite Universe and Worlds.

luminous in itself and hot in itself; and such a thing cannot be unless it is constant, thick, and dense. For a rare and thin body <note>In Renaissance physics, "rare" refers to low density or gaseous states, while "dense" refers to solid matter.</note> cannot be the subject of light or heat, as we have demonstrated elsewhere at the appropriate time. It is necessary, then, that the two foundations of the two contrary primary active qualities <note>The "active qualities" refer to Heat (associated with fire/sun) and Cold (associated with water/earth).</note> be similarly solid, <margin>**79**</margin> and that the sun—at least in those parts which are luminous and hot—be like a stone or a most solid glowing metal. I do not mean a fusible metal <note>original: *liquabile*</note> like lead, bronze, gold, or silver; but rather an infusible metal—not like glowing iron, but like iron that is fire itself. And just as this star upon which we live <note>Bruno refers to the Earth as a "star" or "astro," a radical idea for his time.</note> is in itself cold and dark, sharing in no heat or light except what is heated by the sun; so that other body [the sun] is in itself hot and luminous, sharing in no coldness or opacity except what is cooled by surrounding bodies, and it contains parts of water just as the earth contains parts of fire. And therefore, just as on this coldest body, the "primary cold" and opaque one, there are animals that live by the heat and light of the sun; so on that most hot and shining body, there are those who flourish by the cooling <note>original: *refrigeratione*</note> of surrounding cold bodies. And just as this body is, by a certain participation, hot in its dissimilar parts; so that other body is, by a certain participation, cold in its own.

*Elpino.* Now, what do you say of the light?

*Philotheo.* I say that the sun does not shine to the sun, the earth does not shine to the earth, and no body shines unto itself; rather, every luminous body shines in the space around it. Therefore, although the earth is a luminous body due to the sun’s rays on its crystalline surface, <note>Bruno suggests the Earth's atmosphere or water acts as a reflective "crystalline" layer that makes it look like a star from a distance.</note> its light is not perceptible to us, nor to those who are on that surface; but rather to those who are opposite | to it. <margin>**80**</margin> Consider how, although the entire surface of the sea at night is illuminated by the splendor of the moon, it does not appear so to those who travel upon the sea, except in a certain space that is opposite the moon. If those travelers were granted the ability to rise higher and higher into the air above the sea, the dimension of the light would always increase for them, and they would see a larger space of the luminous field. From this, one can very easily deduce how those who are on luminous or even illuminated stars do not perceive the light of their own star, but that of the surrounding ones; just as in the same common space, a particular location takes light from a different particular location.

<margin>5</margin> that moves naturally has a circular displacement <note>original: "delation circulare"</note>, either around its own center or around another's center. <margin>10</margin> it is seen only in those parts that are, as it were, "excrements" <note>Bruno uses "excrements" in the biological sense of matter being expelled or absorbed by a larger organism.</note> that flow out from worldly bodies, or flow into their kindred spheres and continents from elsewhere—just as we see with water that, thinned into vapor by heat, rises on high, and then, thickened into its proper form by the cold, returns to the depths. <margin>15</margin> when we consider motion. As for the arrangement of the four bodies they call earth, water, air, and fire, I would like to know what nature, what art, or what sense-perception establishes it, verifies it, or demonstrates it?

<margin>20</margin> natural things as they please; but I deny this order, this arrangement—namely, that the earth is surrounded and contained by <margin>87</margin> water, the water by the air, the air by the fire, and the fire by the heaven. <margin>25</margin> field. Here, each of these bodies, stars, worlds, and eternal lights is composed of that which is called earth, water, air, and fire. <margin>30</margin> condition, which shines by reflecting another's light, as has been said. <margin>35</margin> This is no different from how the heterogeneous <note>original: "etherogenee"</note> parts in animals are arranged according to various and diverse compositions of bones, intestines, veins, arteries, flesh, and nerves; of lungs and members of one shape or another—presenting its own mountains, its valleys, its recesses, its waters,

<meta>This page continues the Third Dialogue of Giordano Bruno's "On the Infinite Universe and Worlds." Following the previous discussion of the Earth as a living organism, the speakers Fracastoro and Burchio now debate the nature of the elements—earth, water, and air—and their hierarchical arrangement. Fracastoro argues against the traditional Aristotelian view that earth is the "heaviest" element, proposing instead a more fluid and integrated understanding of the planetary body.</meta>

# On the Infinite Universe and Worlds.

<margin>1</margin> and thick like ours, so we live in a more vaporous air than those who are in a purer and more tranquil region; and just as the Ocean is to the air as impure water, so is our misty air to that other truly pure air? From such a sense and saying, what I wish to infer <margin>5</margin> is this: that the sea, the springs, the rivers, the mountains, the stones, and the air contained within them and comprised in them up to the middle region (as **92** they call it <note>The "middle region" refers to the *media regio*, a division in Aristotelian meteorology where clouds and storms form.</note>) are nothing other than parts and | dissimilar members of the same body, of the same mass, very much proportional to the parts and members that we commonly know as composite animals: of <margin>10</margin> which the boundary, convexity, and ultimate surface is terminated by the extreme margins of the mountains and the tempestuous air, so that the Ocean and the rivers remain in the depths of the earth, no less than the liver—esteemed the source of the blood <note>In ancient medicine, particularly Galenism, the liver was believed to be the organ where blood was produced.</note>—and the branching veins are contained and extended through the most minute parts.

<margin>15</margin> *Bvr.* Then the earth is not the heaviest body, and therefore in the middle, next to which the water that surrounds it is heavier and closer [to the center], which in turn is heavier than the air?

*Fra.* If you judge the heavy by the greater aptitude for penetrating parts and moving toward the middle and from the center, I will say air is the <margin>20</margin> heaviest, and air is the lightest, among all these called elements: because just as every part of the earth, if given space, descends to the middle, so the parts of the air will run more quickly to the middle than the parts of any other body whatsoever; for it falls to the air to be the first to succeed to a space to prohibit a vacuum <note>original: "uacuo" - Fracastoro refers to the *horror vacui*, the Aristotelian principle that "nature abhors a vacuum" and will immediately fill empty space.</note> and to fill it. Not so <margin>25</margin> quickly do the parts of the earth succeed to a place, for ordinarily they do not move except by penetrating the air: because to make the air penetrate, neither earth nor water nor fire is required, nor do any of these prevent it, nor do they overcome it by being more ready, apt, and swift to **93** fill the corners of the containing body. Furthermore, if the earth, which is <margin>30</margin> a solid body, departs, the air will be that which occupies its place; the earth is not so apt to occupy the place of the air that departs. Therefore, since it is proper to the air to move itself to penetrate every site and recess, there is no body lighter than air, and no body heavier than air.

*Bvr.* Now what will you say of the water?

<margin>35</margin> *Fra.* Of the water I have said, and I say again, that it is heavier than the earth; because we see the moisture descend and penetrate the dry [earth] more powerfully toward the middle than the dry penetrates the water; and furthermore, the dry taken by itself without the composition of water will come to float upon the water, being without the aptitude to penetrate <margin>40</margin> within; and it does not descend unless it is first soaked with water and condensed.

<margin>20</margin> # Dialogo Quarto. <margin>105</margin>

*Philotheo.* There are not, therefore, a finite number of worlds of the sort imagined as a composite of this earth surrounded by so many spheres, some of which contain one star, and others innumerable stars; for space is such that many stars can pass through it. # On the infinite universe and worlds.

<margin>1</margin> We shall understand that the orbs and spheres are not arranged in the universe as if they were contained one within another—the smaller always being contained by the larger, like the <term>layers</term><note>original: "squogli." <margin>15</margin> *Elpi.* We must see (he says in the first book of his *On the Heavens <margin>107</margin> and the World*) whether there be another world outside this one.
*Phil.* Concerning this question, you know that he uses the name "world" differently than we do. For we add world to world, as star to star in this most spacious ethereal breast—just as it is <margin>20</margin> fitting that all those wise men understood it who esteemed the worlds to be innumerable and infinite. He, however, takes the name "world" to mean an aggregate of these arranged elements and <term>fantastic orbs</term><note>Bruno considers the literal celestial spheres of the Ptolemaic/Aristotelian system to be imaginary "fantasies."</note> up to the convexity of the <term>primum mobile</term><note>original: "primo mobile." In traditional cosmology, this was the outermost moving sphere that carried all others around the Earth.</note>, which, formed in a perfectly round shape, revolves everything with a most rapid motion (as it revolves itself) around the center <margin>25</margin> toward which we are. Therefore, it would be a vain and childish pastime if we wanted to regard such a fantasy reason by reason. Instead, it will be good and expedient to resolve his arguments insofar as they may be contrary to our senses, and to disregard that which does not wage war against us.
<margin>30</margin> *Fra.* What shall we say to those who might reproach us, claiming that we are arguing based on an <term>equivocation</term><note>In logic, using a single term with two different meanings to confuse the issue.</note>?
*Phil.* We shall say two things: first, that the fault lies with him who has taken "world" according to an improper meaning, forming for himself a fantastic corporeal universe; and second, that our answers are no less <margin>35</margin> valid when assuming the meaning of "world" according to our adversaries' imagination as they are according to the truth. For where the points of the ultimate circumference of *this* world (of which this Earth is the center) are understood, there can be understood the points of innumerable other Earths which exist beyond that imagined circumference—since they <margin>40</margin> really exist there, though not according to the condition imagined by [our opponents].

# On the infinite universe and worlds.

<margin>1</margin> **Fracastoro.** ...storo, <note>Likely the end of the name "Fracastoro," continuing from the previous page.</note> which, however it may be, does not add or take away a single point from what concerns the quantity of the universe and the number of worlds.

<margin>5</margin> **Elpino.** "Every body" (he says) "either moves or stands still: and this motion and state of rest is either <term>natural</term><note>Natural motion: In Aristotelian physics, the tendency of an object to move toward its "proper place" (e.g., earth moves down).</note> or <term>violent</term><note>Violent motion: Movement caused by an external force that goes against an object's natural tendency.</note>. Furthermore, wherever a body does not stay by violence, but naturally, it does not move there by violence but by nature: and where it does not move violently, there it naturally resides. Thus, everything that is moved violently toward the top, naturally moves toward the bottom, and vice versa. From this, it is <margin>10</margin> inferred that there are not many worlds. For we must consider that if the earth which is outside this world moves to the center of this world violently, then the earth which is in this world would move to the center of that other world naturally. And if its motion from the center of this world to the center of that one is violent, then its motion from the center of that world <margin>15</margin> to this one will be natural. The cause of this is that if there are multiple earths, one must say that the power of one is similar to the power of the other—just as the power of that fire would be similar to the power of this fire. Otherwise, the parts of those worlds would be similar to the parts of | **109** this world in name only, and not in being; and consequently, that world <margin>20</margin> would not truly be one, but would be called a 'world' just as this one is. Furthermore, all bodies that are of one nature and one species have one motion (because every body naturally moves in some manner). If, therefore, there are earths there just as there is this one, and they are of the same species as this one, they will certainly have the same motion. Conversely, if they have the same motion, they are the <margin>25</margin> same elements. This being so, the earth of that world would necessarily move toward the earth of this one, and the fire of that one toward the fire of this one. From this, it follows that earth would move naturally toward the top no less than toward the bottom, and fire toward the bottom no less than toward the top. Now, such things being impossible, there must be only one earth, one <margin>30</margin> center, one middle, one horizon, and one world."

**Philotheo.** Against this, we say that just as in this infinite universal space our earth turns about this region and occupies this part, so in the same way the other stars occupy their own parts and turn about their own regions in the immense field. Wherein, just as <margin>35</margin> this earth consists of its own members, has its own alterations, and has <term>ebb and flow</term><note>original: "flusso et reflusso." Referring to the tides.</note> in its parts (as we see happen in animals, humors, and parts, which are in continual alteration and motion), so too the other stars consist of their own similarly affected members. And just as this earth, moving naturally according to its whole mechanism, has no motion | other than <margin>40**110**</margin> one similar to the circular, with which it revolves around its own...
