# On the infinite universe and worlds.

<margin>1</margin> ...center, and circles around the sun: so necessarily do those other bodies that are of the same nature. And in the same way, the individual parts of those bodies, which by some accident are distanced from their place (which, however, should not be considered principal parts or members), naturally <margin>5</margin> return there by their own impulse. Just as parts of the dry land and water, which through the action of the sun and the earth had been distanced in the form of exhalation and vapor toward the higher regions of this body, return there once they have reacquired their proper form. And thus, those parts do not stray from their containing body beyond a certain limit, just as these on our Earth do not; this will be manifest when we see that the matter <margin>10</margin> of comets does not belong to this globe <note>Bruno suggests that comets are not "exhalations" of the Earth's atmosphere (as Aristotle thought) but are celestial bodies in their own right.</note>. Thus, just as the parts of one animal, although they are of the same species as the parts of another animal, nevertheless, because they belong to different individuals, never do the parts of one (I speak of the principal and distant parts) have an inclination toward the place of those of the other. Just as <margin>15</margin> my hand would never be suitable for your arm, nor your head for my torso. Having established such foundations, we say truly that there is a similarity among all the stars, among all the worlds, and that this earth and the other "earths" <note>Bruno uses "earths" to refer to other planets or celestial bodies of a similar material nature.</note> have the same logic. However, it does not follow that where this world is, <margin>111</margin> all others must <margin>20</margin> be; or that where this one is situated, the others must be situated. Rather, one can well infer that just as this one exists in its own place, all the others exist in theirs. Just as it is not right that this earth should move to the place of the others, it is not right that the others should move to the place of this one. Just as this one is different in matter and other individual circumstances from those, those are different from this. Thus, <margin>25</margin> the parts of this fire move toward this fire, just as the parts of that fire move toward that one; thus the parts of this earth move toward this whole, just as the parts of that earth move toward that whole. Thus, the parts of that earth (which we call the moon), along with its waters, would move toward this one against nature and violently; just as the parts of this earth would move toward <margin>30</margin> that one. That moon naturally dwells in its own place and occupies its region which is there; this earth is naturally in its region here. And so, its parts refer to that earth, as these parts refer to this one; you should understand the same regarding the parts of those waters and those fires. The "down" and the lower place of this earth is not some point of the ethereal <margin>35</margin> region outside and beyond it (as happens to parts that are cast out of their proper sphere, if such a thing occurs), but is in the center of its own mass, or roundness, or gravity. Likewise, the "down" of that other earth is not any place outside of it, but is its own middle, its own center. <margin>1</margin> it is not its primary and principal <term>continent</term><note>The "continent" refers to the larger body or "home" that contains and sustains a part, such as the Earth for a stone</note>: and sometimes to another thing that preserves and nourishes it, though not of a similar species: because the <term>intrinsic impulsive principle</term><note>An internal drive or soul-like force that moves an object from within</note> does not proceed from the relation it has to a determined place, a certain point, or its own proper sphere: but from the natural impulse <margin>5</margin> to seek where it might best and most promptly maintain and preserve itself in its present being; which (however lowly it may be) all things naturally desire: just as those men most desire to live, and those who lack the light of true philosophy and apprehend nothing other than the present most fear dying, <margin>10</margin> thinking that nothing else can follow that pertains to them: because they have not come to understand that the vital principle does not consist in the <term>accidents</term><note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities (like color or shape) that can change without destroying the thing itself</note> that result from composition: but in individual and indissoluble substance, in which, if there is no perturbation, there is no appropriate desire to preserve oneself, nor fear of being lost: but this is appropriate <margin>15</margin> to composite things, *as* composites, that is, according to symmetrical, temperamental, and accidental reasoning: because neither the spiritual substance that is intended to unite, nor the material that is intended to be united, can be subject to any alteration or passion: and consequently they do not seek to preserve themselves, and therefore to such substances no movement is appropriate <margin>20</margin> at all: but rather to the composite ones. Now, if distance does not destroy the principle of <term>gravity</term><note>In this context, gravity refers to the Aristotelian tendency of heavy objects to fall toward the center of the Earth</note>, for what **121 |** reason does such a body not only fail to fall to the bottom or remain stationary, but instead circles the earth? If it is said that it does not circle by itself, but because it is <term>swept along</term><note>original: "rapito"; refers to the belief that the celestial spheres physically drag objects along with them</note>, I <margin>5</margin> will insist further that in that case, each of its heavens and stars (which they claim are neither heavy nor light nor of similar matter) are also swept along; I will set aside the fact that the motion of these bodies appears to be their own, because it never conforms to the daily rotation, nor to that of other stars.

<margin>10</margin> *Phi.* The reasoning is excellent for convincing these people by their own principles; for we shall speak of the true nature of comets when we make a specific study of them. There, we will show that such ignitions are not from the <term>sphere of fire</term><note>In Aristotelian physics, this was a layer of fire supposed to exist between the Earth's atmosphere and the Moon</note>, because they would then be ignited on every side; seeing as they would be contained within the air rubbed by heat (as they say) or the sphere of fire <margin>15</margin> along the entire circumference or surface of its mass. But we always see the ignition occurring on one side. We shall conclude that the said comets are a species of star, as the ancients well said and understood. We shall conclude that such a star, by its own motion, approaches and moves away from <margin>20</margin> this star [the Earth]; by reason of this approach and retreat, it first appears to grow as if it were igniting, and then fades as if it were being extinguished. It does not move around the Earth; rather, its own motion is that which is beyond the daily rotation proper to the Earth, which, revolving on its own back, causes all those lights **122** that are outside its circumference | to rise and set. <margin>25</margin> And it is not possible that such a terrestrial and great body could be swept along and held suspended against its nature by such liquid air and subtle body [the atmosphere], which offers no resistance at all. If its motion were true, it would only conform to that of the <term>prime mover</term><note>The outermost sphere in the geocentric model that was thought to drive the motion of all others</note> by which it is swept along, and it would not <margin>30</margin> imitate the motion of the planets, where it is sometimes judged to be of the nature of Mercury, sometimes of the Moon, sometimes of Saturn, and sometimes of others. But we shall speak of this at another time when it is appropriate. It is enough for now to have said this much as an argument against him [Aristotle], who, based on proximity and distance, does not want one to infer a <margin>35</margin> greater or lesser capacity for the motion he calls proper and natural. This is against the truth, which does not allow a motion to be called "proper and natural" to a subject in a state that can never suit it. And therefore, if parts from beyond a certain distance never move toward the <term>continent</term><note>The larger body to which the parts belong, like the Earth</note>, it should not be said that such motion is natural to them.

<margin>40</margin> *Elp.* He who considers well knows that this man had principles...

# On the Infinite Universe and Worlds. 373

<margin>1</margin> ...all contrary to the true principles of nature. He <note>Referring to Aristotle, whose arguments Philotheus is refuting</note> further replies that if the motion of <term>simple bodies</term><note>In Aristotelian physics, the four elements (earth, water, air, fire) were called simple bodies</note> is natural to them, it would follow that the simple bodies existing in many worlds—being of the same species—would move toward the same center or the same extremity.

<margin>5</margin> *Phi.* This is what he will never be able to prove: namely, that they must move to the same particular and individual place; <gloss>| 123</gloss> because from the fact that bodies are of the same species, it is inferred that they require a place of the same species and a center of the same species—which is their own proper center—and it should not and cannot be inferred <margin>10</margin> that they require the same <term>numerical location</term><note>A "numerical" difference refers to individual identity (this rock vs. that rock), whereas "specific" difference refers to the kind of thing they are (a rock vs. a flame)</note>.

*Elp.* He was somewhat expectant of this response, and therefore out of all his vain effort he asserts this: he wants to prove that numerical difference is not the cause of the diversity of locations.

*Phi.* Generally we see the complete opposite; but tell me, how does he <margin>15</margin> prove it?

*Elp.* He says that if the numerical diversity of bodies were to be the cause of the diversity of locations, then of the parts of this earth—diverse in number and weight—each would need its own center within the same world, which is impossible and inappropriate; <margin>20</margin> since the number of centers would then match the number of individual parts of the earth.

*Phi.* Now consider what a beggarly persuasion this is. Consider if you could ever be moved from the contrary opinion, or rather be confirmed in it. Who doubts that it is inappropriate <margin>24</margin> to say there is one center for the whole mass, and for the body and the entire animal, to which all parts refer, gather, and by which they are united and have their foundation? And yet there can be positively innumerable centers, just as from the innumerable multitude of the parts, in each one we can seek, or take, or suppose a center? <margin>30</margin> In a human <gloss>| 124</gloss> there is simply one center called the heart; and then there are many other centers according to the multitude of the parts, where the heart has its center, the lung its own, the <term>liver</term><note>original: "epate"</note> its own, the head, the arm, the hand, the foot, this bone, this vein, this joint, and these particles that constitute such members; and they have <margin>35</margin> a particular and determined site, both in the primary and general sense—which is the whole individual—as well as in the immediate and particular sense—which is this or that other member of the individual.

*Elp.* Consider that he might mean not simply that each part has a center, but that it has a <margin>40</margin> center *toward which it moves*.

<summary>Philotheus argues against Aristotle's claim that all matter of the same kind must fall toward a single center of the universe. # On the Infinite Universe and Worlds. 374

<margin>1</margin> *Phi.* In the end, everything leads to one conclusion: just as in an animal, it is not required that all the parts move toward the middle and the center—for this is impossible and unsuitable—but rather that they refer to the center for the union of the parts and the constitution of the whole. For the life and consistency <margin>5</margin> of <term>divisible things</term><note>Things made of separate parts</note> is seen in nothing other than the proper union of their parts, which are always understood to have that boundary which is itself taken as the middle and center. Therefore, for the constitution of the entire whole, the parts refer to a single middle; but for the constitution of each member, the particles of each refer to the <margin>10</margin> particular middle of each. Thus the <term>liver</term><note>original: "epate"</note> subsists through the union of its parts, and likewise the lungs, the head, the ear, the eye, and others. See then how it is not **125** | only not unsuitable, but most natural that there should be many centers according to the logic of many parts and particles of those parts, if you please. For by these, one center is constituted, <margin>15</margin> subsisting and consistent through the consistency, subsistence, and constitution of the others. Truly, the intellect is indignant at such <term>nonsense</term><note>original: "frascharie," meaning trifles or worthless talk</note> as this philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> brings forward.

*Elp.* This must be endured because of the reputation he has gained, more for not being understood than for anything else. But please, <margin>20</margin> consider for a moment how much this gentleman pleased himself with this poor argument; see how, almost triumphantly, he adds these words: *“If therefore the opponent cannot contradict these discourses and reasons, there is necessarily only one center and one Horizon.”*

*Phi.* He speaks very well; continue.

<margin>25</margin> *Elp.* Next, he proves that <term>simple motions</term><note>In Aristotelian physics, the natural straight-line movement of elements (up for fire, down for earth)</note> are finite and determined, because what he said about the world being one and simple motions having their own proper place was founded upon this. He speaks thus: every mobile thing moves from a certain <term>starting point</term><note>original: "termine onde"</note> to a certain <term>endpoint</term><note>original: "termine oue"</note>; and there is always a specific difference between the starting point and the endpoint, <margin>30</margin> since every change is finite. Such are disease and health, smallness and greatness, "here" and "there," because that which is being healed does not tend toward wherever it wants, but toward health. The motions of the earth and of fire are not, therefore, infinite, but toward certain terms different from those places from which they move. **126** | For upward motion is not downward motion, and these two <margin>35</margin> places are the <term>horizons</term><note>The boundaries or limits</note> of motions. See how rectilinear motion is determined. No less determined is circular motion; for that too moves from a certain term to a certain term, and from contrary to contrary, if we wish to consider the diversity of motion which is in the diameter of the circle. This is because the motion of the entire circle as a whole has no contrary (since it <margin>40</margin> does not terminate at any point other than that from which it began), but in its parts...

<margin>3</margin> *Phil.* That motion is determined and finite according to such reasons, there is no one who denies or doubts it; but it is false that it is simply <margin>5</margin> determined as "high" and determined as "low," as we have said and proved at other times. For every thing moves indifferently here or there, wherever the place of its preservation may be. And we say (even assuming the principles of Aristotle and others like him) that if there were another body inside the <margin>10</margin> earth, the parts of the earth would remain there by force; and from there, they would naturally "rise." Nor would Aristotle deny that if the parts of fire were above its sphere (as, for example, where they intend the heaven or dome of Mercury) they would naturally descend. You see, then, how well they naturally determine <margin>15</margin> "up" and "down," "heavy" and "light," once you have considered that all bodies, wherever they may be and wherever they move, retain and seek <insert>127</insert> <note>This number refers to the original page or section marking in the manuscript.</note> as much as possible the place of their preservation. And it does not destroy the fact that the motion of any particular act is simply infinite—by which that spirit (as we might call it) which creates and contributes to this composition, union, and vivification, can and will always be in other and other <margin>25</margin> infinite compositions. It can therefore be the case that every motion is finite (speaking of current motion, not absolutely and simply of each particular, and in the whole) and that there are infinite worlds. This is because, just as each of the infinite worlds is finite and has a finite region, so to each of <margin>28</margin> those belong the prescribed limits of its motion and its parts.

# On the Infinite Universe and Worlds. 376

<margin>1</margin> in this or that configuration through the immense space of the universe; they will certainly come to have infinite local motion, traversing <note>original: "moto locale" — refers to change of place, or physical movement through space.</note> infinite space, and contributing to infinite alterations. From this, however, it does not follow that they possess infinite gravity, levity, or velocity. <note>In the physics of this time, "gravity" was the tendency to move toward the center of the world, and "levity" (lightness) the tendency to move upward.</note>

<margin>5</margin> *Phil.* Let us set aside the motion of the primary parts and elements, and consider only the proximate parts <note>The specific, organized matter that makes up a body.</note> determined to a certain species of being—that is, of substance—such as the parts of the earth which are themselves earth. Regarding these, it is truly said that in those worlds where they exist, and in those regions where they dwell, in the form they maintain, they <margin>10</margin> do not move except from a certain limit to another certain limit. From this fact, the conclusion that "therefore the universe is finite and the world is one" follows no more logically than these other conclusions: "therefore monkeys are born without tails," "therefore owls see at night without glasses," or "therefore bats produce wool." <note>Bruno uses these absurd analogies to ridicule the logical leaps made by his Aristotelian opponents.</note> Furthermore (regarding these specific parts), one can never make such an <margin>15</margin> inference: "the universe is infinite, the earths are infinite; therefore a part of earth could move continually into infinity, and must have an infinite impulse toward an infinitely distant earth, and thus infinite gravity." 

<insert>129</insert> This fails for two reasons. The first is that | such a transit cannot occur; for since the universe consists of opposing bodies and principles, such a <margin>20</margin> part could not travel far through the ethereal region <note>The "ethereal region" refers to the vast space between planets or "earths."</note> without being overcome by its contrary. It would eventually reach a state where that earth-part no longer moves, because that substance is no longer earth—having changed its temperament and form due to the victory of its opposite. The other reason is that we generally see that it is far from true that <margin>24</margin> an impetus of gravity or levity can exist from an infinite distance, as they claim. Rather, such an impulse of parts can only exist within the region of its own continent <note>original: "proprio continente" — here meaning the "containing" sphere or local system that a body belongs to (like the Earth's atmosphere or gravitational field).</note>. If they were outside that region, they would no longer move toward it. This is similar to the fluid humors <note>In Renaissance medicine, "humors" were the fluids (blood, phlegm, etc.) that governed the body.</note> (which in an animal move from external to internal parts, and from upper to lower, according to all differences, rising and <margin>30</margin> falling, moving from this part to that, and from that to this). Once placed outside their own "continent"—even if they remain next to it—they lose that natural force and impulse. Therefore, such a relationship holds only for as much space as is measured by the semidiameter <note>The radius.</note> from the center of that particular region to its circumference. 

<margin>34</margin> Near the circumference, gravity is at its minimum; near the center, it is at its maximum; <note>Bruno's theory of gravity is unique: he suggests gravity is a pull toward the center of a specific world-system to maintain its integrity, not an absolute force in the universe.</note> and in the middle, according to the degrees of proximity to one or the other, it becomes greater or lesser. This appears in the present demonstration, in which **A** signifies the center of the region, where (speaking <insert>130</insert> commonly) the stone is | neither heavy nor light. **B** signifies the <margin>40</margin> circumference of the region, where likewise it will be neither heavy nor light.

# On the Infinite Universe and Worlds.

...it is impossible <note>The OCR 'sibile' is likely the end of 'impossibile'.</note> for a spherical body to change its location: because just as it is impossible for it to change its center, so it is also impossible for it to change its site. This is because a body cannot be outside its proper site except by violence <note>In Aristotelian physics, 'violence' refers to an external force acting against a thing’s natural inclination.</note>, and such violence can exist in it neither actively nor passively.

5 Similarly, it is not possible that outside the heaven there exists a simple body <term>simple body (corpo semplice): the basic elements—earth, water, air, fire, and aether—which were thought to make up the universe</term> capable of moving in a straight line: whether it be heavy or light, it could not naturally be there, given <margin>142</margin> that the proper locations of these simple bodies are different from those locations said to be "outside the world." Nor could you say they are there by accident, because that would imply that other bodies are there by nature. Now, since it has been proven 10 that there are no simple bodies other than those that go into the composition of this world—which move according to three types of local motion—it follows that outside the world there is no other simple body. If this is so, it is also impossible for any composite body to be there, because the composite is made from simple ones and into them it is resolved. Thus it is manifest 15 that there are not many worlds, because the heaven is unique, perfect, and complete, and there is not, nor can there be, any other like it.

From this it is inferred that outside this body there can be no place, nor plenum <note>original: 'pieno'; a space entirely filled with matter</note>, nor void, nor time. There is no place, because if it were full, it would contain a body, either simple or 20 composite; and we have already said that outside the heaven there is no body, neither simple nor composite. If it were a void, then according to the definition of a void (which is defined as a space in which a body *could* be), a body could exist there; but we have shown that outside the heaven no body can exist. 25 There is no time, because time is the number <note>or 'measure'</note> of motion, and motion belongs only to a body. Therefore, where there is no body, there is no motion; there is no number or measure of motion, and where this does not exist, there is no time. Furthermore, we have proven that outside the world there is no body; and consequently, we have 30 demonstrated that there is neither motion nor time there. If this is so, there is nothing temporal <margin>143</margin> nor anything mobile; and consequently, the world is one.

Secondly, the unity of the world is inferred primarily from the unity of the mover <term>mover (motore): the 'Primum Mobile' or First Mover that initiates all motion in the Aristotelian cosmos</term>. It is a conceded fact that circular motion is truly one, uniform, and without 35 beginning or end. If it is one, it is a single effect which cannot come from any cause other than a single one. Therefore, if the first heaven is unique, under which are all the inferior heavens that all conspire in a single order, it is necessary that the governor and mover be unique. This mover, being immaterial, 40 is not capable of being multiplied in number by matter. If the mover is one, and from one mover there is but one motion, and one motion (whether complex or simple) exists only in one mobile thing, whether simple or composite—it remains that the mobile universe is one; therefore there are not many worlds. 

Thirdly, from the locations of mobile bodies, one concludes that the world is one. 45 There are three species of mobile bodies: the heavy in general, the light in general...

Ninth, the plurality of worlds is a thing contrary to reason, because in them there would be no civil goodness, which consists <margin>5</margin> in civil conversation <note>The term "civil conversation" refers to social interaction and the shared moral life of a community</note>: and the creator gods of diverse worlds would not have done well by not ensuring that the citizens of those worlds had reciprocal commerce. Eleventh, from one thing a plurality of individuals cannot proceed, except by such an act through which nature multiplies itself by the division of matter, and this is no other <margin>15</margin> act than that of generation. This is what Aristotle says with all the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle's philosophy, named for his habit of walking while teaching</note>.

<margin>149</margin> A multitude of individuals is not made under one species, except by the act of generation. But those who speak of more worlds of the same matter and form in species, do not say that one is converted into the other, nor generated from the other. Twelfth, to the perfect no addition is made: if therefore this world is perfect, it certainly does not require <margin>20</margin> that another be added to it. The world is perfect: first as a species of the continuous <term>continuous (continuo): a philosophical term for something that can be divided infinitely without gaps</term> which does not end at another species of the continuous: Because the mathematically indivisible point runs into a line, which is one species of the continuous; the line into a surface, which is the second species of the continuous; the surface into a body, which is the third species of the continuous; the body does not <margin>25</margin> migrate or pass into another species of the continuous: but if it is part of the universe it ends at another body: if it is the universe it is perfect and does not end except by itself. Therefore the world and universe is one if it must be perfect. These are the twelve reasons which I wish to have produced for now: if you satisfy me in these: I wish to <margin>30</margin> hold myself satisfied in all.

Of all these, there is one prince upon whom all depend; there is a first who <margin>1</margin>
grants the power of motion to the spirits, souls, gods, deities, and movers;
and grants mobility to matter, to the body, to the animated being, to the lower
nature, and to the movable. There are, therefore, infinite movable things and movers, which
all reduce back to one passive principle and one active principle, just as <margin>5</margin>
every number reduces to unity; and infinite number and unity
<margin>156</margin> coincide, | and the supreme agent, capable of doing all, coincides in one with the
possibility of all being done: as is shown at the end
of the book *On Cause, Principle, and Unity*. <note>Bruno refers to his own previous work, *De la causa, principio et uno* (1584), where he argues that in the absolute, possibility and actuality are the same.</note> In number, therefore, and multi-
tude, there is an infinite movable and an infinite mover: but in unity and singu- <margin>10</margin>
larity, there is an infinite immobile mover and an infinite immobile universe; and this
infinite number and magnitude, and that infinite unity and simplicity,
coincide in one most simple and individual principle, truth, and being.
Thus there is not a "first movable" <note>A reference to the *Primum Mobile* of Aristotelian cosmology, the outermost sphere that supposedly moved all others.</note> which is followed in a certain order by a se-
cond down to the last, or even into infinity: but all movable bodies are <margin>15</margin>

mover: just as (speaking logically) all species have an equal rela-
tionship to the same genus, and all individuals to the same species.

infinite universal motion upon which depend infinite movable things and infinite movers, <margin>20</margin>
each of which is finite in mass and efficacy. As for the third argu-
ment, I say that in the ethereal field <note>The "ethereal field" refers to the vast expanse of space or the heavens.</note> there is no determined point
toward which, as to a center, heavy things move, and from which, as toward
the circumference, light things move away; because in the universe there
is neither center nor circumference: but (if you like) the center is everywhere, and in every <margin>25</margin>
point one can take a part of some circumference in respect to

<margin>157</margin> call "heavy" | that which moves from the circumference of this globe
toward the center; and "light" that which moves in the opposite way, toward

light; because all parts of the earth successively

centuries, there is no central part that does not become circumferential, nor
circumferential part that does not become the center, or move toward it. We shall see

their own container and preserver wherever it may be; therefore these are not

# On the Infinite Universe and Worlds

<margin>1</margin> Therefore, no less from the circumference of the moon and other worlds similar to this one in species or in kind, parts move toward the center of the globe to unite as if by the force of gravity; and toward the circumference, the thinned parts move as if by the force of levity. And it is not because <margin>5</margin> they flee the circumference or cling to the circumference: for if this were so, the closer they approached it, the more swiftly and rapidly they would run toward it; and the further they moved from it, the more strongly they would hurl themselves toward the opposite site. We see the contrary of this <note>Bruno is arguing against the Aristotelian view that objects have an inherent "desire" to reach a specific place in the universe.</note>, seeing that if they are moved beyond the terrestrial region, <margin>10</margin> they will remain balanced in the air, and will neither mount on high nor descend to the bottom, until—either by acquiring greater weight through the addition of parts or by thickening from the cold—they divide the air beneath them and return to their containing body, or, dissolved by heat and thinned, they disperse into atoms.

<margin>15</margin> **Albert.** Oh, how much this will sit in my mind once you have more clearly shown me the indifference <note>The lack of fundamental physical difference</note> of the stars from this terrestrial globe.

**Philotheus.** Elpino can easily repeat this to you, in the way he has heard it from me; and he will make you hear more distinctly <margin>20</margin> how no body is heavy or light in respect to the region of the universe, but rather parts are so in respect to their whole, their own container, or their preserver. Because out of a desire to preserve themselves in their present being, they move toward every local difference, they huddle together as do the seas and drops, and they scatter, as do all <margin>25</margin> liquids from the face of the sun or other fires. For every natural motion that comes from an intrinsic principle is nothing other than to flee the inconvenient and contrary, and to follow the friendly and convenient. Therefore, nothing moves from its place unless driven out by its contrary; nothing in its own place <margin>30</margin> is heavy or light, but the earth raised into the air, while it forces itself toward its place, is heavy and feels heavy; likewise, water suspended in the air is heavy; it is not heavy in its own place. Therefore, to those submerged, all the water is not heavy, yet a small vessel full of water above the air, outside the surface of the dry land, weighs down. One's own head is not heavy to its own torso, but the head of another will be heavy if it is placed upon it; the reason for which is its not being in its natural place. If, therefore, gravity and levity are an impulse toward a preserving place and a flight from the contrary, nothing naturally situated is heavy or light; and nothing has gravity or levity when very far from its own preserver and very removed from its contrary, until it feels the benefit of the one and the annoyance of the other. But if, feeling the annoyance of the one, it despairs and is perplexed and irresolute regarding the contrary, it comes to be overcome by it.

<summary>Philotheus explains that gravity and levity are not absolute properties of matter but relative tendencies of parts to seek their "whole" or "natural place" for self-preservation. He argues that the Earth is not unique and that the same physical laws of attraction and repulsion apply to all celestial bodies.</summary>

Furthermore, it is entirely false that contraries <note>Opposite qualities, such as hot and cold, or heavy and light.</note> are most distant from one another; because in all things, these come together naturally joined and united. The universe—as much in its principal parts as in its secondary ones—consists only through such conjunction and union. Consider that there is no part of earth that does not have water most closely united within it; without which it would have no density, no union of atoms <note>Bruno uses "atomi" to refer to the smallest indivisible particles of matter, a concept revived from ancient Lucretius.</note>, and no solidity. Where, then, is there a part of this "cold and dry" body of yours <note>Referring to the element of Earth in the Aristotelian system.</note> that does not have joined | to it this other "moist **162** and hot" body <note>Referring to the element of Air.</note>? This distinction of elements is therefore not natural, but merely logical. And if the sun is in its own region far from the region of the earth, the air and water are no further from it than from this body [the earth]; for the sun is a composite body just as this one is, although of the four mentioned elements, one predominates in that and another in this. 

Furthermore, if we want nature to conform to this logic—which demands the maximum distance between contraries—it would be necessary that between your fire (which is light) and the earth (which is heavy), your "heaven" <note>The "Aether" or fifth element, which Aristotle claimed was unchanging and moved only in circles.</note> be interposed, which is neither heavy nor light. Or, if you wish to restrict yourself to the order within the so-called elements, it would be necessary to order them differently: I mean to say that it would fall to water to be in the center and place of the heaviest thing, if fire is in the circumference and place of the lightest thing in the elementary region. This is because water, which is cold and moist, is contrary to fire in both qualities, and thus should be furthest from it. Likewise, the air, which you call hot and moist, should be furthest from the cold and dry earth. Do you see, then, how inconsistent this Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note> proposition is, whether you examine it according to the truth of nature, or measure it by its own principles and foundations?

From this coincidence, we believe it is finally divinely stated and considered that "contraries are within contraries." Thus, it is not difficult to reach the point of knowing how "every thing is in every thing"—something that Aristotle and other Sophists <note>Here used as a derogatory term for those who use clever but false arguments.</note> could not understand.
